closure.residual: The private Browser Harness/Stagehand services and authenticated owner profile have not yet been deployed and live-certified on Trading Core with a real model/provider credential and target browsing canaries.
closure.residual_reason: Repository closure now contains the services, authority boundary, deployment units and fail-closed tests. Live process/model/profile behavior requires the external Trading Core runtime and credentials.

findings.title: workspace_studio, which has no implementation, is selectable as a routing fallback
findings.description: The Google mesh can select a capability with no gateway code at all as the fallback for workspace_operation.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Restrict fallback selection to capabilities with a readiness source and an implementation.

closure.summary: Every Google capability declares an executor — gateway, hermes, or null for a surface nothing in VAN can run — and the router skips a capability with none, as a direct candidate or as a fallback. workspace_studio, the fallback for workspace_operation whose primary is gateway code, is one of the three with none.
closure.residual: The 'hermes' executor is taken from what the registry declares, not from anything this repository can verify.
closure.residual_reason: Hermes is an external runtime that is not in this repository, so which workers it actually implements cannot be checked here. What can be checked, and now is, is that a capability declaring no executor at all is never routed to — which is the case the finding names.
closure.posture: Offering a capability nothing can execute as a fallback turns 'the preferred surface is unavailable' into 'the operation was planned', which is worse than an honest refusal. The test that changed most is the old one, which asserted `planned` on workspace_studio as correct behaviour.

findings.title: Nothing expires: ten-year grants, no rotation, 825-day PKI with no renewal
findings.description: Enrollment grants are minted with a ten-year expiry; the ingress token, internal token, device secrets and commander tokens are never rotated; make-bridge-pki returns early if the certificate exists.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Add expiry and rotation for every long-lived credential and a PKI renewal path with monitoring.

closure.summary: Enrolment grants are a year rather than a decade and carry a renewal path with a reportable RENEW_SOON state. Credential age is tracked by fingerprint, so a rotated value restarts its own clock without anybody telling the gateway, and /health reports anything past its policy. make-bridge-pki.sh re-issues a certificate inside its renewal window instead of returning early whenever the file exists, and --check exits non-zero for a monitor.
closure.residual: The gateway reports credential age but does not rotate anything itself, and a static token's age is measured from when the gateway first saw it rather than from when it was issued.
closure.residual_reason: Rotating the ingress token means updating the gateway, the phone and the tunnel at the same instant; a process doing that unattended would lock the owner out far more reliably than it would stop an attacker. A token in an environment file carries no issue date the gateway can read, so the age is a floor — the report says so in age_basis rather than implying precision it does not have, and a test asserts that wording is there.
closure.posture: An expired grant is deliberately not renewable: re-pairing is the path back, and silently reviving one the owner let lapse would make the expiry decorative. The PKI test proves the fix rather than the intent — it builds a PKI, confirms --check is clean, then re-runs with the window widened and asserts the certificate bytes actually changed.

findings.title: A live to fake Google transport swap route exists on the production app
findings.description: POST /v1/google/test-transport replaces the live transport and clears the OAuth client with no undo route; outside pytest it fails closed as an unhandled 500.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Remove the route from the production application.
findings.progress_note: tools/ci/maturity_gate.py now reports the forbidden /v1/google/test-transport route as scheduled. Removal is Gate 1 work; this stays OPEN.

closure.summary: The /v1/google/test-transport route, which allowed the live Google transport of a running production app to be hot-swapped for a fake, is deleted. The maturity gate asserts it stays deleted.
closure.posture: Tests that needed a fake transport now install it on app.state directly, so the test seam no longer has to exist as a production route.

findings.title: No speaker verification on voice commands
findings.description: Voice commands previously carried no speaker provenance into the authoritative gateway. The device now computes local speaker similarity when a provisioned sherpa embedding bundle is available, signs that fixed-point evidence in command envelope v3, and the gateway enforces it only after deterministic action resolution.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Compute speaker similarity locally as provenance, sign it with the paired-device command envelope, and enforce the evidence at the gateway after deterministic action resolution without replacing biometric approval.

closure.summary: Speaker similarity is now a signed provenance signal on the real voice-command path, not an Android-side authority decision. Android computes a bounded local similarity score when a checksum-pinned sherpa speaker bundle and owner embedding are provisioned, converts it to fixed-point speaker_evidence_milli, and signs it in command envelope v3. The gateway rejects unsigned/tampered/non-voice speaker claims, resolves the command's true action class first, then applies one canonical speaker policy: A1/A2 never gain authority from voice identity; A3 with MATCH may proceed under its normal policy, while missing/inconclusive evidence tightens it to exact owner biometric approval; a consequential MISMATCH is refused; A4 still requires biometric approval even on MATCH. Speaker evidence therefore can only preserve or tighten authority, never mint it.
closure.residual: The trained speaker-embedding ONNX model and owner reference embedding are deployment artefacts and are not committed to the repository. Without them Android emits no positive speaker evidence, so consequential voice actions fail safe into biometric approval or refusal according to the gateway policy.
closure.residual_reason: A trained acoustic model and an owner-derived embedding are runtime/deployment artefacts. Repository closure consists of the pinned runtime, checksum-confined loader, signed transport, authoritative policy, and fail-safe behavior when those artefacts are absent.

findings.title: Full field geometry is rebuilt every frame with no frame-budget measurement
findings.description: The geometry engine allocates fresh lists and rebuilds all 35-point polylines per frame; frameBudgetMissed has no producer and thermal state is sampled once per composition.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Cache stable topology and update only dynamic coordinates; add frame-time sampling.

closure.summary: The silhouette is built once and the frame budget finally has a producer. `VanBodyExclusionProfile.compact` was called on every frame for a value that depends only on the body's size and position and was identical each time; it is now memoised on a quantised key, so sub-pixel layout wobble does not defeat the cache, and a test asserts one rebuild across 120 frames *and* that the strands still move — caching the wrong thing would freeze the aura. Separately, `VanEffectConditions.frameBudgetMissed` had no producer at all: the ladder knew what to do about a device that could not keep up and nothing ever told it. `VanFrameBudgetSampler` reports on a sustained fraction of a rolling window rather than one slow frame, because a single long frame happens on every device and degrading on it would make VAN flicker between effect budgets, and it recovers with hysteresis so a cooled device gets its field back without oscillating.
closure.residual: The field's per-frame strand coordinates are still recomputed each frame, and no on-device frame-time measurement exists in this environment.
closure.residual_reason: The strand coordinates are the animation; caching them would stop the motion, which a test asserts against. Real device frame times arrive through POST /v1/observability/device-telemetry (P3-OBS-002) once the client posts them, and the gateway reports them as unobserved until then rather than inventing values.

findings.title: No correlation identifier spans command to mission to execution to verification
findings.description: Identifiers exist per subsystem but nothing joins a hermes_run_id to a later verification, and mission changes never reach the event bus.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Introduce a single correlation id propagated across every subsystem and log sink.

closure.summary: One correlation id now spans the chain the blueprint names, and the join an operator used to do by hand is a single call. The id is derived from the command id rather than minted as a new random value: a random id has to be carried from the first hop by every subsystem, and propagation is the thing that gets forgotten, whereas a derived id lets a subsystem that forgot still be joined after the fact. It is filled in by a validator on CommandResult rather than at the orchestrator's twenty-one construction sites, so it is present on every result including the refusals — the case an operator most needs. GET /v1/observability/trace/{command_id} performs the six joins across five tables, two of them through JSON, that answering "what happened to the thing I asked for" previously required.
closure.residual: The correlation id reaches Hermes in the run metadata, but the external agent runtime is not in this repository, so whether it echoes the id back on its callback is not verifiable here.
closure.residual_reason: Hermes is an external system outside the repository boundary; asserting its behaviour from here would be asserting something unverified.

findings.title: Eleven parallel work-status vocabularies with no owner-facing projection
findings.description: MissionState, ActivityState, ExecutionStatus, RunStatus, BrowserTaskStatus, DecisionStatus, IdempotencyStatus, AttentionState, KnowledgeOperationStatus, OperationState and the Android command status all describe work in progress.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Define one owner-facing work status projection and map every subsystem onto it.

closure.summary: One owner-facing status vocabulary, and a total mapping onto it from nine of the eleven subsystem vocabularies the audit named. The mapping is driven off the enums themselves in test, so adding a subsystem status without deciding what it means to the owner fails CI. The projection is served on the mission list, the mission detail and the activity feed, and the device consumes it rather than deriving its own.
closure.residual: IdempotencyStatus, the eleventh vocabulary, is deliberately not projected.
closure.residual_reason: It describes a claim on a request key, not a piece of work: COMPLETED means the gateway finished handling the request, which is equally true when the command was denied. Mapping it would put a reassuring word next to a refusal. The exclusion is recorded in NOT_OWNER_WORK with its reason and asserted by a test, rather than left as a silent omission.
closure.posture: The projection keeps apart exactly what the audit proved gets confused: verified, partial and unverifiable stay three answers; only a verified outcome reads as DONE; a refusal is not a failure; a verification failure is not an execution failure; a stale attention item is not 'handled'. Each of those is a test, not a comment.

findings.title: AttentionScorer and VerifierRegistry are 2.0 implementations built beside live 1.0s
findings.description: decisions/service uses the older AttentionEngine while AttentionScorer is isolated; AutomationDispatcher uses its own WorkflowVerifier while VerifierRegistry is test-only.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Migrate to one attention engine and one verification system.

closure.summary: Two 2.0 implementations were sitting beside live 1.0s. Verification: verification/observations.py is now the single answer to 'what can VAN independently observe?', and both VerifierRegistry and WorkflowVerifier are built from it in verification/production.py. Attention: AttentionScorer is now on the live path — every AttentionEngine.upsert is scored, and the disposition, score and reason are stored with the item — rather than being reachable only from the understanding report's metrics.
closure.residual: The two verification systems still persist different record shapes, VerificationResult for automation runs and VerificationRecord for missions.
closure.residual_reason: Each subsystem stores its own and neither shape is wrong; collapsing them would be a large migration for no behavioural gain. What was genuinely duplicated was the observations, and those now exist once, so adding a way to observe the world is one change rather than two.
closure.posture: The direction of each merge is the part worth defending, and in both cases it is towards the better implementation rather than the incumbent. The scorer decides and the engine stays the durable queue, because retiring §29's five dispositions, deduplication and recorded reasons in favour of a severity enum would have been a downgrade dressed as consolidation. A severity now maps to written-out dimensions that a test holds monotonic, so the bridge cannot silently invert the enum, and an item written before this was wired still interrupts rather than being silenced by a missing decision.

findings.title: No application logging anywhere in the gateway
findings.description: The gateway emits no structured logs. The audit table is the only trace and it is shallow. A developer cannot reconstruct a request without reading SQLite directly.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
repository_evidence: backend/van_gateway/ (no logging configuration or logger usage on request paths)
findings.remediation: Add structured logging with timestamp, service, mission id, command id, correlation id, action class, principal, result, degraded code and error class. Never log secrets.

closure.summary: The gateway emits structured JSON logs with the nine context fields Gate 11 names, always present as keys so an absent field is distinguishable from a logger that does not emit it. Secrets are removed recursively by field name at any depth, because the way secrets reach logs is not that somebody logs a password on purpose but that somebody logs a dict they had not looked inside. Command outcomes are logged by wrapping `handle` rather than by a call at each of its twenty-one returns: most of those returns are refusals, and a refusal nobody logged is the 'VAN did nothing and said nothing' report this gate exists to make impossible. The command text is deliberately not logged.

findings.title: Metrics are collected in-process and exported nowhere
findings.description: Automation telemetry and trading observability compute metrics that no endpoint or exporter publishes.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Export the metric set named in blueprint Gate 11 to a scrape endpoint or push gateway.

closure.summary:
All sixteen metrics Gate 11 names are declared in a closed catalogue and exported at GET /v1/observability/metrics in Prometheus text format. The catalogue names a producer for each metric and records whether it is produced by the gateway, the device or the trading process, because declaring sixteen metrics and exporting them all as zero would have closed the finding on paper while leaving the instruments unwired. `van_metric_unobserved` reports the declared metrics that have never received a sample, so a metric at zero because nothing happened is distinguishable from one at zero because nothing writes it. Device-produced metrics — aura frame time, wake/ASR/TTS latency, battery and memory — are ingested through POST /v1/observability/device-telemetry rather than invented, and trade halt latency is recovered from the two ledger events that bracket it. Route labels use the matched route template, not the path, so a mission id cannot become an unbounded set of time series.

The device half is here too. The six metrics the catalogue marks `MetricSource.DEVICE` — wake, ASR and TTS latency, aura frame time, battery and memory — had a declaration and an ingest route and no producer, so the scrape reported them as `van_metric_unobserved` forever. `DeviceTelemetryReporter` posts them, bounded and behind the gateway's own circuit breaker, because a phone that cannot reach its gateway should spend its radio on the owner's queued commands rather than on frame times. `DeviceMetric` mirrors the gateway's `DEVICE_HISTOGRAMS` and `DEVICE_GAUGES`, and `tests/contracts/test_device_telemetry_contract.py` parses both and fails on drift — the route refuses a name it does not know, so a device that invents one has its telemetry counted as refused and silently disappear, which is the state this finding was about.

findings.title: No alerting thresholds exist for any runtime failure
findings.description: Nothing defines what constitutes an actionable production failure, so no operator is ever paged.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Define actionable alert thresholds for the critical runtime failures enumerated in Gate 11.

closure.summary: Nine alert rules are defined and evaluated in process against the same registry the scrape renders, and GET /v1/observability/alerts returns the ones firing now. Writing a YAML file for a monitoring system nobody has installed would have closed the finding and left VAN exactly as unalertable as before. Every rule names the operator action, because a threshold with no action is a notification and an operator who cannot act on a page learns to ignore pages. Every ratio rule carries a sample floor so one denied command out of one is not a 100% error rate. INSTRUMENT_SILENT fires on the failure the other rules cannot see: an exporter that has gone blind reports every threshold as healthy.
closure.residual: The rules are served on an endpoint; nothing in this repository pages a human, because no notification transport is deployed.
closure.residual_reason: Choosing and configuring a paging transport is an owner deployment decision, not a repository one. The actionable condition is now computable and served, which is what was absent.

findings.title: No retention policy on any table
findings.description: A repo-wide search for retention, prune, vacuum, purge or logrotate finds one setting in the whole system: n8n's own 168-hour execution retention. The audit table, event table, knowledge_evidence, research_evidence, eval_runs and context_snapshots grow forever in the SQLite file that serves live requests.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Add a retention policy and a prune job to every unbounded store.

closure.summary: Every table in the schema carries a retention class, and a test reads the live schema and fails if any table is unassigned — the reason one n8n setting was the only retention in the system is that nothing ever compared the policy to the schema. The policy is six classes with stated meanings rather than seventy hand-chosen day counts, so it can be argued with. OWNER_STATE never prunes because the owner's record of their own life is not the system's to expire; deletion there is the owner's, through context/forget.py. The audit log is pruned only as an anchored prefix: a hash chain cannot be cut in the middle or from the end, but it can be cut from the start if the verifier is told where the surviving chain begins and what hash it links back to, so `verify_chain` still reconciles afterwards and the anchor itself records how much was removed.
closure.residual: n8n's own 168-hour execution retention is unchanged and remains the automation runtime's setting rather than VAN's.
closure.residual_reason: It is configuration of an external runtime that already has a bounded policy; duplicating it in VAN would create two sources of truth for the same horizon.

findings.title: No backup, no restore path and no restore drill
findings.description: No Postgres dump, no SQLite backup, no volume snapshot and no snapshot policy exists anywhere in deploy, tools or systemd. Loss of the gateway host is loss of all owner state and the entire audit history.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Automate backups for databases, configuration, evidence and project state; run an actual restore drill and record it.

closure.summary: Backup, restore and a drill that actually restores. The database is copied with SQLite's own backup API rather than with cp: the gateway runs in WAL mode while serving requests, and copying the file without its -wal sidecar produces something that opens cleanly and is missing the most recent committed transactions — a backup that restores to a plausible past. All four parts Gate 11 names are covered, every artefact is digested, and the manifest is verified before any restore touches a target. A restore refuses to overwrite an existing database unless told to, because replacing live owner state over a mistyped path is worse than the disaster being recovered from. `tools/ops/backup.py drill` takes a backup, restores it to a scratch location and compares schema version, every table's row count and the audit chain tip, exiting non-zero on any difference — the recorded run is a real one against this repository.
closure.residual: The scheduler's own backup job is off by default and no offsite destination is configured.
closure.residual_reason: A backup written by the gateway to the same disk as its database is not a backup; choosing an offsite target is an owner deployment decision. The mechanism, its verification and the drill are complete and runnable.

findings.title: Bridge PKI expires silently with no renewal path
findings.description: make-bridge-pki.sh uses 825 days and its issue() returns early when the certificate already exists, so re-running bootstrap never renews. No expiry monitoring exists. At day 825 commander mTLS and the MT5 worker link both break without warning.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Add a renewal path and expiry monitoring for all PKI and long-lived credentials.

closure.summary: Expiry is now a number a monitor can ask for, not only a script it can run. The renewal path landed under P2-SEC-008: make-bridge-pki.sh re-issues anything inside its renewal window instead of returning early because the file exists. This closes the other half: ops/pki.py reads the certificates directly and reports days remaining per certificate and the minimum across them, which the PKI_EXPIRING rule thresholds at thirty days, and the scheduler re-reads it hourly. A missing or unreadable certificate reports as already past due, because it is more urgent than any expiry. A deployment with no trading PKI reports absence rather than expiry: paging an operator about a system they do not run is how alerts get muted.
closure.residual: The certificates in these tests are generated by the tests; no live trading PKI exists in this environment to read.
closure.residual_reason: Reading a real deployment's /opt/van-trading/secrets/pki is an owner-host action. The parser is exercised against real X.509 that the test mints, which is what makes it more than a fixture comparison.

findings.title: fire_due has no scheduler
findings.description: The reminder firing routine exists and nothing calls it on a schedule, so due reminders are never dispatched by the system itself.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Give reminder and attention dispatch a real scheduler with ownership and observability.

closure.summary: `fire_due` has a caller. The scheduler sweeps due reminders every minute, publishes a reminder.fired event the device replays and raises one attention item per reminder — firing a reminder and telling nobody is the same as not firing it. It also runs retention daily and re-reads PKI expiry hourly. It remembers when each job last ran in `scheduler_runs`, so a restart does not re-run everything, which in a restart loop would mean firing the same work forever; a job that has never run is due immediately, so a first boot fires the reminder that came due during installation. A failing job is recorded with its error class and the loop continues: a scheduler that dies on one bad job and one that swallows errors are both failures, and `status()` reports which jobs ran and how they ended.

findings.title: Reminder and attention dedupe are in-memory only
findings.description: Deduplication state is lost on restart, so a restart can re-surface an already dismissed item.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Persist dedupe and suppression state.

closure.summary: Dedupe and suppression are in the database. `notification_suppressions` records the channel, the subject and how long the suppression lasts — the third of which an in-memory set cannot express at all, since a set entry is forever or gone. A null expiry means the owner said never again and is deliberately distinguishable from a long one. An expired suppression keeps its row, so 'I already told you about this yesterday' stays answerable. The attention engine's `upsert` had a second, non-restart-specific form of the same defect: it wrote the caller's state unconditionally, so any source re-reporting a condition moved an item the owner had acknowledged back to OPEN. A re-report no longer overrides the owner's disposition, while a caller that explicitly resolves an item still can.
closure.residual: DegradedRegistry._active remains in memory.
closure.residual_reason: It is live health state, not a dismissal: a subsystem's degradation should be re-detected on boot rather than remembered from before the restart. Remembering it would report a subsystem as degraded after the fault was fixed.

findings.title: Blocking sleep inside an async retry loop
findings.description: The n8n client calls a blocking sleep on an async path, stalling the event loop for the duration of every retry.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Use awaitable bounded exponential backoff with jitter.

closure.summary: The retry backoff awaits instead of blocking. `time.sleep` inside an `async def` inside the gateway's single event loop meant that one n8n call receiving a 503 stopped every other request the gateway was serving, including the owner's, for the duration of the backoff. The test does not grep for the call: it runs a companion task alongside a failing request and asserts the companion kept running while the retry waited, which is the property that matters and the one a source-text check cannot establish.

findings.title: n8n client calls an endpoint that is not a real n8n API
findings.description: POST /workflows/{id}/run has no counterpart in the n8n API or anywhere in the repository.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Replace with a real n8n execution call or remove the method.

closure.summary: The invented endpoint is gone and execution goes where n8n actually accepts it. n8n's public REST API can create, update, activate, deactivate and read a workflow; it has never had `POST /workflows/{id}/run`. The only thing that ever exercised that call was a test fake that answered it, which is how it survived: the call and its test agreed with each other and neither agreed with n8n. Every workflow VAN compiles for dispatch is built on a webhook trigger, so invocation now reads the trigger path from the *deployed* workflow — a workflow edited in the n8n UI is exactly the case where VAN's compiled path and the live one differ — and POSTs the same run envelope and run-scoped grant to its production webhook URL. A workflow with no trigger is refused rather than invoked by some other means, and an inactive workflow gets its own error code because that is a deployment fault with a specific remedy.
closure.residual: No live n8n instance exists in this environment, so the call is verified against a fake shaped like the documented n8n API rather than against n8n itself.
closure.residual_reason: n8n is an external runtime that is not deployed here. The fake was rewritten to the real API's shape, which is the correction the finding asked for; asserting against a live instance requires the owner's automation host.

findings.title: No retry or backoff anywhere in the Android client
findings.description: VanGatewayClient uses raw HttpURLConnection with no retry, no backoff and no circuit breaker.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Add bounded exponential backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker.

closure.summary: `VanGatewayClient` retries with bounded full-jitter backoff behind a circuit breaker. It had none: one `HttpURLConnection` per call, so the first request after a tunnel drop failed, the owner tapped again, that failed, and VAN looked broken. Two rules the naive version gets wrong are in `GatewayRetryPolicy`, which is pure and executed in the harness: not everything is retryable — a 409 means the command already exists and retrying it is how one command becomes two — and jitter is not decoration, because every screen refreshes on the same tick. The breaker is advisory rather than a hard block: a refresh loop honours it, the owner pressing send is not told no by a client-side guess about a server they can see is up. Fixing this exposed a second defect in the same file: `VanGatewayClient` had two `companion object` declarations, which Kotlin does not permit, so the class could not have compiled. Introduced by commit d25ad15 in this remediation and undetectable here because the Android toolchain cannot be fetched in this container; merged.

findings.title: /v1/events is polled once with a hardcoded cursor
findings.description: There is a single events(0) call in the activity feed's initial composition; the cursor is hardcoded to zero and never persisted, so the event stream is effectively unused.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Replace with the semantic state subscription from Gate 6 and persist the cursor.

closure.summary: The event stream is streamed. There was a single `events(0)` in the activity feed's initial composition with a literal zero cursor that was never persisted and never polled again, so anything the gateway published afterwards never reached the owner until they left the screen and came back. `EventStream` is a pure state machine that advances and persists the cursor, merges pages by sequence so a restored cursor slightly behind does not produce duplicate rows, refuses to rewind on a low cursor from the gateway, bounds what the client retains, polls again immediately on a truncated page — waiting the idle interval per page would make catching up take pages x interval — and backs off exponentially to a ceiling on failure. A feed that failed is distinguishable from a feed with nothing in it, which is the distinction that was collapsed.
closure.residual: The SharedPreferences-backed cursor store and the Compose polling loop are not compiled here.
closure.residual_reason: Both need the Android toolchain. The paging, cursor and backoff arithmetic — the whole of what was wrong — runs in the JVM harness.

findings.title: 18 declared gateway client methods are never called
findings.description: All four mission methods, needsYou, activityFeed, the six understanding methods, permissions, autonomy, technology radar, eval report, briefing and attention are dead code.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Wire them into the mission surfaces built in Gate 2, or delete any whose capability was removed.

closure.summary: Two capabilities that existed end to end apart from the last ten lines are wired, and the rest of the list turned out to be already closed. The finding named 18 dead client methods; Gate 2 wired the mission surfaces, Gate 6 wired the event stream, and a re-check against the current tree found four candidates, two of which — `contextTrustFor` and `hasIngressToken` — are called from inside the client itself and were never dead. The two that were are `attention()` and `briefing()`: the gateway maintained an attention queue and built a briefing, and the app had methods to fetch both and no surface that read either. The home screen now shows what is waiting. The summarising lives in `OwnerOverview`, pure and executed on the JVM, because its decisions are worth holding to a test — the governing one being that an empty queue and an unreachable gateway must never produce the same sentence: 'nothing is waiting for you' is a claim about the world and VAN may only make it when it has looked.
closure.residual: The composable that renders the summary is not compiled here; the summariser it renders is.
closure.residual_reason: The Android Gradle Plugin cannot be fetched in this environment. The decisions — what counts as waiting, what to say when nothing does, what to say when VAN could not look — are all in the pure module and all executed.

findings.title: Five degraded subsystems are hardcoded healthy
findings.description: Overlay, queue, notifications, voice and biometric are declared in the degraded model and never written, so they always report WORKING regardless of reality.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Drive all five from real signals.

closure.summary: The five subsystems have a producer. `overlay`, `queue`, `notifications`, `voice` and `biometric` were in `defaultSubsystems()` and nothing anywhere called `markBroken` or `markWorking` for any of them, so all five reported WORKING on a phone that had granted nothing — which is worse than having no health page, because an owner who checks and is told nothing is wrong stops checking. `DeviceSignals` reads the device; `SubsystemHealth` turns those facts into verdicts and is pure, so the mapping is executed rather than inspected. Two distinctions the rule keeps: an overlay the owner turned off is WONT_DO, not a fault, and a few queued commands with no failures is VAN working offline, which is the feature rather than a defect. `DegradedModeStore.mark` exists because the old pair could not express either.

findings.title: All seven RestoreAction values are defined and never rendered
findings.description: The degraded contract carries an actionable restore instruction that no screen shows the owner.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Render the restore action wherever degraded state is shown.

closure.summary: `RestoreAction` reaches the owner as a button. All seven values were defined, carried through the degraded-mode contract and rendered by nothing, so VAN knew what the owner should press and never said so. `DegradedPanel` renders the label, the sentence describing what pressing it will do, and nothing at all when nothing is wrong — a permanent 'all systems nominal' banner is how an owner learns to stop reading that part of the screen. `DeviceSignals.perform` is the other half, and it returns false for CONTACT_SUPPORT rather than pretending: the screen then says so, because a button that silently does nothing is worse than one that admits it. `CLEAR_QUEUE` needed `EncryptedCommandQueue.clear`, which did not exist.

findings.title: Offline queue never replays on connectivity recovery
findings.description: replayAsync is called exactly once at application start, with no connectivity or health trigger.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Trigger replay on connectivity and gateway health recovery, with duplicate suppression.

closure.summary: The queue drains when connectivity or the gateway comes back. `replayAsync()` was called exactly once, at application start, so a command the owner issued in a tunnel sat in the queue until they next killed and reopened the app — which for a resident floating assistant is approximately never. A `ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback` and the health poll now both drive it. The care is in the duplicate suppression: connectivity callbacks arrive in bursts, so `ReplayTrigger` fires on the edge into availability rather than on the level, and debounces at three seconds. Relying on the gateway's idempotency keys for a client-side stampede is how a backstop becomes load-bearing. Writing the test found a real boundary defect: `lastReplayStartedAtMs` defaulted to `0L`, which against `elapsedRealtime` means 'replayed at boot' and would have suppressed the first replay on a phone that had just started — exactly when the queue is fullest. It is nullable now, and null means never.

findings.title: No state restoration anywhere
findings.description: A repo-wide search for rememberSaveable, onSaveInstanceState, ViewModel and configChanges over the main source set and manifest returns zero hits. Rotation destroys the selected module, the chat draft, every module's fetched data and the onboarding position.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Introduce ViewModels and rememberSaveable throughout.

closure.summary: Owner state survives rotation and process death. Everything was held in `remember`, so rotating the phone, changing the font size or having Android reclaim the process dropped the owner back on Home with their typed text gone; on an assistant meant to stay resident, process death is what happens overnight, not an edge case. `CommandCentreViewModel` holds the selected module and the draft in a `SavedStateHandle`, the permissions the owner said "not now" to are persisted by `VanAsks` (there is no longer a pairing form or a step list to lose), and the chart keeps the owner's place in the series. The navigation rules are in `CommandNav`, which is pure: saved state is keyed by id rather than ordinal, because ordinals restore the wrong screen the first time a module is inserted into the enum, silently, to an owner whose process Android had just killed.

findings.title: No light theme and a deprecated parent theme
findings.description: darkColorScheme is hardcoded in all three activities, there is no isSystemInDarkTheme branch and no values-night; Theme.Van extends a deprecated platform parent.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Support a coherent light mode unless canon explicitly elects dark-only, and update the parent theme.

closure.summary: One theme, following the owner's system setting, and a parent theme the platform still ships. Three activities each built `darkColorScheme(primary = ACCENT_CYAN)` inline, so there was no theme to change; the window theme inherited from the deprecated `android:Theme.Material.NoActionBar` and hardcoded the dark field, and there was no `values-night`. `VanTheme` and `VanPalette` replace all three call sites. The light scheme is deliberately not the dark one with the background flipped: VAN's `#00DAFF` is a glow colour and is 1.8:1 on white, so using it as a light-mode primary would ship white label text nobody can read. `VanPaletteTest` computes WCAG contrast for every foreground and background pair a screen actually puts text on, and parses both `themes.xml` files to catch drift between the window colour and the palette — the navy flash on every launch of a light-mode app, which owners notice and builds never do. It found one real defect: the dark outline was 2.9:1 against its surface, a card boundary you can only see if you already know it is there. `DayNight` is deliberately not used; it arrived in API 29 and this app supports 26, so the split is done with the `night` resource qualifier.

findings.title: Two god files carry the app's owner surfaces
findings.description: CommandCentreActivity is 1238 lines with 13 module composables, no ViewModel, no NavHost and no repository; FloatingOverlayService is 1031 lines holding windows, gestures, chat draft, trade view and every composable.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Split per blueprint Gate 10 and Rev 3.0 s41.

closure.summary:
Both god files are split, and both splits are contracts rather than tidy-ups.

`CommandCentreActivity.kt` was 1,342 lines carrying the Activity, the navigation, fourteen module bodies, the shared components and two JSON helpers. It is now nine files, the largest 403 lines, and `tests/contracts/test_android_dashboard_navigation.py` fails if any of them passes 450. That is not a style rule: the status projection P0-EXEC-003 found painting unverified outcomes in the working colour sat at line 1,310 of that file, and the reason nobody had seen it is that nobody reads to line 1,310.

`FloatingOverlayService.kt` was 1,096 lines and was, at once, a foreground service, a WindowManager client, a drag controller and an entire Compose tree, with every panel reading the service's own mutable fields and calling its private methods. It is now 420 lines — window, lifecycle, composition host, state persistence and interaction routing, which is what Rev 3.0 s41 says a service with a window is for — beside eight files that each do one job. `VanOverlaySurface` and `VanOverlayWorkboards` draw from a state snapshot and act through a callback bundle, so `MaximizedWorkboard` no longer sizes itself from the service's display metrics and the chips no longer call `startActivity` on it. `OverlayDragController` owns the drag behind an `OverlayWindowPort`, which is the boundary that makes the gesture sequence executable: the haptic fires on the arming edge rather than on every frame, a cancelled drag never leaves the overlay armed to close on the owner's next unrelated touch, and a lift over the dismiss target returns null rather than a state update for a window that is going away. `VanOverlayController` and `EdgeDocking` hold the geometry; `EdgeDocking` had to leave `OverlayStateStore.kt`, where it sat below a `SharedPreferences` class in a file that imports `android.content`, which is exactly why none of that arithmetic could be executed anywhere.

`tests/contracts/test_android_overlay_split.py` holds the boundary: no file in the package over 450 lines, no drawing in the service, no reaching around the parameters from the surface, and the geometry files kept free of Android imports and present in the harness — because a split that is not asserted is a split that lasts until the next hurried change.

findings.title: Trading UI shows unformatted floats and raw ledger keys
findings.description: Risk caps render as values like 'cap 2.0000000000000004%', and raw ledger keys such as max_open_stop_risk are shown to the owner.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Format numbers for display and map ledger keys to owner language.

closure.summary: Trading numbers are formatted and ledger keys are translated. The risk screen rendered `cap 2.0000000000000004%`, which is a `Double` printed with `toString()` and is the tell that nobody had looked at the screen, and it labelled rows `max_open_stop_risk` in a monospace font, which is the same problem one layer up: the owner reading the trading system's internal vocabulary. `TradingFormat` holds both, with the rounding done on a scaled integer rather than by re-parsing a formatted string, because re-parsing is how a thousands separator ends up inside a decimal. A missing number renders as a dash and never as zero: no exposure and not loaded yet are different facts about the owner's money.

findings.title: Trading empty state instructs the owner to run a Python module
findings.description: The empty state tells the owner to run a python -m vati lake command.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Replace with an owner-meaningful empty state.

closure.summary: The trading empty states say what is true and what, if anything, the owner can do. One of them told them to run `python -m vati lake`; there is no phone on which that is an instruction a person can follow, and an empty state that tells the owner to open a terminal tells them the product is not for them. They are all in `TradingFormat.emptyState` now, and the test asserts no rendered state contains 'python', 'vati', 'cli' or 'terminal'. Empty and unavailable are kept apart: 'No open trades' when VAN cannot read the ledger is VAN reporting an absence it has not established, so `unavailableState` says it cannot see rather than that there is nothing there.

findings.title: android/README.md is stale
findings.description: It claims targetSdk and compileSdk 34 against an actual 36, and omits the trading, mission, control and gateway packages.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Correct the README and add it to the Gate 0 truth sweep.
findings.closure_note: README corrected to SDK 36 and given a package map covering trading, mission, control and gateway.

closure.summary: android/README.md is corrected: SDK 34 becomes SDK 36 to match the build files, and a package map is added so a reader can find the modules the README names.
closure.posture: Corrected against the build files themselves rather than against memory of them.

findings.title: The resolver casefolds command text so sealed titles lose owner capitalisation
findings.description: Extracted parameters are taken from casefolded text, so a title the owner capitalised is sealed lowercase and created lowercase at the provider.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Match case-insensitively but extract from the original text.

closure.summary: The resolver matches case-insensitively and extracts from the owner's own text. It used to match against casefolded text and take the parameters from the match, so a title the owner capitalised was extracted lowercased, sealed lowercase into the authority record, and created lowercase at the provider. Because it was sealed, the corruption was cryptographically bound to the command and nothing downstream could recover the original. The two existing tests asserted the lowercased values, so they encoded the defect; they now assert the owner's capitalisation and say why they changed. The normalised text is still casefolded — that is what matching is done against and what the audit record stores — but it is no longer where parameters come from.

findings.title: Chart text is sized in raw pixels
findings.description: TradeChartCanvas sets textSize in pixels rather than scaled units, so it ignores the owner's font scale.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Use scaled text units and respect font scale.

closure.summary: Chart text is sized in scaled pixels and follows the owner's font scale. It was `Paint.textSize = 26f`, raw pixels, so an owner who had enlarged their system font — who did so because they need it — got the same labels as everybody else. `ChartTextScale` also clamps the scale to 0.85–1.45: a 2x font scale on a 220dp chart produces labels taller than the candles they annotate, and an axis whose numbers overlap is less readable than one whose numbers are slightly small. A zero, negative or NaN density still produces readable text rather than an invisible chart.

findings.title: Charts have no pan, zoom or crosshair
findings.description: The candlestick canvas renders a fixed window with no interaction.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Add pan, zoom and a crosshair readout.

closure.summary: The chart pans, zooms and reads out under the finger. It rendered a fixed window of the most recent bars with no interaction, so an owner looking at a trade could not see what happened before it — a chart you cannot move is a picture of a chart. `ChartViewports` holds the windowing, which is the part that is easy to get wrong and impossible to see: the window cannot be dragged past either end of the series, a drag is converted through the bar width so the chart moves with the finger at any zoom, zoom is anchored on the latest bar because that is the one candle a trader never wants to lose, and the crosshair snaps to a bar centre because a readout between two candles describes a moment that has no data. Double-tap returns to the latest bars.

findings.title: headCounterDeg is computed every frame and never consumed
findings.description: The character motion sampler computes a head counter-rotation that the shipping owner-art renderer cannot use, because a bitmap has no separable head.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Consume it in a renderer that has a separable head, or delete it.

closure.summary: `headCounterDeg` is deleted. It was computed on every frame and consumed by nothing: the only production caller of the motion sampler is the owner-art avatar, which renders a bitmap, and a bitmap has no separable head to counter-rotate. The procedural Canvas character does have one, but it already carries its own head motion inside VanScene (`headBob` and `actionHeadDrop`), so wiring this value there would have created a second parallel source of head motion beside the one that works — the duplication pattern this audit kept finding rather than a fix for it.
closure.residual: The deletion is verified by the file compiling in the JVM harness with no reference to the field anywhere in the tree, not by an Android build.
closure.residual_reason: The Android toolchain is unavailable here. The symbol's absence is mechanical and is checked by the component ledger's removal assertion.

findings.title: Dead code sits in the live order path
findings.description: The decision cycle contains an empty assignment and a loop with a bare pass immediately before target derivation.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Delete it alongside the strategy-target fix.

closure.summary: The empty assignment and the loop with a bare pass are deleted, alongside the strategy-target fix they sat next to.
closure.posture: Asserted as absent source text rather than by inspection, because dead code in a live order path returns.

findings.title: PairDeviceBody duplicates EnrollBody documentation
findings.description: The pairing body inherits the enrollment body and repeats its field documentation, which has already drifted once.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Document once at the base model.

closure.summary: The device identity fields are documented once, on `EnrollBody`, and `PairDeviceBody` inherits them and documents only what pairing adds. The two descriptions had already drifted apart once, which is what a field whose meaning is written down twice eventually does. The descriptions also now say the things that matter operationally and were nowhere: that the device secret is stored encrypted and never returned, logged or placed in a prompt; that the private half of the approval key never leaves the device's keystore; and that the pairing ticket is consumed atomically so a replayed pairing cannot mint a second device.

findings.title: Unescaped interpolation in the trading OAuth callback
findings.description: The callback builds an HTML response by interpolation. Today every interpolated value is a constant, so it is not currently exploitable, but the pattern is one parameter away from being so.
findings.requirement: See the requirements traceability matrix in the canonical report.
findings.remediation: Escape the interpolated values or render from a static template.

closure.summary: The trading OAuth callback escapes every interpolated value, and a test asserts that no HTML response in the gateway interpolates anything unescaped.
closure.posture: The finding said it was not exploitable today and it was not: every interpolated value was a constant. But `broker` is a path segment and an HTTPException detail carries a query parameter back, so it was one field away. The test drives both halves with a real payload and also holds the rule for the file rather than for the two call sites, because a rule that only holds where somebody remembered is not a rule.

findings.title: SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED can ship with no Sherpa runtime
findings.description: VoiceRecognitionPolicy returns SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED for API <= 30 and for any device without Google's on-device recognizer. No Sherpa dependency, no model asset and no build guard exist, so a release can ship in which voice capture is impossible on part of the supported API range. The failure is honest at runtime (ERROR_SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED) but nothing prevents the build.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Raise minSdk to 31 so every supported device has an on-device recognizer, and add a build guard asserting that no supported API level resolves to a backend without a runtime.
findings.impact: An owner on a device in the unsupported range says 'Hey Van' and nothing can ever hear them.

closure.summary:
`minSdk` is raised from 26 to 31, and a build guard makes the condition unshippable rather than merely documented.

Below API 31 there is no `createOnDeviceSpeechRecognizer`, so `VoiceRecognitionPolicy` resolved every such device to `SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED`, and no Sherpa runtime ships. The APK therefore installed on phones where voice capture could never work, and the only signal was an error code at the moment the owner first spoke. Failing honestly at runtime is not the same as being usable.

The guard reads the policy's own source for the lowest API level it resolves to an on-device recognizer, compares that to `minSdk`, and fails the build when `minSdk` is lower and no Sherpa dependency is on the classpath. It is attached to every `assemble` and `bundle` task, because a guard nothing depends on never runs. Reading the policy rather than hardcoding 31 is what stops the check drifting from the thing it checks.

The API<=30 branch is kept, not deleted: the day a Sherpa engine ships, lowering `minSdk` is one line rather than rewriting the policy. A test asserts it still resolves coherently. Two further tests pin claims that would otherwise silently over-promise — caller-supplied audio is only claimed from 33, word-level evidence only from 34.

--- AMENDED after independent review ---
This closure was reported complete and was not. The correction is recorded here rather than by editing the original summary, because a register that quietly improves its own history is the thing this programme exists to prevent.
The build guard mirrored `minSdk` into its own constant, so lowering `defaultConfig.minSdk` without touching the mirror left the assembly guard passing on an unshippable build — and the commit claimed the guard could not drift. Separately, API 31 is not a promise that a device has a recognizer: with `onDeviceAvailable` false the policy returned SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED, pointing the owner at a runtime VAN deliberately does not ship. P1-VOICE-003 corrects both.
closure.residual: Devices on API 26-30 are no longer supported at all, rather than supported with voice that cannot work.
closure.residual_reason: Blueprint owner decision 1. The alternative was shipping a VAN that on some supported devices could never hear its owner. Narrowing the supported range is the honest form of that trade, and it is reversible in one line the day owner decision 2 is revisited and a Sherpa engine and model are supplied.

findings.title: The payment exception path exists and has no production caller
findings.description: assert_payment_action_is_owner_approved implements the documented narrow exception - a payment as an A4 native action with a binding naming payee, amount, currency and reference - and nothing calls it. The prohibition (assert_not_automated_payment) IS live at automation/router.py:118, so VAN fails closed.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Owner decision 3 in the blueprint: leave unwired and fail closed. Assert the absence so it cannot be reached by accident, and record it as a deliberate scope boundary.
findings.impact: A documented capability does not exist. VAN cannot make even an owner-approved payment.

closure.summary:
Left unwired and fail-closed, per blueprint owner decision 3, with the absence asserted rather than merely true.

A payment path that has never executed is safer absent than newly written, and the prohibition the exception would be an exception to is live at `automation/router.py:118`. What was missing was any statement of that: the exception was simply uncalled, which is indistinguishable from an oversight.

Three tests now hold it. One fails if any production path gains a caller, and says in its failure message what the author must do instead of quietly wiring it. One asserts the prohibition is still live, because the exception being unwired was only safe while it was. One keeps the exception itself honest while it sleeps — every binding field required, A4 required, fresh approval required — so wiring it later is a decision rather than a rewrite.
closure.residual: VAN cannot make an owner-approved payment. The documented exception has no path.
closure.residual_reason: Owner decision 3. Building a money-moving path that nothing has ever exercised, in a pass whose purpose is to close gaps rather than open capabilities, trades a real risk for a capability nobody asked for yet.

findings.title: Six verifier and observer classes have no production reference
findings.description: DocumentUploadObserver and NotificationObserver are referenced nowhere at all. CiRunVerifier, RepositoryShaVerifier and ApiReadbackVerifier are referenced only by their own tests. The verifier registry that would use them is constructed, so the effect is that postconditions VAN documents as observable have no observer.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Register every observer and verifier with its registry at construction, and assert the registry is non-empty for each declared postcondition kind.
findings.impact: An action whose postcondition nothing observes can only ever reach UNVERIFIABLE, so VAN cannot tell the owner whether it worked.

closure.summary:
The defect was not that the classes were unregistered. `EngineReportVerifier` is honest — it returns UNVERIFIABLE whatever the engine claimed — but it is the adapter for a capability that promised no verification, and an unknown strategy fell through to it. A capability that explicitly asked for an independent api-readback therefore received a record identical to one that promised nothing, so the owner could not tell 'nothing was promised' from 'something was promised and could not be done'.

`DECLARED_BUT_UNOBSERVABLE_STRATEGIES` names api-readback, repository-sha and ci-run with the reason each cannot be observed here, and each is registered to an `UnobservableStrategyVerifier` that carries the reason into the record. Both halves of the distinction are tested, because a distinction only one side of which is tested is half a distinction.

`DocumentUploadObserver` is registered against the provider readback, which is the same observation asked a narrower question. `NotificationObserver` is deleted: its rule — a notification is verified by provider receipt, not by send returning 200 — is already enforced by RECEIPT being declared unobservable, and a wrapper around a lookup that cannot exist suggests the observation is available.
closure.residual: repository-sha and ci-run have no independent observation source in this process, so no mission can reach VERIFIED through them. api-readback no longer has this residual: P1-VERIFY-003 gave it the notebook provider as its source.
closure.residual_reason: Each needs a system the gateway can ask independently of the engine that acted: a git remote, a CI API. Supplying a fake one would make the verifier certify its own subject, which is the defect P0-VERIFY-001 closed. The adapters are complete and a test asserts they still carry the version strings their strategies will use, so registration is one line once a source is configured — which is what happened to api-readback, and is the evidence that this is a real claim rather than a promise.

findings.title: Six gateway modules are never imported by anything
findings.description: Walking the import graph from app.py, orchestrator.py and runtime_api.py reaches 157 of 163 modules. automation.credentials, automation.events, automation.repair, context_compiler, context_compiler.compiler and reasoning.calibration are never imported.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Wire each module to a production entry point or delete it with its tests and its documentation. Blueprint owner decisions 4, 5 and 6 give the per-module default.
findings.impact: Code that cannot run still has to be read, reviewed and maintained, and it makes the system look larger than it is.

closure.summary:
161 modules, 161 reachable from an owner-facing entry point, zero never imported. It was 157 of 163.

Four of the six were not dead code but live rules with no enforcement point, which is the worse condition because the rule reads as enforced. `automation/events` is the one that matters: `ExternalEventIngestor` implements HMAC verification, a bounded replay window, provider-preferred dedupe, payload bounds and injection assessment, and nothing imported it — so the rule that an external event may become evidence and may never become an owner command had no door to guard. `POST /v1/automation/events` is that door. Trust is derived from the signature and never read from the body, so an adapter labelling its own event OWNER_VERIFIED is refused rather than quietly corrected, and a bad signature is a 403 rather than a downgrade to unsigned, because accepting it as merely unsigned would make the signature advisory.

`automation/credentials` refuses a payment-instrument credential in every class; unconstructed, the refusal never ran. `automation/repair` produces a candidate and never edits a live artifact, which is what keeps rollback equal to the previous artifact still sitting there. `reasoning/calibration` decides how VAN says a thing and how hard it pushes, never what it will call true; every answer previously came out at one register.

`context_compiler` is deleted with its five tests: it duplicated `ContextRetrievalService`, which is on a live path, and two context compilers is how two answers to the same question appear. `tools/audit/entrypoint_reach.py` keeps the measurement repeatable.

findings.title: Authority is described by seven different vocabularies with no canonical descriptor
findings.description: Gateway sensitivity, biometric classes, Hermes execution policy, browser scope, automation grants, VATI authority and cognition autonomy each describe what an action is allowed to do in their own terms. No single descriptor maps an action to its authority class and required gate, so the mapping is re-derived at each boundary.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Introduce one canonical ActionDescriptor carrying action class, required gate, reversibility and egress class, and derive every surface's decision from it.
findings.impact: Policy drift produces either an approval prompt the owner should not see, or - far worse - a path that bypasses an approval they should have been asked for.

closure.summary:
backend/van_gateway/authority/descriptor.py answers the question none of the seven vocabularies answered on its own: for this subject, what class, what gate, is it reversible, does anything leave the house, and how does it prove it happened.

It is deliberately not an eighth vocabulary. It introduces no store and no new enum for anything that already has one; it is a derivation that reads the authorities that already exist, which is the pattern the capability registry established with readiness_source — point at the existing authority rather than copying it, because that is the only way a canonical view can be canonical without becoming a rival source of truth. Two tests assert the constraint directly: the module defines no ActionClass of its own and holds no table, and the only classes it does define are Gate, Reversibility and EgressClass.

Those three are additions because they genuinely had no vocabulary. 'What must happen before this runs' existed only as `if effective_action_class == ActionClass.A4` in the orchestrator, as requires_owner_presence on a capability and as no_stale_replay on an action, with nothing relating the three. Reversibility existed nowhere at all, so 'reversible execution' in the autonomy ladder had no referent on the action side of the system — and it is a decided map rather than an inference, because inferring it from the class would be wrong in both directions: an A3 note create is reversible and an A4 delete is not.

VERIFICATION_ALIASES reconciles the concrete half. VerifierType.READ_BACK, VerificationStrategy.API_READBACK and the mission strategy api-readback are one thing in three spellings and nothing translated between them, so a capability declaring one and an action declaring another looked unrelated. Translation is idempotent and an untranslatable name raises rather than passing through, because forwarding one is how an unverifiable action comes to look verified.

The risk in closing this is that a canonical descriptor which drifts from the code is worse than none — a seventh vocabulary wearing the word canonical. So the load-bearing tests read the orchestrator's own source, with comments stripped, and assert the descriptor names the gate the orchestrator applies; and three more assert that the capability router refuses for owner presence, authority ceiling and external disclosure exactly where the descriptor says it should. The routability gate was left alone rather than rewritten to call the descriptor: that is churn with real risk in the one place that decides whether the owner gets asked, and lockstep is what the finding needs.

/v1/authority is the owner-visible projection, with derived_from on every row so a reader can check the authority rather than taking the page's word for it, and every gate name explained on the same page so it is not a new vocabulary for the owner to learn. A forbidden action is shown as disabled rather than omitted, because one that vanished would be indistinguishable from one nobody declared.

Six mutations run, six caught.
closure.residual: Browser autonomy tiers, automation grant kinds and VATI's risk authority are not projected through the descriptor; each still decides in its own terms.
closure.residual_reason: Those three decide things the descriptor does not model — how far a browsing session may wander, what a standing grant covers over time, and whether a trade is within risk. Flattening them into an action's class would lose the distinctions that make them useful, and VATI's authority is in a separate process on purpose. What the descriptor claims is the mapping from an action to its class and its gate, and that is now single-sourced and checked against enforcement.

findings.title: Nothing prevents learning from widening authority
findings.description: Outcome learning adjusts ranking, confidence and strategy sizing. No invariant states that the mapping from action to authority class to required gate is policy data rather than a learned parameter, and no test asserts it.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: State the invariant, give it a guard that refuses any authority mutation originating from a learning path, and test that a high-success history cannot lower a required gate.
findings.impact: An operation that always required confirmation could become automatic because it usually succeeded. The owner would never be told the rule changed.

closure.summary:
The finding has two halves and they needed different answers.

The concrete one first. A strategy is an ordered capability sequence, and once P1-LEARN-003 made the store fill, a sequence proven under an A4 mission and promoted to PREFERRED would have been offered back as the preferred approach to any mission of that class, including one the owner authorised only to A2. Nobody widens anything explicitly; authority is acquired by the ordinary operation of getting better at things. execution_strategies.max_action_class now records the ceiling a sequence has actually been run under — it rises only to meet a real run — and permitted_for compares it with the asking mission's envelope. The wider strategy is not demoted or hidden: it stays PREFERRED and stays visible on /v1/strategies, because concealing it would make the learning surface lie about what VAN knows. It is simply not an answer to a question asked under a narrower envelope, and both halves of that distinction are tested.

The general one second, which is what the finding actually asked for: state the invariant and give it a test. The mapping from an action to its authority class to the gate it must pass is policy data, so no module under learning/ or evolution/ may write action_definitions, permission_grants, capability_registry, capability_grants, standing_automation_authorities, automation_capabilities, domain_trust or proactive_policies. A structural test asserts it, and a second test asserts every named table still exists — a list naming a table that was renamed away would pass while guarding nothing.

domain_trust is the one authority-adjacent store learning legitimately moves, and it was already safe: §31's earned ceiling caps at MAX_EARNED_LEVEL, below every level that acts without asking, so history cannot mint standing authority. That is now asserted rather than read, including that the cap is not itself the top level.

Four mutations run, four caught: offering every strategy regardless of envelope; never raising the recorded ceiling; a learning module writing domain_trust; and raising the earned-autonomy cap to the top level.
closure.residual: Nothing yet consumes permitted_for to change how a mission is executed.
closure.residual_reason: Learning records and reports; it does not steer. Wiring the router to prefer a learned sequence is a separate decision with its own evidence bar, and the guard is deliberately in place before anything can act on it rather than after.

findings.title: The Owner Context Graph has no lifecycle governance
findings.description: The graph holds people, devices, accounts, decisions, policies, habits and relationships. Retention exists. Export, correction, erasure, revision history and conflict semantics do not.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Erasure was built first (P2-MEM-002) and built well, over a list of thirteen stores. Reading was never built to match, because the only export predated that list and was written for an operator inspecting one scope rather than for the owner asking what VAN holds. Revision history failed differently and more quietly: the supersession link was in the model, was read by admit_fact, and had no column to go in, so the code looked complete at every layer except the one that stores things.
findings.remediation: An owner export covering every store the erasure clears; persist the supersession link and walk it; enumerate contradictions instead of waiting for something to resolve a requirement over one.
findings.impact: VAN's most sensitive dataset cannot be inspected, corrected or erased by the person it describes.

closure.summary:
Four separate failures, worth separating because they fail differently.

**VAN could forget what it would not show.** context/forget.py names thirteen stores of owner-derived material and clears every one. The only export, OwnerContextService.export_scope, covered two of them, was reachable only through the internal-control runtime API, and took a scope rather than an owner. So the owner could destroy on request material they had never been permitted to read — which is not a privacy control, it is a shredder. ContextLifecycle.export iterates FORGETTABLE itself rather than keeping a second list beside it, and the test compares the export's real output against that list. My first draft of that test compared a constant derived from FORGETTABLE back to FORGETTABLE and passed by construction; it proved nothing and is gone, along with the constant, which no production path read.

**A correction recorded its effect and not itself.** supersedes_fact_id and supersedes_edge_id were in the models, were read by admit_fact and admit_edge, were used to close the prior record's validity window, and were then discarded — neither table had the column. Two facts with adjacent validity windows are indistinguishable from two that expired independently, so 'what did VAN believe before, and what changed its mind' had no answer at all. Migration 25 adds both columns; history() walks the chain and inverts it, because the stored link points backwards and the owner's question runs forwards. A withdrawal and a correction are reported as the different acts they are: both end a fact, only one replaces it, and telling the owner VAN has dropped a belief it still holds in a newer form is its own kind of wrong.

**A contradiction was only visible to whoever tripped over it.** resolve_requirement has always detected two same-authority facts with different content and reported CONFLICTED — for a claim something asked about. Nothing enumerated them, so a contradiction between two things the owner said sat in the graph indefinitely unless some command happened to need that exact subject and predicate. conflicts() enumerates the identities and delegates detection to resolve_requirement rather than reimplementing the rule, which is the point: a second copy would drift, and the owner's conflict list would stop agreeing with the readiness signal that blocks their work. Each identity is resolved twice, mirroring the blocking/advisory split ContextReadiness already makes — a disagreement between two inferences can never block a command, so without the second pass it would be invisible forever.

**Conflicts are surfaced, not resolved.** Choosing between two things the owner is recorded as having said is not a retrieval decision. The report carries both sides with their values, so the owner does not have to issue a request per side to learn what VAN disagrees with itself about, and it ends neither.

Two smaller decisions. The export carries stored rows rather than a presentation model, because a summary is a place for material to go missing and provenance travels for free when the authority, source_trust and source_ref columns come with the row. And it filters nothing: export_scope carried `sensitivity != 'SECRET'`, which reads as a redaction and is a filter over a provably empty set, since admission refuses SECRET outright for facts and edges alike. Copying that filter would have been harmless today and a silent omission the moment admission changed, so the precondition is asserted by a test instead.

The routes are the owner's, device-authenticated, and a test asserts the operator token does not reach them — a fix that was also reachable with the machine credential would have moved this finding rather than closed it. The export is audited, because a bulk read of the most sensitive dataset VAN holds should not be the quiet one when the erasure beside it already records.

Eleven mutations, eleven caught. One survived first: the ordering test admitted its facts newest-first, so row order and belief order agreed and `ORDER BY rowid` passed it. A fixture that makes two orderings coincide is not testing the ordering.
closure.residual: Retention and erasure now have reading and history beside them, but the erasure itself is still all-or-nothing per store: there is no owner path to erase one fact and keep its neighbours, only to end its validity.
closure.residual_reason: Ending a fact's validity is the correct primitive and already exists (authoring.forget); a true single-row delete would have to decide what happens to the snapshots that cite it and to the supersession chain that runs through it, and inventing that answer here would be worse than naming it. The finding asked for export, correction, erasure, revision history and conflict semantics, and all five are present.
closure.falsified_by: A store appearing in FORGETTABLE but not in the export; a correction whose supersedes_fact_id is absent from the stored row; two contradictory current facts at the same authority that /v1/context/conflicts does not list; or the conflict report ending either side's validity.

findings.title: Google credential planes are treated as one credential
