findings.description: Refresh-token capability, browser-session capability such as consumer NotebookLM, cloud-project credentials and delegated worker identities expire independently. The health surface reports one Google state.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Model each plane separately, report per-plane state, and degrade only the capabilities that plane serves.
findings.impact: One expired plane makes the whole mesh look offline, so the owner re-authenticates everything or gives up on all of it.

closure.summary:
SEMANTIC REQUIREMENT: an owner whose Google access has partly lapsed can see which credential lapsed and what that costs them, and a credential that is fine for one plane never vouches for another.

PRODUCTION PATH: GET /v1/google/planes (owner device, like /v1/google/status) -> plane_health -> the authority that already owned each plane: GoogleService.status for the refresh token, NotebookEnterpriseProvider.status for the cloud project credentials, NotebookConsumerProvider.status for the browser profile, and GoogleIdentityBroker.principal_status for the runtime entitlement.

GoogleCredentialPlane already named all four and each had a reporter; nothing composed them, so the health surface answered 'is Google connected' with one boolean derived from the refresh token alone. This module composes and composes only — no plane's state is decided here.

Three things the tests pin, because each is a way this surface could lie. CONFIGURED maps to AUTH_REQUIRED rather than READY: a credential that is present and has never been exercised is precisely the one about to surprise someone. UNCONFIGURED and AUTH_REQUIRED stay distinct, because 'set this up' and 'sign in again' send the owner to different places. And which capability rides on which plane is read from registries/google_capabilities.json rather than kept as a second list, with a test that every declared capability is attributed to exactly one plane — drift there means telling the owner the wrong thing is broken.

The summary field is named `capabilities_whose_credential_plane_is_ready`, not `capabilities_available`. A working credential is not a working capability: the runtime can still be unreachable, rate limited or uncertified. The payload says so and points at /v1/capabilities/status for the question it cannot answer. That naming was the first thing a counterexample review of the draft changed.

Both wrong answers are tested directly: a revoked refresh token leaving the other three usable, and a healthy refresh token not vouching for a dead cloud credential or a signed-out profile. The route is exercised through create_app with an enrolled device rather than by calling the composer, and asserts that nothing reports ready in an environment where nothing is configured. Six mutations, six caught.
closure.residual: A plane's state is as good as the reporter behind it, and two of those report configuration rather than a live probe: the cloud and consumer planes are READY only once a certification has been recorded, and neither is re-probed on read.
closure.residual_reason: A live probe means spending a request against the provider on every health read, and the certification records exist precisely so that is not done casually. The conservative direction is already taken — anything short of a recorded READY reports AUTH_REQUIRED — so the surface understates rather than overstates.
closure.falsified_by: A plane reporting READY while its credential is rejected by the provider; or one plane's failure changing another plane's state; or a capability appearing on two planes or on none.

findings.title: No whole-runtime resource envelope exists
findings.description: Always-available voice, the animated embodiment, local indexes, notification processing, context compilation, network connections and trading updates all compete on one phone. Each has its own budget; nothing owns the sum.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: The visual layer got a budget because it was the one subsystem whose cost was visible — a dropped frame is something you can see. Everything else consumed battery invisibly, so nobody wrote it a budget, and the finding's phrasing was generous: it said each subsystem had its own budget, and in fact only one did. The event stream polled on a fixed fifteen seconds, telemetry flushed on a fixed minute, and battery *level* was an input to nothing at all.
findings.remediation: One envelope over battery, charging, power-save, thermal, memory and storage; a declared shed order with a named set that is never shed; and each subsystem's own knob answering to it rather than beside it.
findings.impact: VAN is individually well-behaved and collectively a battery and thermal problem.

closure.summary:
VanResourceEnvelope is not another budget beside the others; it is the one they answer to, and four properties make that true rather than decorative.

**Pressure is the worst input, not the latest.** Each of battery, power-save, thermal, memory and storage contributes a level independently and the envelope takes the maximum, naming which inputs reached it so a CRITICAL reading is arguable rather than mysterious. Charging clears battery pressure and nothing else — a phone charging while hot is a phone getting hotter, and a mutation making the charger excuse the heat is in the suite.

**Some things are never shed.** An envelope that throttles the wake word is worse than no envelope: the owner says 'Hey Van', nothing happens, and the cause is the mechanism meant to protect them. WAKE_WORD, OWNER_COMMAND and DEGRADED_REPORTING are full at every pressure including SURVIVAL. Everything that yields is something VAN does for the owner without being asked. The shed table is exhaustive over the enum with no else branch, so adding a subsystem is a compile error rather than a silent 'unconstrained' — an envelope whose default for anything new is no limit decays back into this finding one subsystem at a time, which is roughly how it got here.

**The subsystems that already had knobs now turn them.** rememberVanEffectBudget resolves through VanResourceEnvelope.effectBudget, which takes the weaker of what VanEffectPolicy decided and what the envelope permits — the sum may veto a subsystem's budget and may never raise it. EventStream.nextDelayMillis takes the pressure and returns null at SURVIVAL, because 'stop' and 'a very large delay' are different instructions and the second keeps a coroutine alive for nothing. DeviceTelemetryReporter re-reads its allowance every iteration rather than capturing it once, so a device that cools down speeds back up without a restart.

**Accessibility is not a cost rung.** Clamping REDUCED_MOTION down to LOW would restore motion on a device whose owner switched it off, because LOW allows motion and REDUCED_MOTION does not. The rank function puts them side by side and a test asserts over every pressure that a still budget is never clamped into a moving one.

The concrete regression this fixes: a phone at four percent with power-save switched off rendered the full field, because battery level was an input to nothing.

Two corrections from the mutation run. Three mutations survived first. Two were bad mutations — one was semantically a no-op, and one attacked an invariant held in two places, which no single edit can falsify; the harness now supports compound mutations so that one can be tested properly. The third was real: an explicit branch exempting catch-up from cadence stretching could not fire, because CATCH_UP_POLL_MS is zero and any scale times zero is zero. A guard that cannot fire is what I had just removed from the clamp for the same reason, so it is gone, and a test now pins the constant with the reasoning that depends on it.

Twenty-three mutations, twenty-three caught: ten against the arithmetic under Gradle, seven against the wiring under pytest, and six existing ones re-run.

CONFIRMED in part by run 35454462305 on a24efec: :app:compileDebugKotlin, :app:testDebugUnitTest, :app:assembleDebug and :app:lintDebug all passed with the envelope wired into VanCanvasFallback, WorkModules and DeviceTelemetryReporter. That settles that the wiring is sound Kotlin and that lint has no objection to the permission-free readings — and nothing about battery or heat, which is what the residual says.
closure.residual: The policy is declared, executed and wired. Whether it keeps a real S24 cool under VAN's actual load is unmeasured, and the thresholds — twenty percent, the thermal bands, the cadence multipliers — are reasoned rather than tuned against a device.
closure.residual_reason: Battery drain and thermal behaviour cannot be measured in this container or on a CI runner; there is no phone. The arithmetic is executed in android/verification with injected readings, which is the whole of what a repository can prove about a policy, and the wiring is compiled by CI. The measurement is Gate 14's, on the owner's device, with the APK run 35452683328 published — and that is where the thresholds should be tuned, because guessing them here and calling it evidence is exactly the substitution the audit brief forbids.
closure.falsified_by: VanResourceEnvelope.allowance returning anything but a full allowance for a NEVER_SHED subsystem; rememberVanEffectBudget calling VanEffectPolicy.resolve directly again; a subsystem added to VanSubsystem without a shed rule; or an S24 measurement showing VAN's drain unchanged between NOMINAL and CRITICAL pressure.

findings.title: No recovery matrix exists for partial-failure paths
findings.description: Tests are overwhelmingly happy-path. Gateway restart mid-command, Android process death while awaiting approval, duplicate provider callbacks, connectivity loss after a mutation but before the receipt, and trading state changing while approval is pending are unexercised.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Build a recovery matrix with a test per cell, and treat an unexercised cell as unshipped.
findings.impact: The failure modes an owner actually meets are the ones nothing has tried.

closure.summary:
backend/tests/test_recovery_matrix.py is the matrix: six cells, 26 tests, each naming what fails and what must be true afterwards. The bar is not 'does not crash' — a recovery that silently repeats a mutation is worse than a refusal.

  1. Gateway restart mid-command. A stale claim is recoverable; a fresh one and one just short of the lease are not; a COMPLETED answer and a CONFLICT are never retaken; age does not make a different request the same request.
  2. Restart after dispatch, before the receipt. The retry gets the mission already open rather than a second one, which is what makes retaking a claim safe.
  3. Connectivity lost after a mutation. The deadline sweeper expires the mission, a mission still inside its deadline is left alone, and an expired one cannot become a verified success.
  4. Duplicate provider callback, terminal and non-terminal, plus a racing writer with a stale expectation.
  5. Process death while awaiting approval. The challenge lives in the database so a restart does not invalidate the owner's decision; it expires on the clock rather than on a session; an expired one is removed rather than left to be read as valid later; it is consumed once; and a device revoked while the approval was pending cannot approve.
  6. Trading state changing while an approval is pending. Stated as the boundary it is rather than a gate the gateway does not have: an approval proves the owner asked for this action on this device, and whether the world still permits it is VATI's decision. A gateway that re-evaluated trading state at approval time would be a second risk authority, which is worse than one.

Writing cell 1 found P0-OPS-011, which was not merely untested. Two mutations survived the first run and both named real gaps: a duplicate terminal callback was refused by the transition table whichever guard was removed, so the terminal guard was untested until the test asserted MISSION_TERMINAL rather than any MissionError — an operator reading MISSION_ILLEGAL_TRANSITION would go looking for a state-machine bug instead of seeing that the provider delivered twice; and the non-terminal duplicate case was missing entirely. Both are now cells. Fifteen mutations, fifteen caught.
closure.residual: The matrix covers the cells the gateway can exercise in-process. Android process death is exercised through the server-side property it depends on — that a challenge outlives any session — rather than by killing an app.
closure.residual_reason: Killing the Android process and resuming is Gate 14 device work, deferred to physical verification. What the repository can settle is the invariant the app relies on, and that is settled here.

findings.title: No machine-checkable map of which document owns which invariant
findings.description: Thirty-one canonical documents, ~13,700 lines. Nothing states which document is authoritative for a given invariant, so two can be locally correct and jointly contradictory.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.remediation: Create docs/project-state/AUTHORITY_MAP.yaml binding each invariant to one owning document, its implementation and its test, and fail CI on an unowned or doubly-owned invariant.
findings.impact: A contradiction between authorities is resolved by whoever read one of them last.

closure.summary:
docs/project-state/AUTHORITY_MAP.yaml binds 36 invariants across 11 domains to the six documents that own them, and tools/ci/authority_map.py enforces the binding.

The design turns on what a machine can actually check. It cannot tell that two prose documents contradict each other. It can tell that two of them claim authority over the same subject, which is the condition under which a contradiction survives — and which is the shape the audit found, a document describing a capability as BUILT living next to one describing the gap because neither owned the claim. So each invariant names a dotted subject, exactly one owner decides it, and a second claim on the same subject fails CI. The same rule restated under a second subject fails too, because one rule owned twice under two names is the same failure in a disguise.

The weaker failure — a map that is decorative — is closed by the rest of the gate: every owner, implementation and test path must exist, every invariant must name at least one of each, and every finding it cites must be in the register and closed. That last check is the one that stops the map being written ahead of the work, which is the failure mode the whole audit is about, one level up.

Nine tests inject each defect and assert the gate rejects it, including the gate's own entry: governance.invariant_ownership is owned by the closure blueprint, implemented by the gate and tested by its own test file. docs/SECURITY_POLICY.md owns six invariants and is not edited — naming an owner is a statement about where authority lives, not a change to it.

One mutation survived the first run and named a real gap: the gate checked that an owner exists, not which documents may own. 'A path under docs/' was the whole check, so a derived document could acquire authority by being cited — which is how docs/IMPLEMENTATION_LEDGER.md came to certify 33 of 36 workstreams against a blueprint it does not own (P1-DOC-001). The map now declares `owning_documents` and the gate refuses an owner outside it, and refuses a declared document that does not exist so the list cannot be padded to make a citation pass. Five mutations, five caught.
closure.residual: The map covers the invariants this programme established and can point at a test. Rules in the canonical documents that nothing enforces are not listed.
closure.residual_reason: An invariant with no test is a claim, and a map that held claims would reintroduce the problem it exists to solve: a reader would not be able to tell an enforced rule from a stated intention. Adding an entry is the same work as enforcing the rule, which is the right cost.

findings.title: No owner command could ever be verified: the mission's success contract was always empty
findings.description: TypedCommandResolver resolves an exact owner phrase to a registered action and copies that action's declared verifier_type onto the CommandResolution. CommandMissionLink.open then created every mission with SuccessContract() — no postconditions, no verifier_class. CommandResolution.verifier_type was therefore written by the resolver and read by nothing anywhere in the tree, and MissionService._perform_verification, which refuses VERIFIED_SUCCESS on a contract that is not checkable, refused every mission that originated from an owner command. The effect was total: no command issued from the phone, however exactly VAN understood it and however readable its result, could reach VERIFIED_SUCCESS.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: RC1's sibling. P0-EXEC-001 found the command path ending at dispatch with no mission; this is the same break one layer on — the mission exists, and carries nothing that would let it be judged.
findings.remediation: Translate an exact resolution into a success contract, using only strategies with a registered independent observation, and record the reason where none exists.
findings.impact: Every owner command terminated at COMPLETED_UNVERIFIED. VAN could not tell the owner that anything had worked, including trading.halt — the one A4 command issued under time pressure, where 'the command returned' and 'the runner stopped' are exactly the two things that must not be confused.

closure.summary:
`command/success_contracts.py` is the missing joint. `contract_for(resolution)` emits a contract only where an independent observation is registered, and `CommandMissionLink.open` now takes the resolution the orchestrator already held.

Two strategies gained a real source. `trading-halt` reads the VATI kill-switch ledger — written by the trading process, hash-chained there, and the only party entitled to say whether the runner stopped; the observation refuses a ledger that is stale (P0-TRADE-004) or whose chain does not verify, because either would confirm a stop that may never have reached the runner. `api-readback` reads the notebook provider, which answers 'gone' and 'I could not ask' differently — only the first is a deletion. That moved ApiReadbackVerifier out of DECLARED_BUT_UNOBSERVABLE_STRATEGIES, which is the first time one of P2-VERIFY-002's 'one line from working' claims has actually been collected.

The contract is deliberately narrow. research.web.search and owner.context.read get no contract, and NO_CONTRACT_REASONS says why for each; the reason rides on the mission's constraints so the owner is told the limitation was decided at the outset rather than inferring it from a status. An enterprise notebook create gets none either: the id does not exist until the provider assigns it, and promising a readback that pointed at nothing would be this same finding one level down.

Five mutations of the invariant were run and all five caught, including the one that reverts the joint itself and the one that cites a genuine-looking ledger:// reference on a mission that failed.

--- AMENDED after independent review ---
This closure was reported complete and was not. The correction is recorded here rather than by editing the original summary, because a register that quietly improves its own history is the thing this programme exists to prevent.
The architecture was right and one contract was semantically wrong. `google.notebook.enterprise.sources.delete` and `.sources.add` were given the postcondition `notebook_exists: True`, because the notebook readback was the observation that existed. Deleting a source does not change whether the notebook exists, so a delete that silently failed satisfied the contract and the mission could reach VERIFIED_SUCCESS with the source still there — VAN telling the owner it had removed something it had not touched. P1-VERIFY-004 corrects it.
closure.residual: A free-form command still cannot be verified, and neither can a web search or a context read.
closure.residual_reason: The gateway does not know how to check an arbitrary instruction, and a search and a read leave nothing it can observe independently. Inventing a postcondition for any of them is how a mission ends up 'verified' on nothing, which is the defect P0-VERIFY-001 closed. Each carries its reason on the mission instead.

findings.title: The Computer Interaction Fabric has no executor, and nothing said so
findings.description: computer_use/fabric.py declares twelve typed operations with no RUN_ARBITRARY, real A4/A5 refusals, a per-type action-class ceiling, a mutation-needs-a-verifier rule and a durable computer_operations ledger. No worker exists for BROWSER, DESKTOP, TERMINAL or MOBILE, and ComputerInteractionFabric was constructed only by its own tests. begin() therefore inserted a PENDING row for an operation nobody would perform, and every capability matrix that listed the fabric read it as built because the module compiles and its refusals pass.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: A boundary written ahead of the thing it bounds, with nothing to mark the gap. That is the right order to build in; what was missing was a way for the system to say so.
findings.remediation: Construct the fabric in production, refuse every surface that has no worker before the ledger write, and report which surfaces are staffed on an internal-control health route.
findings.impact: A caller could record an operation that would never be performed, and the owner would read a PENDING row as queued work. At the programme level it meant a capability matrix that listed a surface VAN cannot act through.

closure.summary:
The recorded disposition was delete — the audit's 'delete or fold' and the closure blueprint's owner decision 6, which described the module as a stub. Reading it corrects that description and therefore the decision: the refusals are real, ordered and tested, the ledger is durable, and what is missing is a worker. Deleting a hardened boundary because the thing it bounds is unbuilt gets the order backwards; re-deriving it later under delivery pressure is how a RUN_ARBITRARY appears. Decision 6 in the blueprint is corrected in place, with the deletion instruction kept as the reversal.

So the module stays and the gap becomes enforced state. SURFACE_WORKERS is empty; begin() raises OPERATION_NO_WORKER_FOR_SURFACE, last among the refusals and before the insert. Last because an absolute prohibition must not read as a configuration gap — 'no worker for DESKTOP' invites someone to start a worker, and an A4 request reported that way would look one worker away from permitted. Before the insert because a PENDING row for work nobody will do is the owner being told it is queued.

ComputerInteractionFabric is constructed in create_app for the first time, /v1/computer-use/health reports which surfaces are staffed under the RUNTIME control scope, and COMPUTER_USE_NO_SURFACE_WORKER names what still works. A test asserts that registering a surface is the whole change needed to make the fabric work, so the guard reports a gap rather than hiding rot. Three mutations run, three caught.
closure.residual: VAN still cannot act on a desktop, a terminal or a mobile surface, and the browser surface is served by the browser fabric rather than this one.
closure.residual_reason: No surface worker has been built, and building one is a programme decision rather than a closure step. The refusal, the health route and the degraded entry make that state observable instead of implied, which is what the finding was about. Routing browser work through this fabric as well would give the owner two accounts of one task, the coherence defect P2-COH-001 closed.

findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: No mission carried a mission class, so StrategyLearning could never hold a row
findings.description: Every method on StrategyLearning keys on mission_class — register, preferred_for, the promotion gate, and §41's 'measurable strategy improvement in >= 3 production mission classes'. The missions table had no such column and the Mission model had no such field. P1-LEARN-001 gave the learning stores a feed and this one still could not fill, because the key it needs did not exist anywhere in the system. The class VAN already establishes is the typed resolver's intent id, which the command path computed and discarded.
findings.root_cause: A store keyed on a concept the rest of the system never named.
findings.remediation: Carry the resolver's intent on the mission, and record the capability sequence a terminal mission actually executed as a strategy outcome for that class.
findings.impact: §25 and §41 were both unanswerable. VAN could not say which approach works for any kind of work, and the eval scoreboard had nothing to score.

closure.summary:
Schema v21 adds missions.mission_class, and CommandMissionLink sets it from the resolution's intent id — a name VAN assigned by understanding the command, not a label anyone typed. Free-form commands share GENERAL_OWNER_INTENT, which is honest: VAN did not establish what kind of work they were, and grouping them by a guess would make the evidence worse than absent.

LearningFeed.record_strategy_outcome reads the capability sequence back from the mission's activities, not from its plan — learning from intentions is how a system concludes an approach works when it never ran. Only VERIFIED_SUCCESS counts as a success, so a strategy cannot accumulate a promotion record out of runs nothing checked. A mission with no activities produces nothing, which is the common case today and the right outcome: recording an empty sequence would make every free-form command look like the same successful approach.

/v1/strategies is the owner-visible projection, reporting the promotion rule alongside the rows so the numbers can be read against the bar they must clear, and reporting no success rate at all for a strategy nothing has exercised rather than a zero that would read as repeated failure.

--- AMENDED after independent review ---
This closure was reported complete and was not. The correction is recorded here rather than by editing the original summary, because a register that quietly improves its own history is the thing this programme exists to prevent.
The comment said only VERIFIED_SUCCESS counts as a success, and the implementation passed a boolean whose False branch incremented `failure_count`. So a cancellation, a policy refusal, an unsafe refusal, an expiry and an UNVERIFIABLE run all recorded as 'this approach does not work'. P1-LEARN-005 corrects it.
closure.residual: Strategies accumulate only for missions that produced gateway activities. Hermes performs most work without creating any, so today most missions record nothing.
closure.residual_reason: The gateway learns from what it can see. Hermes creating specialist work that MissionBinder binds is what produces activities, and where that does not happen there is genuinely no observed sequence. Inventing one from the plan would be the defect this finding is about.

findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: Regression auto-demotion had no caller
findings.description: §41 asks for regression auto-demotion and StrategyLearning.auto_demote implements it correctly, demoting any ADMITTED or PREFERRED strategy below a 60% success rate over at least three runs. Nothing in the gateway called it, so a strategy that stopped working kept its promotion indefinitely.
findings.root_cause: A sweep with no scheduled job — the same shape as P3-OPS-004.
findings.remediation: Add a scheduled job and publish the demotions as events.
findings.impact: The asymmetry §41 depends on — promotion is hard, demotion is automatic — held only on the promotion side.

closure.summary:
learning.auto_demote runs on the retention cadence and publishes strategy.demoted for each one, so a demotion is observable rather than a silent column change. The asymmetry is the safety property and is stated where the job is registered: removing trust from something that stopped working needs no ceremony, granting it does.

app.state.scheduler now exposes the installed jobs, because a job list that exists only inside a closure is how this went uncalled for as long as it did. The test asserts the caller, which is what the finding was about.

findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: The backup drill was written and never run
findings.description: ops.backup.drill takes a backup, restores it into a scratch location and compares row counts, schema version and the audit-chain head with the manifest. It was complete and referenced only by its own tests. Owner decision 10 in the closure blueprint took 'local only, with the drill enabled' as the default, and only the backup half had a scheduled job.
findings.root_cause: The proving half of a two-part guarantee had no caller.
findings.remediation: Schedule the drill, raise attention on failure, and clean up the scratch copy.
findings.impact: A backup nobody has restored is a hypothesis. A format, permission or schema change would have been discovered on the night it mattered.

closure.summary: ops.backup_drill runs weekly wherever a backup directory is configured, on by default and independently of backup_enabled: taking a backup and proving one restores are different decisions, and conflating them is how 'backups are configured' comes to mean 'backups were written'. A failure raises a BLOCKER attention item rather than only logging, because the owner has to act before the next backup is taken. The scratch restore is removed afterwards — it is a second full database, and anyone who found it would reasonably read it as a backup.
closure.residual: The drill proves the backup restores; it does not prove one exists anywhere but this disk.
closure.residual_reason: Owner decision 10: a backup on the same disk is not a backup, and the repository must not pick the owner's offsite target. tools/ops/backup.py already takes one.

findings.title: Three owner-memory stores had no producer and no route
findings.description: IntentContinuityGraph (§77), DecisionFingerprints (§65) and StrategicMemory (§78) were complete, correct and referenced only by their own tests. No mission observed a standing goal, no owner approval recorded a decision, no project rationale had anywhere to live, and IntentContinuityGraph.mark_stale had no caller, so an intent observed once would have stayed ACTIVE forever had one ever been observed. Each was a concept VAN could describe and had never seen an instance of.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Stores designed to be curated, in a system where nobody curates. The events they describe were already arriving on the mission path and nothing connected the two.
findings.remediation: Observe the goal and the approval where they actually arrive, sweep stale intents on a schedule, and give each store an owner-visible surface.
findings.impact: §77's conflict visibility — a newer instruction contradicting an older standing goal should be seen rather than silently winning — could not fire, because there were no intents. §65's falsifiability could not fire, because there were no decisions.

closure.summary:
LearningFeed is the producer, because the mission path is where the owner's instructions and approvals actually arrive; curating these stores by hand is the design that produced empty stores.

Opening a mission observes its goal as a standing intent and links the mission to it. The node is keyed on the goal text, so asking for the same thing again refreshes an existing intent rather than creating a second one — which is what lets STALE mean 'unmentioned for ninety days' instead of 'recorded once'. understanding.mark_stale_intents sweeps on the retention cadence, and /v1/understanding/intents reports each goal with what it conflicts with, plus the statement that STALE is not abandoned.

A decision fingerprint is recorded only where there was a decision: a mission whose envelope required the owner's presence is one they could have declined and did not. Ordinary use is not a choice, and recording it would bury the decisions that were. The mission's terminal state becomes the decision's outcome.

What is deliberately absent is the inference. VAN does not infer why the owner decided anything, so inferred_reason is null and falsified() is empty — and /v1/understanding/decisions says so, because an owner reading 'no falsified patterns' off a silent surface would take it to mean VAN's model of them is accurate, when it means VAN has made no claim. Writing a plausible reason there is exactly §12's warning: a fingerprint store that only accumulates becomes a machine for justifying whatever the owner did last.

StrategicMemory gets owner routes rather than a producer, because the owner is the author of project rationale. Recording something already rejected is answered with the rejection, which is the one place already_rejected can be asked today. §21's separation from Project Truth is stated on the wire so a rationale is not read back as a fact about the code.

Six mutations run, six caught — including inferring a reason the owner never gave, and sweeping the goals just mentioned instead of the forgotten ones.

--- AMENDED after independent review ---
This closure was reported complete and was not. The correction is recorded here rather than by editing the original summary, because a register that quietly improves its own history is the thing this programme exists to prevent.
Every mission goal was promoted straight into the standing-intent graph, so a one-off request stayed an ACTIVE long-term objective until the ninety-day sweep — giving §77's conflict detection transient commands to contradict genuine goals with. P2-MEM-003 corrects it.
closure.residual: VAN records what the owner decided and how it turned out; it does not infer why, so no inferred pattern exists for an outcome to falsify.
closure.residual_reason: §12 requires an inferred pattern to be falsifiable, and the safe order is falsifiability first. The outcome half is wired and the inference half is not, so the day VAN does infer a reason the machinery that can prove it wrong already runs. The surface reports the absence rather than letting an empty falsified list read as an accurate model.

findings.title: The external-reality store had no producer and the benchmark harness no corpus
findings.description: ExternalRealityModel is '§22's mandatory separation' — what available evidence says, kept apart from what the owner believes, so personalization cannot become an echo chamber. Nothing ever wrote to it, so the separation protected an empty store and contradictions() returned nothing in a way indistinguishable from the world agreeing with the owner. BenchmarkHarness declares fourteen VAN-specific suites and none has a task corpus; because AIEvolutionRadar.transition refuses ADMITTED without a benchmark digest, no technology can be adopted at all, and nothing reported that.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: An evidence store with no evidence source, and a benchmark vocabulary mistaken for a benchmark capability.
findings.remediation: Record research results as attributed external claims, and report which suites have a corpus alongside what follows from none having one.
findings.impact: VAN could not say what the world currently claims about anything, and an operator would have learned that no technology can be admitted by watching an adoption fail.

closure.summary:
Web research is external evidence with a citable source, which is the one thing ExternalRealityModel refuses to be written without, so ExaResearchService records one observation per result: the subject is the query, the claim is what the page asserts, the source is its URL. A result with no title claims nothing and records nothing. Confidence is 0.0, matching the UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL trust the evidence row already carries — a friendlier number would make the same source look more credible depending on which table you read.

contradicts_owner_belief is never set, because nothing compares a result with the owner model. Guessing would put VAN in the position of deciding the owner is wrong on the strength of a headline, which inverts §22: the disagreement is meant to be recorded as a fact about the world and reconciled in the open. /v1/external-reality reports that no comparison is performed, so an empty contradiction list is not read as agreement.

BenchmarkHarness.SUITES_WITH_A_CORPUS is empty and coverage() reports it on /v1/eval, separating 'cannot be run' from 'has not been run' — a reader who cannot tell them apart will read the second as the first — and naming the consequence: no technology can reach ADMITTED, which is §23's intended fail-closed state rather than an outage. Two tests assert the consequence rather than describing it, including that a benchmarked technology still needs the owner, because the two requirements fail separately.
closure.residual: No benchmark suite has a task corpus, so no technology can be admitted; and no external observation is compared with the owner model, so none is ever marked as contradicting it.
closure.residual_reason: Writing fourteen task corpora is a programme, not a closure step, and the absence produces the correct fail-closed behaviour rather than a wrong one. Contradiction detection needs a comparison VAN does not perform, and a heuristic one would let a search result overrule the owner. Both absences are now reported on the surfaces where their emptiness would otherwise read as a result.

findings.title: The workflow installer would have deleted most of CI
findings.description: tools/ci/install_github_workflow.py copies tools/ci/github-actions-ci.yml over .github/workflows/van-ci.yml on --apply, and its docstring states the template is 'kept byte-for-byte aligned with the live workflow'. Nothing enforced that. The template had drifted seventy lines behind and was missing the maturity gate, the maturity-gate self-test, the Hermes and trading policy suites, the automation and browser fail-closed proofs, the context-latency evidence step and the pure-Kotlin verification run. Running the installer would have removed all of it, including the gate that exists to stop a capability being described as BUILT with no production path.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: A claim in a docstring with nothing checking it — the audit's own defect shape, applied to the tooling that was supposed to catch it.
findings.remediation: Re-sync the template from the live workflow and assert byte equality, plus the survival of each load-bearing step, in a contract test.
findings.impact: One run of a tool documented as idempotent would have silently disarmed CI, and the next build would have gone green with nothing checking the ledgers.

closure.summary:
The template is re-synced from the live workflow and both now also run the authority-map gate and its self-test. tests/contracts/test_ci_workflow_is_what_it_claims.py asserts the byte equality the installer's docstring already claimed, and separately asserts that each load-bearing step survives an install — named individually rather than counted, so a renamed step is noticed rather than absorbed by a total that still adds up.

Two further checks: the maturity gate must run before the test steps it guards, because a truth gate that runs after the suite reports failures in an order that invites reading the test summary and concluding the system is fine; and the installer must still name the two paths these tests check, so moving its source or destination cannot leave the tests checking nothing.

findings.title: A gateway crash made the crashed command permanently unrepeatable
findings.description: IdempotencyService.begin claimed a key by writing an IN_FLIGHT row and nothing ever released it. A gateway that died between the claim and complete() or fail() left the row IN_FLIGHT forever, so every later attempt at that command raised 'still in flight'. The idempotency key is part of the signed request, so the owner could not work around it by changing it: that command was unrepeatable for the life of the database, and the only cure was editing the table by hand.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: A claim with no lease. P1-SEC-005 made the claim atomic, which was the right fix for the race; nothing addressed the holder never coming back.
findings.remediation: Give the claim a lease, recover a stale one inside the same transaction as the read, and record that it was recovered.
findings.impact: Any crash during command handling permanently burned that command. Found by writing the recovery matrix (P3-OPS-008) rather than by an incident, which is the point of writing one.

closure.summary:
STALE_CLAIM_SECONDS is fifteen minutes, chosen against the execution deadline rather than against how long a request takes: a command handed to Hermes carries a deadline in minutes, and a claim released before that deadline would let a second attempt run beside the first. The cost of the choice is a retry refused for a while rather than one that duplicates work.

Recovery happens inside the same BEGIN IMMEDIATE as the read, because two retries arriving together must not both conclude the claim is theirs — that is the defect P1-SEC-005 closed, and releasing a claim outside the transaction would reopen it. Only an IN_FLIGHT claim with a matching hash is recoverable: COMPLETED and CONFLICT are answers rather than claims, and a different hash under the same key is the conflict the table exists to detect.

Schema v22 adds claim_count, so a recovered claim is visible rather than looking like a first attempt — a command being retried every fifteen minutes forever would otherwise look normal.

Retaking a claim is not a promise that nothing happened; it is a statement that whoever held it is not coming back. What makes it safe is the layer below: CommandMissionLink.existing_for_command returns the mission already opened for that command rather than opening a second one, and a test drives the crash-and-retake sequence end to end to assert exactly that.
closure.residual: A crash after dispatch but before the mission was opened would be re-executed on recovery, because nothing durable records that the dispatch happened.
closure.residual_reason: The window is between the claim and the first durable write, and closing it needs a two-phase record of the dispatch itself. At-least-once with an idempotent mission link is the honest guarantee, and it is better than the alternative the defect produced, which was zero-times-forever.

findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: A notebook source mutation was certified by the notebook still existing
findings.description: P1-VERIFY-003 gave owner commands success contracts. For google.notebook.enterprise.sources.add and .sources.delete the postcondition was notebook_exists: True, because notebook_enterprise_readback was the observation that existed. Adding or deleting a source does not change whether the notebook exists, so a source mutation that silently failed satisfied the contract and the mission could reach VERIFIED_SUCCESS with the source unchanged. The provider already exposed a per-source endpoint and delete_sources used it internally; it was simply not reachable from the verifier.
findings.root_cause: The weaker observation was always available, so the stronger one was never required. The shape of the requirement was satisfied and the meaning was not.
findings.remediation: Bind the contract to the exact source identifiers and read each one back individually.
findings.impact: VAN could tell the owner it had removed a document it had not touched, with a VERIFIED_SUCCESS and a provider-readback evidence reference behind it. That is worse than no verification, because the receipt makes the claim credible.

closure.summary:
SEMANTIC REQUIREMENT: after 'delete source X from notebook N', X is independently observed to be absent from N. After 'add source X', X is observed present. Neither is satisfied by any fact about N itself.

PRODUCTION PATH: POST /v1/commands -> TypedCommandResolver -> contract_for -> CommandMissionLink.open -> MissionService.transition(VERIFIED_SUCCESS) -> VerifierRegistry['notebook-source-readback'] -> notebook_source_readback -> KnowledgeRuntime.notebook_enterprise_source_get -> the provider's per-source GET.

AUTHORITATIVE POSTCONDITION: the exact source list, stated as `sources_present` and `sources_absent` in full rather than as a count — a count is satisfied by the right number of the wrong sources.

`notebook-source-readback` is a separate registered strategy rather than a branch inside api-readback, and its observer raises when the contract names no sources instead of falling back to the notebook. That fallback is how the defect would re-enter through the adapter after being fixed in the contract, and a mutation adding it survived the suite until a test existed for a path the command layer cannot currently reach.

Evidence references cite the sources, not the notebook: an auditor following `provider-readback://notebook/nb-7` on a source deletion would be pointed at the object that was not the subject of the claim.

NEGATIVE AND ADVERSARIAL TESTS: a delete that did nothing cannot succeed; a partial delete is not a success; an unreachable provider is not a deletion; the evidence names the sources; no source action may rest on notebook_exists, asserted over the whole family rather than the one case found. Six mutations, six caught.
closure.residual: A create action still has no contract, because the provider assigns the identifier after the command is accepted. Post-execution contract enrichment is not built.
closure.residual_reason: Binding a created resource's identity back into the mission contract after execution is a real architectural step and is the right next one; it is not a place to guess. Until it exists a create completes unverified and says so, which is the honest state rather than a contract pointed at nothing.
closure.falsified_by: A mission reaching VERIFIED_SUCCESS for a source add or delete while the named source is in the opposite state at the provider; or any source contract whose postconditions can be satisfied without reading the sources.

findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: Every non-verified terminal mission was recorded as a strategy failure
findings.description: MissionService passed `state is VERIFIED_SUCCESS` as a boolean and StrategyLearning.record_outcome incremented failure_count whenever it was False. So UNVERIFIABLE, CANCELLED, BLOCKED_POLICY, BLOCKED_UNSAFE, EXPIRED and PARTIAL_SUCCESS all recorded as evidence that the approach does not work. A policy refusal is a statement about authority, a cancellation is the owner changing their mind, and UNVERIFIABLE explicitly means VAN does not know. The code comments said as much and the implementation contradicted them.
findings.root_cause: A boolean where the domain has three values. UNKNOWN was collapsed into FAILURE because the type had nowhere else to put it.
findings.remediation: Classify terminal states into SUCCESS / FAILURE / INCONCLUSIVE and let only the first two move the counters promotion and demotion read.
findings.impact: auto_demote fires below a 60% success rate over three runs, so three owner cancellations would have demoted a strategy that had never once failed. Promotion needs eval evidence and ten runs while demotion needs neither, which makes that damage cheap to do and expensive to undo.

closure.summary:
SEMANTIC REQUIREMENT: only evidence that says something about the quality of an approach may change the record of that approach's quality.

PRODUCTION PATH: MissionService.transition (terminal) -> LearningFeed.record_strategy_outcome(state=...) -> STRATEGY_OUTCOME classification -> StrategyLearning.record_outcome(outcome=...) -> success_count / failure_count / inconclusive_count -> promote / auto_demote / preferred_for -> /v1/strategies.

Schema v23 adds inconclusive_count so an inconclusive run is recorded rather than discarded: a strategy that keeps being cancelled is worth seeing and is not one that keeps failing. It is excluded from `runs` and from `success_rate` on purpose — including it either way would make VAN's blind spots look like evidence.

DOWNSTREAM CONSUMERS AUDITED: promote() and auto_demote() both compute over success + failure and were already correct once the third counter existed; /v1/strategies reports all three and states that inconclusive counts toward neither.

One of the original tests asserted `failure_count == 1` for an UNVERIFIABLE mission — it pinned the defect rather than catching it. It is replaced, and the replacement is parameterised over every terminal state rather than the one that was found, plus an end-to-end test that ten cancellations cannot demote a strategy with a clean record. Five mutations, five caught.
closure.residual: PARTIAL_SUCCESS is classified INCONCLUSIVE, so a strategy that half-works accumulates no verdict either way.
closure.residual_reason: A partial success is real information about the world and not a clean verdict on the approach. Splitting it would need per-postcondition attribution — which postcondition failed and whether that step is the strategy's — and guessing is how this finding happened.
closure.falsified_by: Any terminal state other than VERIFIED_SUCCESS or FAILED changing success_count or failure_count; or a strategy's promotion state changing on runs that were refused, cancelled, expired or unverifiable.

findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: The voice guard mirrored minSdk, and a missing recognizer was reported as a Sherpa tier
findings.description: Two defects in the P1-VOICE-002 closure. assertVoiceRuntimeIsShippable read the on-device floor from the policy source but mirrored minSdk into its own constant, so lowering defaultConfig.minSdk without touching the mirror left the assembly guard passing on an unshippable build — while the commit claimed the guard could not drift. And VoiceRecognitionPolicy returned SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED both for the designed API 26-30 tier and for a supported device with no recognizer installed, although its own documentation said it distinguished them.
findings.root_cause: A value mirrored instead of derived, and a documented distinction the code did not make.
findings.remediation: Read minSdk from defaultConfig, and return an honest unavailable state with a reason where the device has no recognizer.
findings.impact: A future minSdk lowering would ship an APK that installs where VAN can never hear, with the guard green. And an owner whose speech service was disabled was told they needed a runtime VAN deliberately does not ship — an answer they can do nothing with.

closure.summary:
SEMANTIC REQUIREMENT: the build refuses any configuration where a supported device cannot reach a recognition backend that exists, and the runtime tells the owner the truth about their specific device.

The guard now reads `android.defaultConfig.minSdk` and the policy's own source. Neither value is mirrored, so there is one source of truth for each and no second constant to drift.

The policy returns UNAVAILABLE with an `unavailableReason` where the API level is supported and no recognizer is installed, and keeps SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED for the designed sub-31 tier. The reason names the thing the owner can actually change. Supporting an API level is not a claim that voice works on a device, and a test says so directly so the minSdk raise cannot be read back as one.

NEGATIVE TESTS: every API from 31 to 36 without a recognizer must be UNAVAILABLE with a reason; every API with one must carry no reason. 269 Kotlin tests pass.
closure.residual: The guard's execution within the real release task graph is asserted by parsing the Gradle file, not by running an assemble: the Android Gradle Plugin cannot be fetched in this environment.
closure.residual_reason: dl.google.com is blocked by the proxy, so no AGP task graph can be resolved here. Proving the release task actually executes the guard is Gate 1 work and stays open until an Android build runs.
closure.falsified_by: An assemble or bundle succeeding with minSdk below the policy's on-device floor and no Sherpa runtime; or a device on a supported API with no recognizer being told it needs Sherpa.

findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.title: Every command became a standing owner intent
findings.description: LearningFeed.record_mission_opened put every mission goal into IntentContinuityGraph with no lifecycle distinction, so a one-off request such as 'what is on my calendar' became an ACTIVE long-term objective until the ninety-day stale sweep. §77's value is surfacing a newer instruction that contradicts an older standing goal; a graph full of transient commands gives that detection things to contradict genuine goals with.
findings.root_cause: Mission history and owner intent were the same store with no horizon between them.
findings.remediation: Introduce EPHEMERAL / PROJECT / STANDING and require evidence to promote, recording what promoted each.
findings.impact: The owner model would fill with noise that looks like evidence, and artificial conflicts between errands and objectives would surface as things for the owner to resolve.

closure.summary:
SEMANTIC REQUIREMENT: a request VAN was given once is recorded as a request, and becomes an objective only on evidence that it is one.

Schema v24 adds horizon, observation_count, promoted_reason and promoted_at_ms. Everything starts EPHEMERAL — not 'unless it looks important', because VAN cannot tell an objective from an errand by reading one sentence and a rule that tried would promote whichever phrasing it liked.

Two things promote. The owner declaring it, which needs no corroboration because it is not VAN's inference. Or three separate observations, chosen because two is a coincidence; a goal arriving with a project reaches PROJECT on the second. Every promotion records what caused it, and the two reasons stay distinguishable so VAN's own counting cannot read as something the owner said.

PROVENANCE: the count is of owner-issued commands, and nothing else writes to this graph, so repetition here cannot be VAN agreeing with itself.

/v1/understanding/intents reports standing and one-off requests separately, with the promotion rule, so the two are not one list again at the presentation layer.

The no-demotion invariant is asserted as a property over every combination rather than as an example: two separate guards enforce it and each is redundant with the other, so a mutation of either survived an example-shaped test. An invariant held by coincidence between two conditions is one refactor from being lost. Five mutations caught; the sixth required removing both guards, which the property test catches.
closure.residual: Nothing sets owner_declared_standing yet: there is no owner surface for saying 'this is a standing goal', so promotion happens only by repetition.
closure.residual_reason: The parameter exists and is tested so the path is ready, and inventing a phrase detector to populate it would be the inference this finding is about. An owner surface for declaring an objective is product work, not closure work.
closure.falsified_by: A goal reaching STANDING from a single observation without an owner declaration; or a standing goal appearing in the same list as a one-off request on the owner surface.

findings.title: CI never ran on the branch doing the certifying
findings.description: van-ci triggers on push to main and on pull_request. Every closure in this programme lands on claude/van-system-audit-ysgtcd with no pull request open, so the workflow had zero runs against any of it. The test counts in the commit messages were developer-local evidence, and nothing distinguished them from CI certification.

findings.remediation: Trigger on claude/** as well as main, and keep the installer template in step.

closure.summary:
The push trigger now includes claude/**, and the installer template is re-synced so the byte-equality contract test still holds. A gate that does not run on the head being certified is not a gate.

This is recorded as repository-complete rather than evidenced because the run itself is external: the workflow will fire on the next push to this branch, and until a run exists against a specific commit SHA, every closure in this programme is implementation-complete and CI-uncertified. Those are different states and this register does not merge them.
closure.residual: No workflow run exists for any commit on this branch yet, so no closure in this programme carries independent CI certification.
closure.residual_reason: GitHub Actions runs on GitHub. The trigger is fixed here; whether a run happens, and whether it passes, is observable only after the push and is not something this repository can assert about itself.

findings.title: A contract test passed locally and failed in CI on the first run that reached it
findings.description: tests/contracts/test_device_telemetry_contract.py imported backend.van_gateway.observability.instruments. backend/ has no __init__.py, so that path resolves only when the repository root is on sys.path. `python -m pytest` puts the working directory there; the bare `pytest` binary, which is what the workflow runs, does not. The test therefore passed under every local invocation used during this programme and failed the moment CI first ran against the branch.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: An import that depended on the invocation rather than on the configured path, and a local verification habit that never exercised the other invocation.
findings.remediation: Import van_gateway directly, which pytest.ini's pythonpath already provides under either invocation.
findings.impact: Narrow in itself — one contract file. What it demonstrates is not narrow: local test counts were being reported as evidence for a configuration CI does not run.

closure.summary:
The import is now `van_gateway.observability`, which pytest.ini's `pythonpath = backend` provides whether or not the repository root is on sys.path. A comment at the top of the file records why the short form is the correct one, so it does not get 'fixed' back.

The wider correction is to the verification habit rather than the code. Local runs for this programme used `python3 -m pytest`, which puts the working directory on sys.path and is not what the workflow does. `PYTHONSAFEPATH=1 python3 -m pytest` reproduces CI's import shape on the same interpreter, and both suites pass under it: 1153 backend, 83 contract.

The repository's bare `pytest` is a separate uv-managed install with different packages, so its failures here are a local artefact and not a second defect — worth recording, because mistaking it for one would send the next reader after a bug that is not there.
closure.residual: Nothing enforces that local verification uses CI's import shape; it is a habit, not a gate.
closure.residual_reason: The gate that matters already exists and now runs: CI on the branch. A second local-only guard would be one more thing to keep in step with the workflow, which is the class of problem P3-OPS-010 was.
closure.falsified_by: Any test that passes under `python -m pytest` and fails under the workflow's invocation.

findings.title: The Android app did not compile
findings.description:
Four Kotlin compile errors on the branch. CommandCentreViewModel was public and exposed the internal CommandModule in three signatures — a hard Kotlin error — introduced when the Gate 10 refactor split CommandCentreActivity and made CommandModule internal without changing the view model. And VanGatewayClient.tradingAccountAction called toByteArray on the JsonObject that AccountOnboarding.requestBody returns, so the trading account-action path had never compiled either.

Nothing in this repository could detect it. The Android Gradle Plugin cannot be fetched in the development container (dl.google.com is refused by the proxy), android/verification compiles only the pure decision files and neither of these qualifies, and CI had never run on this branch because van-ci triggered on main alone. Every claim of Android progress in this programme was made against a tree that did not build.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: A refactor that changed a type's visibility without its consumers, and a call site that assumed a serialiser returned a String. Both survived because the only thing that can find them is a compiler, and no compiler had seen this code.
findings.remediation: Make the view model internal, serialise the body before writing it, and run the Android build in CI on this branch.
findings.impact: The app could not be built, so it could not be installed, so no Android finding in this programme had been demonstrated on a device or even in an APK. P3-OPS-011 is why it stayed invisible; this is what it was hiding.

closure.summary:
CommandCentreViewModel is internal, which is the right direction: the navigation surface is app-internal and nothing outside the module has business naming a screen. The trading body is serialised with toString() before it is written, rather than changing what requestBody returns — the JsonObject is what the signing helper produces and what the signature is computed over.

The guard that matters is CI, which compiles the app and now runs on this branch (P3-OPS-011). tests/contracts/test_android_compiles_at_all.py is the cheaper half: the visibility error is statically checkable, so it is caught before a push rather than three minutes into a runner, and the JsonObject call site is pinned at both ends — the caller and requestBody's return type — so the test cannot end up checking a fiction.

Writing that checker took three attempts and each failure is instructive. Looking only at column zero missed the case entirely, because the exposure is in indented *members*. Tracking the enclosing declaration's visibility fixed that and produced false positives on locals inside a top-level composable. Brace-depth tracking separates a type body from a function body and settles it. A static checker written to catch one known error is worth only as much as its handling of everything it must not flag.

One test asserts the honest limit: the verification harness does not compile either file and never claimed to, so its passing was never evidence the app builds.

CONFIRMED by run 35449312512 on 05c6514: :app:compileDebugKotlin, :app:compileDebugJavaWithJavac, :app:dexBuilderDebug, :app:mergeProjectDexDebug, :app:validateSigningDebug and :app:stripDebugDebugSymbols all succeeded. The app compiles and dexes. The run still failed, at :app:testDebugUnitTest, which is a different finding (P0-AND-013) and is itself only visible because the compile succeeded.

This finding claims compilation and nothing more. Whether the resulting APK installs and runs on the owner's device is Gate 14, tracked there and deliberately deferred to last; recording it as this finding's residual would have both overstated what is unfinished here and understated that it is a gate of its own.
closure.falsified_by: The :app:compileDebugKotlin task failing on any subsequent CI run.

findings.title: Two app-module unit tests asserted behaviour that earlier closures had changed
findings.description:
The first CI run to compile the app got as far as :app:testDebugUnitTest, where 2 of 135 tests failed. Both pinned behaviour that a previous closure in this programme deliberately changed.

DegradedModeStoreTest.liveWorkspaceReadyClearsInitialGoogleDegraded asserted that a live Google mesh clears degraded mode entirely. P1-VOICE-001 made wake_word its own subsystem, BROKEN until a model is installed, so the banner correctly stays up.

VoiceRecognitionPolicyTest.modernDeviceWithoutOnDeviceRecognizerRequiresLocalFallback asserted SHERPA_PRIMARY_REQUIRED for a supported device with no recognizer. P1-VOICE-003 changed that to UNAVAILABLE with a reason, and updated the verification harness's copy of the test but not the app module's.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Android tests that no one could run. A closure changed behaviour, the neighbouring app-module test did not, and nothing could report the contradiction because the app did not compile (P0-AND-012) and CI did not run on the branch (P3-OPS-011).
findings.remediation: Assert what is now true, and why it is the better thing to assert.
findings.impact: Both tests would have failed any Android build for months. More to the point, the verification harness's copies passing was being read as Android coverage while the shipping module's copies disagreed with the code.

Both now assert current behaviour, and in both cases the new assertion is worth more than the old one.

The degraded-mode test pins that recovery is *scoped*: Google going READY clears google and leaves the banner up while wake_word is broken. That is the whole reason subsystems are listed separately instead of reported as one health bit, and it was not asserted anywhere. A second test clears the last broken subsystem so 'stays active' cannot be mistaken for 'can never clear'.

The voice test pins that a supported device missing its recognizer is UNAVAILABLE with a reason rather than a Sherpa tier, plus that supporting an API level is not a claim voice works — asserted in the shipping module and not only in the harness, which is the drift that produced this finding.

findings.title: The offline queue could never see the network return, and said nothing
findings.description: VanApplication.startConnectivityMonitor registers a ConnectivityManager network callback, and the manifest did not declare android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE. Lint calls this an error because the call throws at runtime. Here it was wrapped in a bare runCatching { }, so it threw nothing anyone would see: the registration failed, nothing observed connectivity, and the offline queue's replay-on-recovery — the whole of P3-AND-006 — never fired. A queued command would sit until the owner sent it by hand, and no surface would say why.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: A permission-gated API called without its manifest entry, and a catch-all that turned the resulting exception into silence. Either alone would have been survivable; together they made a closed finding untrue without anything reporting it.
findings.remediation: Declare the permission, and report a failed registration through the degraded registry instead of discarding it.
findings.impact: P3-AND-006 was closed as 'the offline queue replays on connectivity recovery' and the mechanism could not work. The owner would see queued commands that never went out.

closure.summary:
ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE is declared — a normal permission, granted at install and never prompted, so there is no runtime request to add.

The second half matters more. The registration result is now bound and a failure marks the queue subsystem BROKEN with a sentence the owner can act on: queued commands wait for them to send rather than going out on their own. The degraded registry exists so VAN says which parts of itself are not working, and a capability that quietly does not exist is worse than one that fails loudly.

The neighbouring sweep asked the more useful question — not 'what other permission is missing', which lint answers across the whole platform, but 'where else is a failure swallowed into silence'. Eleven discarded-result sites exist and ten are teardown: unregisterReceiver, removeView, updateViewLayout, AudioRecord stop and release. Swallowing there is correct, because nothing useful can be done and a throw during teardown is worse. This was the only one on a *setup* path, where the result decides whether a feature exists at all.

tests/contracts/test_android_permissions_match_the_apis_used.py guards the family rather than the instance: permission-gated APIs the app actually calls, checked against the manifest. One mutation survived the first run — dropping the `val registered =` binding left `registered.isFailure` in the source referring to nothing, which my string assertions accepted and only the compiler would have rejected. A static check that leans on the compiler to make it honest is measuring the wrong thing, so the binding is asserted too. Four mutations, four caught.

CONFIRMED in part by run 35451735330 on e64379e, the first fully green run on this branch: :app:lintDebug passed, which is the authority this closure named for the permission. MissingPermission is gone. That settles the manifest half and nothing more — lint reads the manifest against the call sites, it does not observe a phone losing and regaining a network.
closure.residual: That the queue actually drains when a phone regains connectivity. The permission itself is now proven by lint.
closure.residual_reason: Lint has confirmed the manifest declares what ConnectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback requires (run 35451735330). What remains is a real device making a real network transition with queued commands pending — Gate 14 work, and not something any static check or JVM test can stand in for.
closure.falsified_by: :app:lintDebug reporting MissingPermission again, or a queued command failing to replay on a device after connectivity returns with the queue subsystem reported healthy.

findings.title: CI assembled an APK and then deleted it
findings.description:
Run 35451735330 is the first fully green run on this branch: :app:testDebugUnitTest, :app:assembleDebug and :app:lintDebug all passed. assembleDebug writes android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk, and the workflow uploaded preview images and a latency JSON but not that. The APK was destroyed with the runner workspace.

So the only machine in the programme that can build the Android app produced a build nobody could obtain. findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: The Android job was written while it could not get past compilation, so what to do with a successful build was never a live question. It became one the moment the job went green, and nothing was watching for that.
findings.remediation: Upload the debug APK as a workflow artifact, with if-no-files-found: error so a run that stops producing one fails rather than publishing an empty artefact.
findings.impact: Gate 14 could not begin. Every ENVIRONMENT_UNVERIFIED residual waiting on a physical device was blocked behind an artefact that existed for four minutes and was thrown away.

closure.summary:
The workflow now uploads android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/*.apk as van-debug-apk, with if-no-files-found: error. That setting is the part worth arguing for: an empty artefact named van-debug-apk is worse than no artefact, because the owner downloads it, finds nothing, and cannot tell whether the build stopped producing an APK or the upload points somewhere wrong.

tests/contracts/test_the_apk_leaves_ci.py guards it, and the interesting problem was writing a path assertion that does not merely agree with itself. Asserting that the workflow contains the path I put in the workflow proves nothing. So the path is tied to facts outside my belief: the module segment must be a real directory with a build.gradle.kts, that module must be the one settings.gradle.kts includes as :app — the name in the Gradle invocation CI runs — and it must apply com.android.application, because a library module emits an AAR and the path would be a fiction. A test also asserts no APK is committed anywhere: the repository ignores *.apk, and a checked-in binary would not be evidence that the current tree builds.

Both workflow copies were changed together; test_ci_workflow_is_what_it_claims.py already fails on drift, since install_github_workflow.py --apply would otherwise delete the step.

CONFIRMED by run 35452683328 on 62b42b1: van-debug-apk published, 30,821,691 bytes, sha256 80c7d48be8df99273d45a0615a61e61a97d62f1a37a146e75f7e85ed94b723ff, retained until 2026-12-18. Gate 14 now has an artefact to install, which it did not before this commit.

findings.title: §15's gate had no producer, no consumer and no door
findings.description:
CriticalReasoningKernel.assert_safe_for_irreversible_work implements §15 — irreversible work waits until a mission's HIGH or CRITICAL assumptions are settled. It had no production caller. record_assumption, which is the only way the ledger it reads gets a row, also had no production caller. And there was no runtime route through which Hermes — the only system that does the reasoning an assumption comes from — could have supplied one.

Three absences that each look small and together made the mechanism unreachable. The assumption_ledger table was referenced in production by exactly one thing: the retention sweep that prunes it.

Separately, resolve_assumption demanded evidence for VERIFIED only. FALSIFIED, EXPIRED and SUPERSEDED all clear ACTIVE and all were settable by assertion, so the actor the gate restrains could record a CRITICAL assumption and clear it a moment later with nothing to show.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: The kernel was built as a library for a caller that was never written, and the caller could not have been written because the ingress did not exist. Nothing in the repository could notice: the code is correct, tested, and imports cleanly.
findings.remediation: Give Hermes the routes, enforce the gate where irreversible work is requested, and make clearing an assumption cost what the claim being made costs.
findings.impact: VAN would carry out an irreversible action — deleting an enterprise notebook, deleting sources — while its own planner held an unsettled critical assumption about whether it had the right target. The mechanism designed to stop exactly that could not run.

closure.summary:
Three things, because wiring the consumer alone would have produced a gate that can never fire — a placeholder wearing a check's clothes.

**The door.** POST /v1/runtime/reasoning/assumptions records one, GET /v1/runtime/reasoning/assumptions/{mission_id} lists what is blocking so a planner can find out before it is refused rather than by being refused, and POST /v1/runtime/reasoning/assumptions/{id}/resolve clears one. Internal-control, because an assumption is a statement about a plan and that is the runtime's to make; it is emphatically not a statement about the owner, which P0-COG-001 keeps on the owner's side.

**The enforcement point.** /v1/runtime/actions/begin, not the orchestrator's authorization path. Assumptions are recorded during planning, which happens after the orchestrator has handed the mission over, so a check at authorize time would always find an empty ledger and always pass — green, and worthless. The descriptor decides what is irreversible, and UNDECLARED is treated as irreversible, matching the descriptor's own stated reasoning. An irreversible action arriving with no mission is refused rather than exempted: that is either a bug or a path around the ledger, and neither is the thing to wave through.

**The price of clearing one.** Falsifying is verifying with the opposite sign and it is the direction that unblocks work, so it needs evidence too. SUPERSEDED must name the replacement, on the same mission, not itself — the difference between a correction and a deletion — and a test asserts that superseding a blocker with another blocker leaves the work blocked, because otherwise 'supersede it with something trivial' is the way through. EXPIRED is not a claim at all but the passage of time, so it is the kernel's to decide on the clock and not a caller's to assert. Migration 26 stores the supersession link.

Along the way, P1-COH-003's own claim turned out to be false. The authority map states that the descriptor's gate 'is the gate the orchestrator applies', and gate_for had no production caller — the orchestrator branched on `== ActionClass.A4` and `== A5` directly. They agreed, because both derive from the action class, but nothing made them agree. The orchestrator now asks. Worse, the test guarding it asserted that the orchestrator *contains* the hardcoded comparison, so it pinned the duplication as proof of agreement and failed when the duplication was removed. A test that fails when a finding is fixed was testing the finding; it now asserts derivation and that no second copy exists.
