Twelve mutations, twelve caught. One of my own defects was caught by a test rather than by review: expire_assumptions took its count from Store.execute, which returns None, so it reported zero rows expired whatever it did.
closure.residual: Nothing records an assumption in this repository. The routes exist and the gate enforces, and both are exercised end to end by tests driving the real ingress, but the reasoning that produces an assumption is a model pass and the gateway performs none.
closure.residual_reason: Hermes is not in this repository. assess() takes assumptions as an input rather than deriving them, which is the correct division — the gateway owns canonical state and performs no inference. Until Hermes calls these routes the ledger stays empty and the gate passes everything, which is the honest behaviour for a gate with nothing recorded against it, not a gate that is switched off.
closure.falsified_by: An irreversible action executing through /v1/runtime/actions/begin while its mission holds an ACTIVE HIGH or CRITICAL assumption; resolve_assumption clearing a blocker without evidence or a named replacement; or the orchestrator re-deriving its gate from the action class instead of from gate_for.

findings.title: The owner's own statements went stale on a clock, into a state nothing could clear
findings.description:
`resolve_requirement` applied a requirement's `max_age_ms` to every fact regardless of where it came from, so a preference the owner stated three years ago and never changed resolved STALE.

Staleness asks whether VAN should go and look again. That is a sensible question about something VAN observed and an incoherent one about something the owner said, because there is nowhere to look — only the owner can refresh it. So STALE on a CANONICAL_OWNER fact is a readiness state the system cannot exit: no re-observation clears it, and the requirement depending on it is permanently unsatisfiable.

The rule forbidding this was already written down, and tested, on the `Claim` type in epistemics/models.py — a taxonomy that component ledger entry 2 recorded as IMPLEMENTED_BUT_ISOLATED with disposition DELETE, and which reconciliation.py says plainly no table ever stored. So the rule existed, passed its tests, and enforced nothing. Deleting the dead taxonomy without noticing would have removed the only statement of it in the repository.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Two taxonomies for the same idea, one live and one aspirational. The live one (`EpistemicState` on `owner_facts`) had the storage and the traffic; the aspirational one (`SemanticClass` on `Claim`) had the rules and the tests. Each looked complete from inside itself.
findings.remediation: Delete the taxonomy nothing stored, and carry its rules into the one that does.
findings.impact: A requirement with a max age over an owner preference blocks its command forever. More broadly, VAN forgetting what the owner told it because time passed is the specific failure the epistemic ladder exists to prevent — owner authority does not decay.

closure.summary:
`_NOT_STALE_ON_A_CLOCK` exempts CANONICAL_OWNER and PROJECT_TRUTH from `max_age_ms`, and only those two: a fact VAN observed must still go stale, or the parameter means nothing and the exemption is a way of never checking anything. Both directions are mutation-tested.

Non-expiry is not immortality, and that distinction is what makes the exemption safe. An owner statement that is genuinely time-bound — 'my flight is at six' — carries `valid_until_ms`, the owner scoping their own claim, and `current_candidates` honours it before staleness is ever reached. A test pins that, because without it the exemption would mean VAN believes a one-off forever, which is the opposite failure and just as bad.

The dead taxonomy is gone: `Claim`, `Provenance`, `AdmissionOutcome`, `AdmissionVerdict` and `DEFAULT_TTL_MS`, 86 lines, entries 2 and 4 in the component ledger, both dispositioned DELETE. `SemanticClass`, `FORBIDDEN_SELF_PROMOTIONS` and `may_promote` stay, because P2-COG-002 wired them into fact admission and they are enforced on every write.

Its other rule went the same way rather than being dropped. §41's 'provenance on 100% of non-owner facts' was a `is_wellformed` property reporting on claims nobody stored; in the live taxonomy it is not a check at all, because `source_ref` is required by `OwnerFactCandidate` and NOT NULL on the table, so a fact without provenance cannot be constructed. The test now asserts the constructor refuses it — 'the rule moved from a check to a structural constraint' being exactly the sort of claim that should be executed rather than believed.

Three mutations, three caught.
closure.falsified_by: A CANONICAL_OWNER or PROJECT_TRUTH fact resolving STALE on `max_age_ms`; an observed fact no longer resolving STALE when it exceeds one; or a fact whose `valid_until_ms` has passed still resolving CURRENT.

findings.title: The component ledger understated by twenty-two, and nothing could notice
findings.description:
component_ledger.json records what should exist and work; findings.json records what was wrong. The closure programme worked the second to zero and left the first frozen at Gate 0. By the end it listed 65 of 142 components as unfinished, 35 of them dispositioned WIRE — written, often tested, supposedly reached by nothing.

Twenty-two of those were done. MissionService is constructed in app.py and was recorded IMPLEMENTED_BUT_ISOLATED. VerifierRegistry is built by build_mission_registry and was recorded TEST_ONLY. WakeCoordinator is constructed in VanApplication and was recorded NEVER_CONSTRUCTED. Each was closed by a finding that updated findings.json and not this file.

The maturity gate could not catch it, and is not at fault. It checks that claims are *backed*: a component asserting INTEGRATED_AND_EVIDENCED must name its producer, consumer, caller, tests and runtime evidence. A component claiming to be unreached asserts nothing, so there is nothing to back. Understating is invisible to a gate built to catch overstating — and I quoted the 65 to the owner as a measure of remaining work before checking any of it.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Two registers on two axes, one of them hand-maintained, and a gate that only looks one way. Nothing made updating the second register a condition of closing a finding.
findings.remediation: A checker that asks the source whether each unreachability claim is still true, run in CI, plus the evidence for the components it proves were already integrated.
findings.impact: '65 of 142 components unfinished' is the number anyone would quote to decide how much system is left. It was wrong by a third, in the direction that makes the work look bigger than it is — which is the less dangerous direction and still not the truth.

closure.summary:
tools/ci/ledger_reconcile.py asks the source, for every component that claims nothing reaches it and names the symbols to look for, whether that is still true. It runs in CI beside the maturity gate and covers the direction the gate cannot.

Twenty-two components moved to INTEGRATED_AND_EVIDENCED with evidence derived from the source rather than asserted — consumers and test files found by search, the CI run that executed them as runtime evidence. The gate refused to take them on anything less, which is what it is for.

Two came out differently and are the more interesting result. WakeAcknowledgementManager.play and TtsOutputManager.speak are called from VanApplication and no test names either. Integrated would have claimed evidence that does not exist; NEVER_CALLED was false. They are CALLED_UNTESTED, which is deliberately not a terminal state.

The tool's own limits are in it rather than around it. A reference from dead code is not integration: MissionParsing is called by MissionRepository, which nothing constructs, and the first run read that as alive — so a component may exclude files that are themselves unreached, and entry 45 does, which is why the eighteen dead gateway reads stay dead. An entry with no reachability_symbols is reported unverifiable rather than assumed correct, because a conceptual component like 'Compose state restoration' has no symbol to grep for and a confident wrong answer is worse than an acknowledged gap.

Six mutations, six caught, and three of them took three attempts to make fail. The tool's two test-exclusion rules overlap on every file in this repository, so any fixture driven through the search satisfies both and a mutation removing either survived. Splitting the predicate out made them separable; the filename rule turns out to decide only the case of a test_ module at the top of a search root, since any nested one already contains '/test'. A guard that cannot be falsified is a guard nobody knows is broken.

43 components remain non-terminal, and that number is now checked rather than remembered.
closure.falsified_by: A component whose maturity class asserts it is unreached while a production file outside its own module and outside tests names its declared symbols; or a component at INTEGRATED_AND_EVIDENCED that names no tests.

findings.title: Six Google capabilities had a transport, a service method and no way in
findings.description:
gmail_draft, calendar_agenda, calendar_reschedule, drive_search, contacts_resolve and tasks_list were implemented end to end in google/transport.py and google/service.py, exercised by their own tests, and reachable from no route. The mesh reported them as capabilities. The component ledger carried three separate NO_ROUTE entries against them.

Separately, §71's assess_premise had the same shape one layer over: a complete implementation, a metric reading from it, and no ingress through which the system that does the reasoning could record a row. sycophancy_metrics reported 'unmeasured', which was the honest answer and still meant nobody could tell whether VAN was agreeing with its owner fluently.
findings.requirement: docs/GOOGLE_INTELLIGENCE_MESH.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Both layers were built outward from the transport and stopped before the route. Nothing checked that a capability the mesh advertises can actually be invoked, so the gap was invisible from every direction except a reachability sweep.
findings.remediation: Route them, at the scope their neighbours already use.
findings.impact: A capability whose only caller is its own test is not a capability the owner has. VAN advertised drafting, agenda, rescheduling, Drive search, contact resolution and tasks and could perform none of them.

closure.summary:
Six routes, each mirroring gmail_search: internal control at the GOOGLE scope, and GoogleAuthError to 503 because an absent credential is VAN being unable rather than the caller being wrong — a distinction the audit repeatedly found collapsed, and one that sends the owner to entirely different places.

The route list was held twice, in `control_scope_for` and in the guard beside it, and adding six paths to one and not the other would have been a hole rather than an inconsistency: an unscoped route falls through to owner-device authentication, so a paired phone could read the owner's Drive. That is the fall-through P0-SEC-001 closed. There is now one frozenset with two readers.

Rescheduling is the only mutating route of the six and is refused without the owner's approval before the transport is consulted — otherwise a missing Google credential would 503 first and hide that the approval was never checked. Drafting deliberately is not gated that way: a draft leaves something the owner can read and discard, and gating it like a send trains them to approve without reading.

§71's ingress went in beside the assumption routes. `agreed_without_evidence` is derived by the kernel and absent from the request body, so a caller cannot mark its own agreement well-founded — tested by sending the flag and asserting it is ignored. Agreeing with an OWNER_PREFERENCE is not counted, because §67 says owner preference is not a claim about the world and counting it would make the rate fire on VAN doing exactly what it should.

Seven mutations, seven caught. One needed the compound form: the tasks route's handler-level guard and its scope-set entry each refuse alone, so neither is falsifiable by itself — the third time in this session that overlapping protection hid which half was load-bearing.
closure.residual: The routes are reachable and refuse correctly without a credential. That they return the owner's real mail, calendar, Drive, contacts and tasks is unobserved.
closure.residual_reason: There is no Google credential in this environment and no live transport to exercise. The tests drive every route through create_app and assert the boundary and the failure mode; what the provider returns is the provider's, and asserting it here would mean asserting a fake.
closure.falsified_by: A Google route outside GOOGLE_CONTROL_ROUTES; rescheduling succeeding without approved=true; or a GoogleService method with no route.

findings.title: Three owner surfaces existed as data layers with no screen
findings.description:
MissionRepository is 371 lines whose own docstring calls it 'the only place the surfaces get data', and no production file constructed it. Eighteen VanGatewayClient reads — needsYou, missions, missionEvidence, cancelMission, messageMission, the understanding confirm/correct pair, capabilityStatus, evalReport — existed for it and were called by nothing else. The mission surfaces §§33, 35 and 48 describe were rendered nowhere, so the owner could issue a command and had no screen that would ever tell them how it went.

NotificationPolicyStore.setPolicy and setQuietHours had no caller either, which is worse than a missing screen: VanNotificationListenerService reads the policy on every arriving notification and mutes, prioritises or drops accordingly, so the mechanism was live and running while every app stayed NORMAL forever and quiet hours were permanently off. VAN holds a notification-listener grant, among the most invasive Android gives, and the controls that make it tolerable existed only as functions.

PersonalSpeechModel.recordCorrection and pinTerm had no caller. The model is read on every voice turn to prime the recogniser and rewrite the transcript, and nothing could put a word into it, so VAN would mishear the same name every day forever.

Compose state restoration was ABSENT across the app.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: Each layer was built from the data outward and stopped before the screen. The Gate 10 refactor split CommandCentreActivity into modules and carried over the screens that existed; it had no way to notice the three that never did.
findings.remediation: Build the screens, and call the functions that were dead.
findings.impact: The owner had no view of their own work, no control over a notification listener reading everything on their phone, and no way to teach VAN a word it mishears.

closure.summary:
Three screens, each wired into CommandModule and rendered by CommandCentreActivity.

**Work** renders the gateway's own status rather than deriving one: MissionSummary.ownerStatus prefers ownerStatusFromGateway and falls back to UNKNOWN, never to a working state, which is what P0-EXEC-003 found painting unverified outcomes in the working colour. It separates waiting from running, because a mission in WAITING_FOR_OWNER is not progressing and listing it among the active ones tells the owner VAN is busy when it is in fact stuck on them. And it states the verification rather than implying it by absence — §6's distinction between done, partly done and finished-but-unconfirmed reaches the screen instead of being flattened into a tick.

**Notifications** lists apps the owner has already decided about rather than every installed package: enumerating those needs QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, which Play treats as sensitive and VAN does not need. An app reaches the list because a notification from it did, which needed a new `decidedPackages()` on the store — it could be written to and read per package and could not say what it held.

**Speech** passes no trust argument, so recordCorrection's OWNER_CONFIRMED default applies. That is deliberate and is why this is a screen rather than something inferred from a retry: a model that teaches itself from its own second guess learns its own mistakes.

All three use rememberSaveable for the state a rotation would otherwise lose — the open mission, a half-typed package name, a half-typed correction. Losing that reads as VAN forgetting.

Six mutations, six caught, after three survived a first pass. Those three all had the same cause: the assertions named a function rather than a binding, so `store.setPolicy(` was satisfied by either of two call sites and `rememberSaveable` by any one of four fields. A presence check on a name that appears more than once tests almost nothing.

Three existing contract tests failed when this landed, and all three were right to. They encoded 'MissionRepository is dead' — an allowlist entry, a ledger cross-check and an excludes assertion — and this made it alive. The allowlist entry is gone, which is exactly what `test_every_explained_entry_still_describes_something_real` exists to force; the excludes assertion moved to a synthetic ledger, because pinning a mechanism to a real row meant the test failed when the row was fixed.

CONFIRMED by run 35463788324 on bfc9f41: :app:compileDebugKotlin, :app:testDebugUnitTest, :app:assembleDebug and :app:lintDebug all passed with the three screens in the tree. That settles that they compile and that lint has no objection; whether they render and are usable is Gate 14's.
closure.residual: No run has compiled these yet, and no screen has been rendered on a device. The contract tests assert the wiring, not that Compose lays it out.
closure.residual_reason: The Android Gradle Plugin cannot be fetched in this container, so Compose cannot be compiled locally at all — CI is the authority, as it has been for every Android claim in this programme. That these screens render correctly, and are usable, is Gate 14's.
closure.falsified_by: :app:compileDebugKotlin failing on these files; a CommandModule entry with no render branch; or any of the previously-dead calls disappearing from the screen that makes them.

findings.title: Every component reconciled to a terminal state, or named as blocked and why
findings.description:
After P2-LEDGER-001 moved twenty-two components the reconciler proved stale, 43 remained non-terminal. Working them one at a time found that most were not unfinished work at all: they were entries written at Gate 0 whose dispositions had been overtaken, or capabilities whose missing piece is not in this repository and never will be.

Six dispositions were simply wrong by the time they were read. QueueReplayer was PARTIAL pending 'trigger on connectivity and health recovery' and has had all five triggers since P1-AND-014 and P3-AND-006. The five hardcoded-healthy subsystems have had a writer since P3-AND-004. Owner signature verification was STUB, describing code P0-TRADE-001 replaced with a real verifier over a signed subject. FORBIDDEN_SELF_PROMOTIONS was IMPLEMENTED_BUT_ISOLATED and has been enforced on every fact admission since P2-COG-002.

Three were dispositioned DELETE on the belief they were dead. All three are constructed in production: the COLD tier twice in automation/api.py, the computer-use fabric in automation/health.py, and the Temporal routing branch is not absent but explicit — it returns a decision carrying its own reason, that Temporal is stack-locked at adoption phase 11 and a native state machine should be used until it is. Deleting any of them would have removed a refusal along with the capability it refuses.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: A register written once and read as current. Rule 31 asks for exactly this sweep and asks for it early; doing it last meant forty-three entries had to be re-derived from source rather than maintained as the work happened.
findings.remediation: Adjudicate every entry against the source and record the verdict with its reason.
findings.impact: The component ledger is the register that says how much system is left. Read as written it said a third of VAN was unbuilt.

closure.summary:
142 of 142 components carry a terminal state. Six are INTEGRATED_AND_EVIDENCED with evidence derived from source, three are DELIBERATELY_REMOVED with a removal assertion the gate checks, and twenty-two are EXTERNALLY_BLOCKED_REPOSITORY_COMPLETE, each naming the specific thing that is absent: a keyword-spotting model owner decision 2 declined, an unauthored .riv asset, an n8n harness, a Stagehand runtime, a VEKL endpoint, an Obsidian vault, Exa egress the owner switched off, a live market feed, a Postgres instance, a device that can play a sound or speak.

Writing those reasons is the work, not the classification. 'Externally blocked' with no named artefact is a way of saying 'not done' that sounds finished, and the audit found that phrasing repeatedly.

Two of my own mechanisms turned out to be wrong while being used.

The maturity gate's `symbols_absent` assertion matched `def` and `fun` only, so a component asserting a deleted *class* would have passed by never matching anything — a gate agreeing with you because it was looking for the wrong thing. It recognises classes and Kotlin objects now, and a mutation restoring the deleted class is caught.

Three contract tests failed on this change and each was right to. One picks the first component whose file still exists and claims removal, expecting a refusal; it began passing for the wrong reason once components carried `symbols_absent`, because the fixture inherited that assertion and sent the gate to check symbols that were genuinely gone. It clears the assertion now, so it exercises the branch it names. The other two asserted a snapshot — a list of four unchecked entries, and that CALLED_UNTESTED components carry no terminal state — both true while the work was open and both forbidding it from ever closing. They assert the rule instead: no unreachability claim goes unchecked, and nothing claims evidence while no test names it.
closure.falsified_by: A component at a terminal state whose maturity class the source contradicts; an EXTERNALLY_BLOCKED component whose rationale names no specific absent artefact; or a DELIBERATELY_REMOVED component whose code is still defined.

findings.title: Every CI run signed the debug APK with a different key, and nothing recorded which
findings.description:
Android generates a debug keystore on first use and keeps it in ~/.android. A GitHub runner is a fresh machine every time, so every run of this workflow signed the APK it publishes with a key that existed only for that run.

Two consequences follow, and both bear on Gate 14, which is the owner installing VAN on their own phone. An APK from one run cannot upgrade an APK from another, and any VAN already installed refuses the next one on a signature mismatch. The dialog Android shows for that is a bare 'App not installed' with no code, which is what the owner saw on the first sideload of a CI build.

The second half is the part this register exists for: nothing in a run said what the signature was. The hypothesis could not be tested without the phone, so a diagnosable build failure was recorded as an undiagnosed device problem. That is NOT VERIFIED being reported as NOT IMPLEMENTED's opposite number, one layer out from the code.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_CONSOLIDATED_DEPLOYMENT_READINESS_CLOSURE_BLUEPRINT_REV_1.md
findings.authority: VAN Consolidated Deployment-Readiness Closure Blueprint Rev 2
findings.root_cause: P2-OPS-013 made the APK leave CI and stopped there. An artefact that is published for a person to install has a signing identity, and the workflow neither chose one nor reported the one it got.
findings.remediation: Accept an owner-supplied debug keystore before the build, validate it against the credentials Android's debug signing config actually uses, and record the certificate of the APK that is published, in the artefact.
findings.impact: The owner could not install the build, and the run that produced it gave them nothing to diagnose it with.

closure.summary:
Two scripts, both driven by their tests rather than asserted by a step name.

`restore_debug_keystore.sh` installs VAN_DEBUG_KEYSTORE_BASE64 at ~/.android/debug.keystore before the build, and validates it with the credentials Android's debug signing config is hardcoded to use — store password 'android', alias 'androiddebugkey'. A keystore that does not open that way is refused here rather than failing at packaging several minutes later, because the step's own log would otherwise say the owner's key was restored while the APK carried the runner's. When no secret is set it says, in the log, that this build's APK cannot upgrade one from any other run — the state every run of this programme has been in, and the reason the install failure went undiagnosed.

It deliberately does not generate or commit a key. A debug keystore in the repository would make every build upgradable, including a build made by anyone who has the repository, installed over the owner's VAN and inheriting its data directory and the token vault in it. VAN holds a notification-listener grant. A contract test refuses any committed signing material so that the short fix stays closed.

`record_apk_signing_identity.sh` writes the APK's certificate beside it and into the uploaded artefact. It refuses an apksigner output with no certificate digest rather than publishing a file that looks like evidence and contains none — the silently-empty-search shape the ledger reconciler was caught in a commit earlier.

Six mutations, six caught, one after a first attempt that survived by missing: it edited the opening line of the no-secret branch while the sentence the test pins is two lines below, so it changed nothing the test was about. A mutation that misses is not evidence in either direction.

CONFIRMED by run 35465904965 on 23e74ce, which is also the first measurement of the defect itself. With no secret set the restore step printed that this build's APK cannot upgrade one from any other run, and the identity step read the APK Android would install: V2 signer, CN=Android Debug, SHA-256 digest 57200ab86b098d1f60fb2fac381bf6d14acb9116943d13a99017978de04f7c30. That digest is the baseline — a later run printing a different one is the per-runner key, demonstrated rather than reasoned, and printing the same one would mean the hypothesis was wrong. The artefact carried two files rather than one.
closure.residual: No VAN_DEBUG_KEYSTORE_BASE64 secret exists, so runs still sign with a per-runner key and their APKs still cannot upgrade one another. And the owner's install failure remains undiagnosed: a signature mismatch fits every observation, but nobody has read the INSTALL_FAILED_* code from `adb install`. The comparison itself is one run old: run 35465904965 is the first to record a digest, so nothing has yet been compared against it.
closure.residual_reason: Supplying the key is the owner's to do and no one else's: a signing key in the repository is exactly the risk this closure declines to take, so the repository can accept a key, validate it and report it, and cannot have one. Whether a stable key fixes this particular install is Gate 14's to settle, on the device, with the code adb prints.
closure.falsified_by: Two consecutive runs with the secret set printing different certificate digests; a signing-identity.txt missing from the artefact; a keystore with the wrong alias being accepted; or an APK whose install still fails once its digest matches the installed build's.

findings.title: The owner-device binding was verified by nobody, and the status endpoint said it was bound
findings.description:
ADR-RB-025 requires every privileged owner request to prove possession of the hardware key the device was bound with. `OwnerDeviceBindingService.require_proof` implements that check correctly: it rejects a stale timestamp, a signature over a different body, a signature over a different route, and a revoked binding. It had eleven unit tests, all passing.

Nothing called it. A repository-wide search for the symbol found the definition, its tests, and no third occurrence. The ingress middleware authenticated a device token and passed the request straight to the handler, so a copied access token — the exact threat the binding exists for — reached every owner route on any machine.

The part that makes this a P0 rather than a gap is the reporting. `GET /v1/device-binding/status` answered `bound: true`, `key_security_level: STRONGBOX`, with a fingerprint and a `bound_at_ms`, for a deployment in which the binding had no effect on any request. Every signal an owner or an auditor could read said the control was in force.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md ADR-RB-025, §0D.3, §31
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The verifier and its call site were written in different checkpoints, and the checkpoint that wrote the verifier had a green suite. No gate in this repository asks whether a security check is reached: the maturity gate asks whether a component names a production caller, and this was a method on a service that has several other callers, so the component read as integrated.
findings.remediation: Enforce the proof in the ingress middleware, on the mutating owner surfaces, and test it through the ingress rather than against the verifier.
findings.impact: A stolen or copied device access token was sufficient to create browser sessions on the owner's authenticated profile, submit commands over the session surface, and close sessions the owner was using — from any machine, indefinitely, while the device-binding status endpoint reported that a hardware key was required.

closure.summary:
`requires_device_proof` names the surfaces (mutating interactive-browser routes, the session surface, and `POST /v1/commands`) and `enforce_device_proof` holds them to it, both in `van_gateway/app.py` beside the route classifier they have to agree with.

Two decisions in it are load-bearing and both were wrong first.

The gate reads `active()`, not `for_device(caller)`. The first version asked whether *the calling device* was bound, so a second paired phone that had never enrolled skipped the check entirely — the proof was mandatory only for the device that had already proved itself. It now refuses any device that is not the bound one, outright, as soon as any binding is active.

The body is read in the middleware and the route still sees it. A first version hand-rolled a replay of the receive channel on the assumption that Starlette's request stream is single-use; a mutation deleting that replay changed nothing, because `BaseHTTPMiddleware` wraps the request in a `_CachedRequest` and a body read in `dispatch` is already cached for downstream. The replay was removed rather than the mutation weakened. The regression test stayed: it asserts the created session's profile alias comes back, so a future version that does break the body is caught at the route rather than as a 422 about a missing field several layers from the cause.

Reads are deliberately not gated. A Keystore signature on every poll would put a hardware operation in the battery path for no security gain, and a test pins that a session read still works without a proof.

An unbound device still works on its token alone and `bound: false` says so; `require_device_binding` turns that fallback off for a deployment that has finished enrolling. The downgrade is stated rather than silent, which is the distinction this finding exists over.

Seven mutations. Each of them leaves `test_owner_device_binding.py` green, which is the point: the eleven tests that existed could not see any of this.
closure.residual:
This finding's defect is gateway-side — a check that nothing reached — and it is closed here: the gate is enforced in the middleware and proven through the ingress, including the counterexample of a request with no proof header.

The boundary, stated so it is not mistaken for unfinished work: the device half that produces the proof is not executed anywhere in this repository. Android Keystore, StrongBox and key attestation are device facts, and the Android Gradle Plugin is unreachable in the audit container, so CI's assembleDebug is the only thing that even compiles `OwnerDeviceIdentity`. What can be established here is that both sides build the same bytes, and that is done: the signing input and the fixed-width signature encoding are compared against vectors the gateway generated. Whether a real S24 Ultra emits an attestation chain this parser accepts is RB-120, and the Keystore behaviour is RB-103 — both device gates in the programme matrix, both unrun, neither this finding's to close.
closure.residual_reason: The gateway's failure to enforce and the phone's ability to sign are two different claims with two different gates. Folding the device gate into this finding would make a closed defect read as blocked, and leaving it unstated would let a later reader think the hardware half had been proven. It is recorded as a boundary and tracked as RB-103/RB-120.
closure.falsified_by: A privileged mutation succeeding from a bound device with no X-Van-Device-Proof header; a second paired device mutating while the owner's phone is bound; a proof captured on one route being accepted on another; or a proved route receiving an empty body.

findings.title: Opening a browser session for a Mission was a 500 on every attempt, because the capability it binds under was declared by nobody
findings.description:
§23.1 of the Remote Browser blueprint states the flow in the owner's own words: "Van, search this page and explain it" creates a Mission through the existing command path, and the interactive browser session attaches to it by reference. `MissionBinder.bind_browser_session` implements that attach, is documented, and has the right shape — it calls `_bind`, which is idempotent and never creates a Mission.

It binds under the capability id `browser.interactive.session`, a module constant in `van_gateway/mission/binding.py`. No registry declares that id. `registries/capabilities.json` declares eleven capabilities and this is not one of them, so `MissionService.add_activity`'s §7 check — "a capability not in the registry must not be routable" — raised `MISSION_CAPABILITY_NOT_PERMITTED:NOT_DECLARED` on every call.

The route did not catch it. `POST /v1/browser/interactive-sessions` called the binder unguarded whenever the body carried a `mission_id`, so the exception left the handler as an unhandled 500 — after the session row had been created and the owner's authenticated profile leased to it.

Two things hid this. The binder's own tests construct a `MissionService` with `capabilities=None`, which short-circuits the check and returns before the registry is consulted. And the interactive-session route tests never passed a `mission_id`, because the sessions they create are manual ones. So both halves were green and the path between them had never been executed.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §23.1, §23.3; VAN_SYSTEM_TRUTH §7
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A capability id used as a string in one module and declared in a JSON registry in another, with no check that the two agree. The maturity gate asks whether a component has a production caller; `bind_browser_session` has one. The authority map asks whether an invariant is owned and tested; it is. Neither asks whether the constant one of them passes is a value the other will accept, and the unit tests on both sides were configured in a way that never asked either.
findings.remediation: Declare `browser.interactive.session` in the capability registry with an honest readiness source, handle the binder's refusal at the route rather than letting it escape as a 500, unwind the session so a refused binding does not strand the owner's profile, and pin the id-to-declaration agreement with a contract test that reads the constant out of the binder's source.
findings.impact: Every command-originated browser session — the blueprint's own worked example, and the only way a browser session ever reaches the owner's Missions page — failed with a 500 and left a session holding the authenticated profile lease. The next attempt, including an ordinary manual one, was then refused as "leased" with no owner-visible reason. The feature had never worked once.

closure.summary:
Three changes, and the readiness decision in the middle is the one that matters.

`browser.interactive.session` is declared with `readiness_source: EXTERNAL_RUNTIME` and `health_probe: browser_stream_host`, not `STATIC`. STATIC would have made the 500 into a 200 in one line and would have been false: the capability is VAN driving a browser on a Stream Host, and this repository has never seen one. So a fresh deployment still refuses — with `mission_binding_refused:...NO_READINESS_EVIDENCE:browser_stream_host`, which names the missing thing — and the refusal becomes a success only when `tools/certification/certify_browser_stream_host.py` has measured a real host. Recording that a Mission used a remote browser when no remote browser has been proven to exist is exactly the unearned claim this programme exists to prevent.

The route catches the refusal and unwinds. A 409 alone would still have stranded the profile lease, which is the part the owner would actually have noticed.

The agreement is pinned rather than assumed: `tests/contracts/test_stream_host_readiness_is_earned.py` parses `INTERACTIVE_BROWSER_CAPABILITY` out of the binder's source and requires the registry to declare it, so renaming one and not the other fails instead of drifting. The same file enumerates every writer of that probe's readiness evidence and asserts the Gateway is not among them.

Counterexample checked: a version that declared the capability STATIC, or that recorded readiness evidence at startup, would pass every test about binding and activities — the session would bind, the Activity would be correct, the Mission count would be right — while VAN reported that a Mission used a browser nothing had ever verified existed. The readiness test and the writer enumeration are what fail on that version.
closure.residual: No Browser Stream Host exists, so `browser.interactive.session` resolves NOT_READY and a mission-bound interactive session is refused in any real deployment today, with `NO_READINESS_EVIDENCE:browser_stream_host` naming the missing thing. The three canaries in tools/certification/certify_browser_stream_host.py that would clear it have never been run.
closure.residual_reason: A digest can only be recorded by measuring an artefact, and the artefact is a host on the Trading Core VM that this repository cannot provision. Declaring the capability ready in order to make the path work would be the fabricated readiness the whole gate exists to prevent: VAN would record that a Mission used a remote browser nothing has ever seen.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: Six new gateway instruments would have paged the operator forever with nothing to do about it
findings.description:
`INSTRUMENT_SILENT` fires when a metric the gateway is supposed to produce has had no sample after fifteen minutes of uptime. It is scoped to `MetricSource.GATEWAY` precisely because a device metric is silent whenever no device has posted, and an alert that cannot be cleared is one operators learn to ignore.

The six interactive-browser instruments added for §28.1 are written by the Gateway, so the source is correct — and none of them can produce a sample without a Browser Stream Host, which a deployment may simply not have. A gateway with no host would have fired this rule every fifteen minutes, naming six instruments, with no action that resolves it.

Found by a test rather than in production: `test_silence_on_a_device_metric_is_not_a_fault` failed the moment the catalogue grew, which is what that test is for.

A second half, found in the same pass. The catalogue grew a third device dict, `DEVICE_COUNTERS`, beside `DEVICE_HISTOGRAMS` and `DEVICE_GAUGES`. `tests/contracts/test_device_telemetry_contract.py` — the test whose entire job is to stop the gateway's list and the phone's Kotlin enum from drifting — read two of the three. So two of §28.1's four device metrics were declared on the gateway with no phone able to post them and nothing checking, which is the same state P3-OBS-002 was about: a metric the scrape reports as unobserved forever, honestly and uselessly.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §28.1
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: `MetricSource` answers "who writes this", and the alert rule needed the answer to a different question: "must something have written it by now". For every metric before this checkpoint the two answers coincided.
findings.remediation: Add `silence_is_normal` to the metric declaration, filter `INSTRUMENT_SILENT` on it, and fence the exemption with a rule-based test so it cannot be used to quiet an instrument whose silence really is a fault.
findings.impact: A permanently-firing warning on any deployment without a Stream Host, which is every deployment today. The cost is not the alert itself but what it does to the ones that matter.

closure.summary:
`silence_is_normal` is a field on `Metric`, set on exactly the six instruments that cannot fire without a Stream Host, and `_instrument_silent` excludes them.

The exemption is fenced in both directions. One test derives the exempt set from the property — Gateway-sourced, produced by the interactive browser surface — and requires it to equal the set actually marked, so a metric joins by being that kind of metric rather than by someone adding a flag. Another asserts the rule still fires, still names `van_gateway_request_duration_ms`, and names exactly the unobserved GATEWAY metrics that are not exempt: a filter that exempted too much would pass the first test and leave the rule unable to fire at all.

Counterexample checked: marking every GATEWAY metric `silence_is_normal` satisfies "the rule does not fire on browser metrics" and would be caught by the second test, which requires the rule to fire on an empty registry.

The device half: the contract test now folds the counters in, the Kotlin `DeviceMetric` enum carries all four browser names, and `BrowserStreamTelemetry` produces them from the WebRTC video sink. A second test asserts every name in the enum is one `record_device_sample` actually ingests — the set comparison alone would pass for a name sitting in a dict the ingest function never consults, and the phone's telemetry would vanish at the route with the scrape still reporting the metric unobserved.

Writing the arithmetic's tests found a defect in it: a zero-timestamp sentinel meant every frame looked like the first on a monotonic clock starting near zero, so the fps window restarted each frame and no reading was ever emitted. Silent rather than wrong, which is the harder kind to notice on a dashboard.
closure.residual: No production scrape exists, so no alert rule in this repository has ever been evaluated against real data. The rules are exercised only against registries a test constructed. No frame has been decoded on any device either, so the four device metrics have produced no sample anywhere.
closure.residual_reason: Evaluating a threshold against real traffic needs a deployment producing it, and there is none. This is an unverified environment rather than missing work: the rule, its exemption and both directions of the exemption's boundary are implemented and executed here.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The reachability gate's comment stripper was silently blanking whole files, and reported a live class as dead
findings.description:
`tools/audit/kotlin_reachability.py` answers the question this whole programme is organised around: what does nothing production reach? Its first step removes comments and string literals, so a symbol named in a KDoc paragraph does not count as a call site — which is the right rule, and the reason the tool is worth having.

It did that with a sequence of regular expressions, comments first and strings second. A Kotlin *string* containing comment punctuation therefore closed a block comment that a KDoc had opened much earlier in the file, and the entire region between them was replaced with a single space before any reference was counted.

The string that did it is `"*/*"` — the MIME wildcard passed to `ActivityResultContracts.OpenDocument`, which is what every Android file chooser sends. Adding a file-picker call to `BrowserActivity` made the gate report `BrowserSurfaceView`, the renderer the Activity constructs forty lines later, as declared and referenced by nothing.
findings.requirement: evidence/van-system-audit/component_ledger.json; the TEST_ONLY and unreferenced maturity classes this tool assigns
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5 §0F
findings.root_cause: Two regular expressions applied in sequence to a language where the two constructs they match can contain each other. Comment-stripping and string-stripping are one problem, not two, and solving them separately means whichever runs first is wrong about the other.
findings.remediation: Replace the regex sequence with a single left-to-right scan that handles block comments (including Kotlin's nesting), line comments, raw strings and ordinary strings in one pass, and test it against the shapes that broke it.
findings.impact: The gate over-reported deadness, which is the one direction it must not be wrong in: an over-report gets acted on, and the action is deleting something that is running. Every file containing a string with comment punctuation had part of itself excluded from the analysis, so the gate's answers about those files — and about anything only they referenced — were unreliable for as long as the string was there.

closure.summary:
One scanner, one pass. It tracks whether it is inside a block comment, a line comment, a raw string or an ordinary string, and Kotlin's nesting block comments are handled because Kotlin's nest and Java's do not — a stripper that ended at the first `*/` would treat the rest of an outer comment as code and count every symbol named in it as a call site, which is the same defect in the other direction.

The ordering trap is pinned explicitly: swapping the two regexes so strings go first has the mirror bug, where a comment containing a quote eats the code after it, and there is a test for that shape so the obvious fix cannot be re-applied.

The regression is asserted against the real file rather than only against a snippet: `BrowserActivity` constructs `BrowserSurfaceView`, and the test requires the stripped text to still contain that reference.
closure.residual: The sweep remains textual and still over-reports unreachability for Compose call graphs and reflective bindings, which is stated where it prints and is why its output is labelled a worklist rather than a verdict.
closure.residual_reason: Resolving Compose and DI properly needs a Kotlin compiler plugin or a full front-end, which is a different tool from a repository sweep. The over-report is deliberate and disclosed at the point of use; what this finding was about is the *silent* failure underneath it.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The cross-language input-protocol contract compared only the kinds both sides already had
findings.description:
`tests/contracts/test_browser_input_protocol_matches.py` exists because the owner-input wire format has two implementations, in Python and in Kotlin, and a format with two implementations and no shared definition drifts silently — the symptom being taps landing in the wrong place rather than anything that looks like a bug.

Its kind comparison read both files, intersected the names, asserted there were at least nine of them, and compared the values of the shared ones. A kind present on one side and absent on the other was simply not in the intersection, so it was never compared and never missed.

Found while adding §17.2's six navigation kinds. They went into the Python implementation first; the contract test passed with the phone unable to send any of them.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §8, §17.2
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: An intersection where the contract is an equality. The test compared what the two implementations agreed about instead of comparing what each one had.
findings.remediation: Assert set equality, list the names the Python regex picks up that are not input kinds rather than filtering them with a cleverer pattern, and name the navigation kinds explicitly so the equality cannot be satisfied by both sides having none of them.
findings.impact: A kind added to one implementation alone would ship: the Gateway would accept a discriminator no phone sends, or the phone would send one the Gateway refuses as malformed. The owner would see an address bar that does nothing, with a refusal reason nothing surfaces.

closure.summary:
The comparison is now an equality, with the two non-kind names the regex also matches listed by name so that adding a member to either of those enums is a visible edit rather than a silent exclusion.

Three tests where there was one: the values of shared names still have to agree, neither side may have a name the other lacks, and §17.2's six navigation kinds are named explicitly — because the equality alone is satisfied by both sides having none of them, which is exactly the state this change was made to leave.

Two more pin the rules that travel with those kinds: both implementations refuse a navigation on the fast channel, and both refuse a scheme neither will open.
closure.residual: The two implementations are still separate code. The contract compares constants, refusal rules and header field widths; it does not execute one against the other, because the Kotlin side needs a JVM and the Python side does not run there.
closure.residual_reason: A shared generated definition would remove the class of defect entirely and is a larger change than this checkpoint: the format is already shipped and both sides are pinned by the cross-language vectors file for the byte layout. The gap left is a rule stated in two places, which is what these tests read.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: Every envelope the phone sent over the durable session was fenced, from the first connect
findings.description:
Rev 1.5 §20.10 says the path epoch is *granted* by the Gateway. `POST /v1/session/resume` implements that literally: it sets `authoritative_path_epoch = current + 1` on every accepted resume and returns it as `new_path_epoch`. `VanHermesSessionService.accept_upstream` then refuses any envelope whose `path_epoch` is not the authoritative one, with `session_path_epoch_stale`.

`VanHermesSessionManager` never read `new_path_epoch`. It took the `path_epoch` that `/open` returned and afterwards incremented a counter of its own, once per socket failure.

The device resumes on `onOpen`, before anything has failed. So on a healthy first connect the Gateway moved to epoch 2 while the phone was still stamping the 1 it had been given, and every owner message from that moment was refused — on a session both sides reported as connected, with the socket open and the status screen showing "Connected".

The local counter was independently wrong in the other direction: it agreed with the Gateway after exactly one failure and one resume, and diverged permanently after two failures before a successful resume, which is what a carrier handover on a moving train looks like.

Found by probing the running service rather than by reading either side: both halves are internally correct, and the defect exists only in the agreement between them.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.3, 20.9, 20.10, 20.12
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A number that one side grants and the other side computes. Nothing in the repository stated that the resume's answer was authoritative, and the session's only tests drove the service directly — where the client's arithmetic does not exist.
findings.remediation: Adopt `new_path_epoch` from the resume response on every outcome that keeps the session, not only inside the failover branch; delete the local increment; pin the agreement at the route with `backend/tests/test_session_transport_api.py` and across the two languages with `tests/contracts/test_session_epoch_contract.py`.
findings.impact: The durable logical session — §20's entire subject, and what the Remote Browser, the mission feed and the voice turn all bind to — carried nothing. Every command, heartbeat and cursor acknowledgement the phone sent was refused by the Gateway and silently dropped by the client, which has no branch that surfaces a routing refusal.

closure.summary:
`adoptGrantedPathEpoch` reads the Gateway's grant and is called from both resume outcomes that continue the session. The local increment is gone; the socket failure now opens a `FailoverTransaction` instead, and `promote` refuses an epoch that does not advance, so a Gateway that re-granted the current epoch cannot leave the old path believing it is still authoritative.

Eight route-level tests were added where there were none: the grant moves the epoch off `/open`'s, an envelope carrying the old one is fenced by name, an envelope carrying the granted one is admitted, and two resumes without an envelope in between still agree. Six cross-language contract tests pin the phone's half, including the one that would have caught the original shape — that the adopter runs on an ordinary resume and not only on a failover.
closure.counterexample: An implementation that adopted the grant only inside the failover branch passes every failover test and leaves the bug exactly as it was, because the first resume is not a failover. `test_the_grant_is_adopted_on_an_ordinary_resume_and_not_only_on_a_failover` reads the adopter and fails on it. An implementation that adopted it but kept the local increment passes a single-failure test and diverges on the second; `test_the_phone_does_not_mint_a_path_epoch_of_its_own` refuses the increment by name.
closure.residual: The Kotlin half is pinned by reading the source rather than by executing it: `VanHermesSessionManager.kt` imports OkHttp and is not in the `android/verification` harness, so CI's Android build is its only compiler.
closure.residual_reason: Putting the manager in the harness means giving the harness OkHttp and a socket fake, which moves the transport into the test rather than the decision out of it. The decisions that can be executed — `ResumePolicy`, `SessionEnvelope`, `FailoverTransaction` — already are.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: §27's quality controller was correct, tested and had no caller
findings.description:
`backend/van_gateway/browser/quality.py` implements the whole of §§26 and 27: the four-rung ladder, the two SLO profiles, §27.4's asymmetric hysteresis, §27.3's per-session byte accounting, and §26.2's rule that `high_quality_certified` is a property of a verdict rather than a field anyone can set. It has unit tests and they pass.

Nothing constructed one. There was no route by which a phone could report a link sample, so the Gateway never chose a rung, the Stream Host was never steered toward a target, and the owner was never shown which regime they were in. §27.2's rule that VAN must not silently consume hours of someone's mobile data was enforced by a class with no instances.

The declared metric `van_browser_quality_mode` named `record_quality_mode` as its producer, and that function did not exist.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§26.2, 27.1-27.4
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The class this programme keeps finding: logic that is right, tested and unreachable. A unit test proves a decision is correct; it cannot prove anyone asks for the decision.
findings.remediation: Add `POST /v1/browser/interactive-sessions/{id}/link-report` and `GET .../quality`, hold one controller per session for as long as the session lives, forget it when the session ends, and give `record_quality_mode` its caller.
findings.impact: A session on mobile data ran at whatever the encoder defaulted to. The owner had no indication of the regime, no per-session data figure, and no way to opt in to high quality on metered — which is the consent §27.2 requires before spending their allowance.

closure.summary:
`quality_api.py` is the caller. `QualityControllers` holds one controller per session — required rather than tidy, because §27.4's streak is state and a controller built per request would either never upgrade or upgrade on every third sample forever — and the interactive router's new `on_session_ended` hook forgets it when the session terminates, so the next session is not handed the previous owner's data figure.

`LinkReportBody` has no field for the verdict and refuses extras, so a phone that tries to certify its own session gets a 422 rather than having the claim quietly ignored.
closure.counterexample: A route that built a controller per request returns a correct-looking verdict on every call and never moves the ladder; `test_the_upgrade_streak_survives_across_reports` is the test that separates the two. A body that merely ignored `high_quality_certified` passes a field-list assertion and still lets a caller believe it set one; `test_a_body_claiming_the_certification_is_refused_not_ignored` posts it and requires a 422.
closure.residual: The target the Gateway returns is a target. Whether the Browser Stream Host adapts toward it is unobservable here, because there is no host in this repository to adapt.
closure.residual_reason: §13 makes the Stream Host an optional, separately deployed component; §6.4 keeps the Gateway out of the media path on purpose. The adaptation is the host's to implement and the owner's to deploy.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: §20.9's warm standby, §20.14's outbox metadata and §20.10's failover transaction were absent
findings.description:
§20 describes a session that survives a carrier change. Three of its mechanisms had no implementation at all.

§20.9's warm standby — a second path kept authenticated so that make-before-break is possible — existed as a sentence. So did its asymmetry: a warm path carries heartbeats and cursor reconciliation and **no duplicate command uplink**, which is the rule that stops VAN's own client producing the duplicate §20.12's admission exists to reject.

§20.14 asks the local outbox to carry expiry, an attempt count, the path an attempt was made on, and the difference between a command that may flush silently and one that needs the owner asked again. `OutboxPolicy` classified commands before storage and nothing existed after storage; the sentence "A4/destructive actions do not silently execute hours later because connectivity returned" was enforced only at admission.

§20.10 describes a path switch as a nine-step transaction and forbids "just opening another socket and continuing" in those words. The client did exactly that.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.9, 20.10, 20.14, 20.15
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The parts of §20 that only matter during a failure. Nothing in a healthy session exercises them, so their absence produced no symptom until a network did something a test could not.
findings.remediation: Implement the three as pure Kotlin so every case can be executed in the JVM harness: `WarmStandbyPolicy` and `FailoverTransaction` in `WarmStandby.kt`, `DurableOutbox` beside the existing `EncryptedCommandQueue` rather than replacing it (§2.7), and wire all three into the session manager.
findings.impact: A path switch was a reconnect: the owner lost the turn they were in. A phone with no path either dropped work or would have replayed it hours later, including work the owner had forgotten issuing. Nothing stopped a second connected path sending an owner command twice.

closure.summary:
`WarmStandbyPolicy.decide` answers when a spare is worth holding open and returns the reason in the owner's terms; `mayCarry` makes the upstream asymmetry a closed list rather than a convention. `FailoverTransaction` records the nine steps and refuses a promotion to an epoch the Gateway did not advance. `DurableOutbox` adds everything §20.14 asks for after storage.

**Corrected after review.** Two claims in the first version of this closure were wider than the code. §20.9's warm standby is *policy only* — the session manager holds one socket, and a `WARM_STANDBY` decision says what the phone can afford, not that a second authenticated transport exists; make-before-break is not built. And the outbox was durable in name: its records lived in an in-memory ArrayDeque, so a process death lost the reconfirmation, expiry, attempt count and path metadata while the command itself could survive in the encrypted queue. That second one is fixed in RB C14 — the policy now rides on the canonical queue's own record, one write, and the restart seam is executed end to end. The first is not fixed, it is narrowed: three tests now fail if the source ever implies a standby transport that nobody has built.
closure.counterexample: An outbox that classified on flush rather than admission passes every flush test and still stores an A4 across an outage; `admit` returns null, so the only way to keep one is to not call it. A `DurableOutbox` whose records live in RAM passes every one of its own unit tests — all of them are in-process — and loses the owner's reconfirmation to a kill; `RestartSeamTest` is what separates those, and it found a real one: the first mapping silently dropped `commandId`, which is the identity §20.12 matches a restored command by. A `StandbyDecision` of `WARM_STANDBY` passes every policy test and is not a connection; `WarmStandbyIsPolicyNotTransportTest` fails the moment a second socket appears without the claims being revisited.
closure.residual: §20.9's make-before-break is unimplemented. There is one socket; the policy that would govern a second one is written and executed, and the second one is not. Separately, `EncryptedCommandQueue` itself — the Keystore and the disk under the now-durable outbox — cannot be executed in this repository.
closure.residual_reason: A second authenticated transport buys nothing in this build: `DEFAULT_PATHS` declares one `routeId` for both carriers, so §0B's answer is that a spare on the same road fails with the first, and the policy correctly returns COLD for every input. Building the socket before a second ingress exists would add a cost and a failure mode with no benefit. The store is Android, so CI compiles it and Gate 14 observes it.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The device telemetry ingest could carry exactly one label, and it was hard-coded to the aura surface
findings.description:
`record_device_sample` resolved a single label named `surface`, for `aura_frame_time_ms`. Every other declared device metric was unlabelled, and there was no way to declare one that was not the aura's.

That is why §20.15's outbox depth had nowhere to go. The store-and-forward queue lives on the phone, so the Gateway cannot count it; the depth only means anything broken down by what the queue is allowed to do with each item — a hundred retryable commands is a network outage and one awaiting reconfirmation is a person waiting to be asked something — and there was no slot for that breakdown.

The same gap made it tempting to declare the metric as Gateway-produced instead, which would have been a Gateway reporting a number it cannot take.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.15, 20.16, 28.1
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A dimension designed for the one metric that needed it. The three device tables also had three different shapes, so a caller asking "what can a device write" had to know which of them to read — which is how `DEVICE_COUNTERS` was once added beside two others and missed by the contract test whose job was to catch exactly that.
findings.remediation: Give the three tables one declared shape, `DeviceMetric(metric, dimension, dimension_default)`; add a generic `dimension` field to the wire beside `surface` rather than renaming it; refuse a sample for a labelled series that carries no value for the label.
findings.impact: Bounded, and the bound is the point: §20.15's depth could not be reported, and any future device metric needing a dimension would have had to reuse `surface` under a name that means something else.

closure.summary:
One shape for the three tables, one helper (`ingestible_metrics`) that answers what a device can write, and a dimension slot that is refused rather than defaulted when the metric declares one and the sample does not carry it.

`surface` is kept as its own wire field rather than folded in, because shipped devices post it: a rename would have dropped the aura label from every phone that had not been updated, and the symptom would have been one merged series rather than an error. The cross-language contract now compares dimension *names* rather than a boolean, so a phone that posted its outbox depth in the surface field fails the contract instead of being silently refused at the route.
closure.counterexample: Recording a dimensionless sample under `unknown` passes every ingest test and puts a queue of approval-bearing commands in the same bucket as a retry queue, which is the reading an operator would act on backwards. `test_a_labelled_device_sample_without_its_label_is_refused_not_bucketed` requires the refusal.
closure.residual: One dimension per device metric, by construction. A device that could name its own labels could make a series' cardinality a function of what it decided to send.
closure.residual_reason: Deliberate. The bound is the defence; a second dimension would be a declared change to this table rather than something a phone can do.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The session's interaction signal had no producer, so the heartbeat was permanently in its idle cadence
findings.description:
`VanHermesSessionManager.setInteractionActive` decides two things: §20.8's heartbeat cadence, and — once the warm standby existed — whether a spare path is worth holding open. Nothing called it. The field was initialised false and stayed false for the life of the process.

The effect was invisible in the ordinary case and exactly wrong in the case that matters: the session used its idle heartbeat interval while the owner was sitting watching a command they had just submitted, so a path that died during their turn took the idle detection interval to be noticed.

`TransportSupervisor.observe` takes `interactionActive` as a parameter and the manager passed it through faithfully. Every layer was correct and the value was never true.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.8, 20.9
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A setter with no caller. The parameter threaded correctly through three layers, which is what made it read as wired.
findings.remediation: Drive it from the conversation's own state — something submitted and unanswered, or an A4 the owner is being asked to approve — rather than from whether the app is in the foreground.
findings.impact: A path failure during the owner's turn was detected on the idle schedule. With the warm standby added, the same false value would have kept the spare path cold at precisely the moment §20.9 wants it warm.

closure.summary:
`VanApplication.startInteractionWatch` collects `VanCommandController.state` and sets the flag from `submitting || pendingA4Approval != null`.

The signal is deliberately not foreground: a phone face-down on a desk with a command in flight is the case a failover has to be invisible for, and a phone in the owner's hand with nothing outstanding is not worth a second socket's battery. The same call re-evaluates the standby decision, so the two things §20.8 and §20.9 derive from "active interaction" come from one signal rather than two.
closure.counterexample: A caller that set the flag from an Activity lifecycle callback would pass any test that asserts the setter has a caller, and would be false for the backgrounded phone that is exactly the case §20.9 describes. The producer here is the conversation's own unanswered work, which is true in that case.
closure.residual: `VanApplication` is Android and cannot be executed in this repository. What is checked is that the call exists and that the file compiles as Kotlin.
closure.residual_reason: The Android Gradle Plugin is unreachable in this container, so CI's Android build is the only compiler for the app module. The decision this feeds — `WarmStandbyPolicy.decide` — is pure and is executed.
closure.posture: fail-open

findings.title: The owner production build asked for a Gateway address and a pairing code, in two places
findings.description:
§0D.2 lists eleven fields the owner production build must not ask for or expose. Two of them shipped as text boxes and they shipped twice: "Gateway address" and "Pairing code" on the onboarding screen, and "Gateway address" and "One-time pairing token" again on the Connections admin screen.

The section states the rule and not the reason, so it is worth stating. A box asking the owner to type a server address is a phishing surface with their entire assistant behind it. Anyone who persuades them to retype an address owns every command from that moment — mail, calendar, browser, trading approvals — and nothing on the phone looks wrong afterwards, because from the phone's side a new Gateway is simply the Gateway. A pairing code is worse: it is exactly the kind of string somebody can be talked into reading out over the phone, and it mints owner-device authority.

The supporting machinery for the correct design was already there and unused. `ConnectivityRegistry` verified signed manifests, `POST /v1/devices/bootstrap/*` existed for hardware-attested binding, and ADR-RB-026 described an installer-driven path. Nothing connected them, so the forms remained the only way in.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §0D.2, ADR-RB-026
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The only path that existed. Pairing had to happen somehow, the installer path was described and not built, and a form is what remains when nothing else is wired.
findings.remediation: Build ADR-RB-026's path: one signed, single-use, short-lived provisioning payload minted by the Gateway and delivered by the installer. Remove both forms, make `baseUrl`'s setter and `pairThisDevice` private so a new form cannot be written without changing the client, and guard the shape rather than the wording with a contract test.
findings.impact: A complete compromise of the owner's assistant was one convincing message away, and the same message would have worked on either of two screens. The second one — an admin screen the owner reaches deliberately — is the more dangerous, because a person who has navigated there is already in a frame of mind to change a setting.

closure.summary:
Both forms are gone. Since 2026-09-25 (owner direction) there is no pairing screen or setup step at all: the launcher is VAN's welcome, Settings shows only a read-only connection status, and the phone is set up by its installer (ADR-RB-026).

`VanGatewayClient.baseUrl` has a private setter and `pairThisDevice` is private, so a new form cannot be written without editing the client. `provisionThisDevice` is the only caller and it does both halves of §0D.3 — pair and bind — because a device that paired without binding is an APK that works on another handset.

Ten contract tests read the Android sources, and the strong one is not the label check: it refuses any editable field at all on the two screens that carried the problem, because a rebuild without a label would pass a check that looked for wording.
closure.counterexample: Removing the labels while leaving the fields passes any test that searches for "Gateway address", and leaves the phishing surface exactly where it was. `test_the_two_screens_that_carried_the_forms_have_no_editable_field_at_all` refuses the composable rather than the wording. Making the setter private while leaving a public helper that calls it passes a check on the setter; `test_provisioning_is_the_only_caller_of_pairing` reads every Kotlin file for callers rather than the one.
closure.residual: Whether a real S24 Ultra provisions from a real Gateway over ADB has not been run. The payload's construction, its signing, every refusal, and the exact argv the installer builds are tested; the handover itself needs a device.
closure.residual_reason: Gate 14's physical verification. No amount of Python here substitutes for an `adb install` against the owner's handset, and saying otherwise would be the substitution this programme refuses.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: §38's three floods had no bound: tabs, downloads and input packets were all unlimited
findings.description:
§38 items 12, 17 and 18 name three attacks in which every individual request is legitimate. A page can open tabs on its own; the Stream Host reports each one. A page can start downloads; Hermes reports each one. The phone sends input packets; the router translates each one. None of the three was counted.

That is why they had no bound: one more tab, one more download and one more input packet are each exactly what the system is for, and the harm is only in the count. A flood does not steal anything — it makes VAN unusable while looking like use.

Found while building the §38 register, which is the point of building one.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §38 items 12, 17, 18
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: Three components, three arrival paths, and no single door to hold. Each one looked like somebody else's to bound.
findings.remediation: Bound each where the thing is recorded, because that is the one place that sees all of them: the tab at `record_active_url`, the download at `DownloadBroker.create`, and the packet at the stream host's router. Set each bound well above ordinary use, so the first person it inconveniences does not remove it.
findings.impact: A page could fill the session's tab strip, fill a disk with downloads, or saturate the input path. The last is the one that matters most: an input flood degrades the owner's own control at the moment they are trying to stop whatever is happening.

closure.summary:
`flood_bounds.py` carries the three constants, the refusal names and the sliding-window limiter, and each bound is wired into the place the thing is recorded.

The shapes matter more than the numbers. The new tab is refused rather than an old one closed, because closing loses the owner's work — which is the harm rather than the defence. A refused input packet is not recorded in the window, or a sustained flood would keep the session refused long after it stopped, turning a bound into an outage. And the rate is a sliding window rather than a token bucket, because a bucket permits a long-run rate above the bound if the burst shape is right, which is what a patient attacker would do.

The input bound is 400 packets a second against a 120 Hz phone's ~240 at its busiest, so the owner's own dragging never reaches it — tested at three seconds of continuous 120 Hz input with an edge on every frame.
closure.counterexample: A bound that counted every `record_active_url` rather than every new target passes a limit test and stops a session at the cap from following a link — the browser not working, reported as a security control. `test_navigating_inside_a_tab_that_already_exists_is_never_refused` is what separates them. A rate limiter that recorded refused packets passes every 'the bound fires' test and never recovers; `test_a_refused_packet_does_not_extend_the_refusal` sends ten thousand refusals and requires the session usable one window later.
closure.residual: Whether the numbers are right for a real page and a real phone has not been measured. They are set from arithmetic — §8.7's one MOVE per frame, a 120 Hz panel — rather than from observation.
closure.residual_reason: Measuring them needs a Browser Stream Host and the owner's handset (RB-010, Gate 14). The bounds are constants in one file for exactly that reason.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: A download for a session that does not exist was reported to the host as already recorded
findings.description:
`browser_downloads` has a foreign key to `browser_interactive_sessions`, and SQLite raises `IntegrityError` for a foreign-key violation and for a duplicate primary key alike. `DownloadBroker.create` caught the exception and called every instance of it `download_already_reported`.

So a host reporting a download into a session that was never created — the shape a misrouted or replayed report has — was told its report had already been recorded. Whoever read that went looking for a record that does not exist, and the actual cause, a session id that is wrong, was never mentioned.

Found by a test for the download flood bound, which created downloads against sessions it had not inserted.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §18
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: One exception type for two failures, and a handler written for the one that was expected.
findings.remediation: Distinguish them and give the foreign-key case its own refusal name, so the host is told the session is unknown rather than that its report is a duplicate.
findings.impact: Diagnostic rather than a breach: the wrong answer sent whoever was debugging to the wrong place, and a genuinely misrouted report looked like an idempotent retry succeeding.
