closure.summary: `REJECT_DOWNLOAD_SESSION_UNKNOWN` is its own refusal, and both halves are tested: the orphan report gets the new name, and a genuine duplicate still gets `download_already_reported` — because a fix that renamed both failures would pass a test for either one alone.
closure.counterexample: Catching the foreign-key case and reporting it as `download_already_reported` with a better log line passes any test that only checks the orphan path raises. `test_a_genuine_duplicate_is_still_a_duplicate` is the other half.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: A second parser for the build-time trust anchor would have made every release build unprovisionable
findings.description:
`VAN_CONNECTIVITY_TRUSTED_KEYS` is injected at build time as newline-separated `kid=PEM` pairs. `ConnectivityRegistry` parses that format. The provisioning intake, written in this checkpoint, parsed the same string as JSON.

It would have found nothing, reported the build as having no trust anchor, and refused every provisioning payload. A correctly configured release APK would have installed, opened, and sat on "waiting for the installer" forever — with every test in the repository green, because nothing executed the parser against the real format.

Caught before it shipped, and recorded because the shape is the point: two parsers for one build-time string is the same class of defect as two copies of a wire format, and it is harder to see because the string is injected rather than sent.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md ADR-RB-026, ADR-RB-027
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A format known by one reader and guessed by the next. The value is a build argument, so nothing on either side fails visibly when the guess is wrong.
findings.remediation: One parser, `ConnectivityTrustedKeys.parse`, in the pure package so it is executed in the harness, with both readers calling it.
findings.impact: Would have been total for provisioning and silent: the release build's only way in would have refused everything, and the owner's screen would have said VAN was waiting.

closure.summary: One parser, five tests, and the one that would have caught the original is not the happy path: `escaped newlines inside a PEM are restored`. The value arrives through a Gradle BuildConfig string where a real newline cannot survive, so a parser that did not restore them would hold a PEM no KeyFactory accepts — and every signature would then be reported as invalid for entirely the wrong reason.
closure.counterexample: A parser that accepted `prov-1=hunter2` as an anchor passes every format test and gives the build a key nobody can verify against; `a value that is not a public key is not a trusted key` refuses it, and the Gradle release gate refuses the same shape at build time so the dead APK is never produced.
closure.residual: The parser is executed; the build-time injection that feeds it is not. Whether a release build's Gradle argument arrives intact is CI's to show.
closure.residual_reason: The Android Gradle Plugin is unreachable in the audit container, so `assembleRelease` runs only in CI.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: §38's fifty-nine red-team scenarios had no register, and a register alone would have been fifty-nine unchecked claims
findings.description:
§38 lists fifty release-suite scenarios and sixteen Rev 1.2 continuity attacks, and ends with a rule that is easy to read past: every finding is `PASS`, `FAIL`, `BLOCKED_EXTERNAL` or `NOT_APPLICABLE_WITH_REASON`, and never `assumed`.

Nothing recorded any of them. Much of the behaviour was in fact tested — the suites were there — but no artefact said which scenario each test answered, so "the red team passes" could only ever have been an assertion.

The first version of the register proved the second half of the problem. Every PASS named a test that existed; twenty-five of the fifty-one named it in a form that cannot be run, because the test lives inside a class the citation omitted. Every claim was true and a quarter of them were unusable as evidence.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §38
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A list in a document and tests in a repository, with nothing between them. The mapping existed only in whoever last read both.
findings.remediation: A register as data, and a checker that refuses a status which is not backed: every PASS must cite a runnable pytest node id or a Kotlin test that exists, every BLOCKED_EXTERNAL must name what is missing, and `assumed` in any spelling is a failure.
findings.impact: Documentary, and it is the class of impact this programme exists to remove: a claim about security that nobody can re-check is indistinguishable from a claim nobody made.

closure.summary:
Sixty-six scenarios: 57 PASS, 9 BLOCKED_EXTERNAL, none assumed. Every PASS cites a runnable node id, and all 197 cited Python tests were executed and pass.

The checker resolves a Python citation by walking the module's AST for the `Class::test` chain rather than by looking for the name — which is what turned twenty-five true-but-unusable citations into runnable ones. It is in CI, with its own self-test, because a checker that only ever passes proves nothing.
closure.counterexample: A checker that accepted any citation whose file exists passes a register full of renamed tests; `test_a_citation_naming_a_test_that_was_renamed_is_refused` fails it. A register that dropped an inconvenient scenario would shorten quietly; the numbering is contiguous and read out of the blueprint, so a missing item fails by name.
closure.residual: A PASS means the repository can demonstrate the refusal, not that a live Remote Browser was attacked and survived. Nine scenarios need a Stream Host, a carrier or a handset and say so.
closure.residual_reason: Deliberate, and stated in the register itself. NOT VERIFIED is not NOT IMPLEMENTED and neither is substituted for the other.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: §43's hundred and four acceptance requirements had no register, and a ledger verdict nobody recomputes
findings.description:
§43 says Remote Browser Rev 1.5 is production complete only when one hundred and four specific things are true, and then lists them by category. Nothing recorded a status against any of them.

`docs/PRODUCTION_ACCEPTANCE_LEDGER.md` existed and carried a verdict at the top — written once, by a person, in September, and never re-derived since. That is the shape of claim this entire programme was commissioned to find: true when written, unchallenged afterwards, and indistinguishable from a claim nobody made.

The specific risk with an acceptance ledger is worse than with most documents, because the thing at the top is a *verdict*. A reader acts on it.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §43
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A verdict is written at the top of a document and everything below it is the evidence. Nothing reads upward.
findings.remediation: Make the register data and the verdict a computation. Read §43 out of the blueprint so a requirement cannot go missing, require a proven row to cite evidence that can be re-run, require every other row to name what is missing, and recompute the verdict from the rows — failing if the stored one disagrees.
findings.impact: Documentary and load-bearing: `PRODUCTION_ACCEPTED` is the sentence that would authorise shipping, and nothing stopped it from being true-looking while forty-four requirements were unmet.

closure.summary:
104 requirements, parsed from §43 rather than copied: 60 REPOSITORY_PROVEN, 37 BLOCKED_EXTERNAL, 7 OWNER_DEPLOYMENT_DECISION, verdict REPOSITORY_COMPLETE_PENDING_EXTERNAL.

The verdict is recomputed by `tools/ci/production_acceptance.py` and the checker fails if the stored one disagrees, which is what makes this a program rather than a document. `REPOSITORY_PROVEN` is defined in the register itself as weaker than certification, and a test asserts that definition still says so — because "proven" reads like "certified" to anyone who did not write it.

Fifteen contract tests, and the ones that matter are the negative ones: a verdict that went accepted, a dropped requirement, an invented one, and evidence renamed out from under a proven row.
closure.counterexample: A checker that always reported PENDING would pass every test that asserts the verdict is not accepted, and would be unable to ever say otherwise. `test_accepted_is_reachable_when_every_row_is_settled` settles every row and requires the checker to accept — so the verdict is withheld by the rows and not by the checker.
closure.residual: Sixty rows are REPOSITORY_PROVEN, which is the strongest thing a repository can say and is weaker than certification. Forty-four are not proven at all.
closure.residual_reason: Stated in the register, in the ledger and in the closure record, in those words. The programme's distinction: NOT VERIFIED is not NOT IMPLEMENTED, and neither is substituted for the other.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The dependency admission row read BUILT_UNWIRED while CI had been checking it on every run
findings.description:
RB-003 recorded `BUILT_UNWIRED` with no producer, no consumer and no tests. `registries/remote_browser_dependencies.json` records a digest measured for each admitted artefact, `tests/contracts/test_remote_browser_dependencies.py` compares it against what `build.gradle.kts` actually declares, and that has run on every CI job since it was written.

Understating is the failure the ledger reconciler exists for, and it is invisible to a gate built to stop overstating. The row's own `external_gates` were correct — the webrtc-sdk upstream revision genuinely is unresolved — and the status was drawn from the gates rather than from the work.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §32, §42.5
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A status set from what is still blocked rather than from what is done. An unresolved external gate on a row does not make the repository's half unbuilt.
findings.remediation: Move it to WIRED_UNPROVEN, name the producer, the consumer and the seven tests, and keep the three genuinely external gates stated rather than rounded away.
findings.impact: A reader planning the remaining work would have counted the admission record as outstanding and rebuilt something that exists.

closure.summary: WIRED_UNPROVEN, with the seven tests named. The note keeps the distinction the row lost: `webrtc-sdk` is admitted by a digest measured from the published artefact, and its upstream source revision is not something the publisher states — a weaker claim than a reviewed source, and said rather than implied.
closure.counterexample: Calling it WIRED because the tests exist would ignore that nothing re-downloads: the test compares a recorded digest against a declared coordinate, and treating a test run as a supply-chain check would be §42.5's failure one layer down. The row says so.
closure.residual: The upstream source revision of `webrtc-sdk`, the S24 MediaCodec canary, and the Sherpa runtime owner decision 2 declined.
closure.residual_reason: None is a repository change.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: Three vocabularies spell capability ids the same way and nothing said which was which
findings.description:
`registries/capabilities.json` declares ids the router may route to. `audit.record(capability=...)` takes a label describing what happened. `CAPABILITY = "stagehand"` in the browser adapters names which runtime handled something. All three are written as lowercase identifiers in a field called `capability`, and nothing anywhere distinguished them.

The resemblance is actively misleading rather than merely untidy. Sweeping the Gateway for `capability="..."` returns fourteen strings the registry does not declare, which is exactly what P0's defect looked like — a capability the Mission binder needed and nobody had declared, making every Mission-bound browser session a 500. Acting on that reading and declaring the fourteen would turn descriptions of past events into routable capabilities nothing implements: the same defect facing the other way.

Found by making that mistake during this pass's final wiring sweep.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §42.5
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: One field name for three vocabularies. The only thing separating them in source is whether the value contains a dot, and that was nowhere written down.
findings.remediation: Write the three down and check them: every dotted capability id the router can be asked for must be declared; the audit labels that are not are named so adding one is deliberate; the runtime names are pinned by the property that separates them.
findings.impact: Documentary, and the harm would have been a well-intentioned change: the fourteen audit labels look precisely like the P0 that was just closed, and declaring them would have made fourteen unimplemented capabilities routable.

closure.summary: Five tests. The one that carries the P0's rule forward scans for the constants that hold a capability id rather than only the call sites — because the id that caused the P0 is written as `INTERACTIVE_BROWSER_CAPABILITY` in `mission/binding.py`, and a check matching only `.require("...")` found nothing at all and passed. That is the vacuous-test shape this programme keeps finding, caught here in its own guard.
closure.counterexample: A check that asserted only `asked <= declared` passes when `asked` is empty, which it was on the first run. `assert asked` is what turns a vacuous pass into a failure, and the third vocabulary is pinned separately so an adapter name gaining a dot fails there first, with a message that says why.
closure.residual: The discriminator is a dot in a string, held by a test rather than by a type.
closure.residual_reason: Three separate types across a registry file, an audit column and an adapter constant is a larger change than the defect warrants, and the test states the rule where somebody sweeping for `capability=` will find it.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The durable outbox was durable in name: its policy lived in RAM while the command could survive on disk
findings.description:
`DurableOutbox` decides whether a stored command may be flushed silently, needs the owner asked again, or has expired. `VanHermesSessionManager` held those decisions in an in-memory `ArrayDeque<QueuedMessage>` and never touched `EncryptedCommandQueue` at all.

The class's own docstring said §2.7 forbids a parallel queue so "the queue still owns the bytes and this owns the metadata". That was the design and it was not the code: nothing wrote the session's bytes to the queue either. The whole outbox was RAM.

Android kills backgrounded processes as a matter of routine, so the failure is ordinary rather than exotic. After a kill the reconfirmation the owner gave, the expiry, the attempt count and the path metadata are gone. Worse than losing everything: a command could survive in the pre-existing encrypted queue through another path while the policy governing whether it may be silently replayed did not — leaving the replay decision to be guessed.

Found by external review of checkpoint RB C11.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§2.7, 20.14, 20.15
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: Every test of the outbox was in-process, so every one of them passed. A policy object tested in RAM proves the policy and says nothing about whether the policy is still there tomorrow.
findings.remediation: Carry §20.14's fields on `QueuedCommand` itself so one record and one write hold both the envelope and its policy, wire the manager to persist at admission and reconfirmation and to forget only after a successful send, and execute the restart seam end to end through a fake store.
findings.impact: Store-and-forward did not survive the condition it exists for. A command whose owner had answered a reconfirmation could come back looking as though they had not, or worse, come back looking ordinary and be sent without anyone being asked.

closure.summary:
One record, one write. `QueuedCommand` now carries the storability, the live-owner-context flag, the reconfirmation stamp, the last attempted path, the turn id and the session's own message and command ids; `OutboxPersistence` maps both directions and is pure, so the mapping is executed rather than reasoned about.

The order is the correctness: persisted before it is queued in memory, and forgotten only after the socket write returns — the other order in either case loses the command to a kill one instruction later.

Two real defects fell out of writing the tests. The round-trip silently dropped `commandId`, which is the identity §20.12 matches a restored command by, so a restart would have sent it a second time. And a session envelope in the shared queue was *dispatchable by the replayer* — P0-SEC-002's shape — so `SESSION_ENVELOPE` is now its own kind and named in `NEVER_DISPATCHABLE` rather than relying on `commandTextOrNull` happening to return null.
closure.counterexample: Persisting the entry beside the queue in a second store passes every round-trip test and reintroduces the defect one layer up: two writes, and a kill between them leaves the bytes and the policy disagreeing. One record is what makes it atomic, and §2.7 required it anyway. Reconstructing a missing `storability` on restore would also pass every happy-path test; `a record with no storability is refused rather than reconstructed` requires the null, because the guess is wrong in both directions — guess SAFE_TO_RETRY and an approval-bearing command replays silently, guess NEVER_STORE and the owner's work vanishes without them being told.
closure.residual: `EncryptedCommandQueue` itself is not executed here. The Keystore, the AES-GCM wrapping and the disk are Android; what is executed is every decision either side of them, through `SessionOutboxStore`.
closure.residual_reason: The interface is where the line falls on purpose. A fake implements it in nine lines and the restart seam becomes executable; the adapter that binds the real queue is twenty lines that CI compiles and Gate 14 observes.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: An unreadable battery was read as a full one, authorising optional background spending
findings.description:
`VanApplication.refreshStandbyConditions` converted `RuntimeReading.UNKNOWN` to 100 before handing the reading to `WarmStandbyPolicy`. That is the one value that authorises holding a second authenticated socket open.

The instinct was right and applied to the wrong question. `VanResourceEnvelope` treats an unknown reading as contributing no pressure, and that is correct there: the question is whether to take capability *away*, and an OEM that will not answer the capacity property must not leave VAN permanently crippled. A warm standby is not capability — it is cost, a second socket with its own heartbeats — and the same unknown should answer that question the other way.

The repository already stated the principle three files away: `DeviceRuntimeReadings.networkCost` fails towards restraint because "an unreadable battery costs VAN capability it probably had; an unreadable data plan would cost the owner money they did not agree to spend". The standby path then did the opposite with the battery.

Raised by external review, which also connected it to an earlier finding about unavailable runtime readings as a fail-open risk.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §20.9
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: One sentinel, two questions. Whether to withhold capability and whether to authorise spending both read the battery, and only the first had a stated answer for unknown.
findings.remediation: Pass the envelope's own sentinel through rather than inventing a number, and refuse in the policy — where the decision is, and where it can be executed.
findings.impact: Bounded today, because this build answers COLD on the route check before the battery is reached. It would not have been bounded the moment a second ingress existed, which is precisely when nobody would be looking at this line.

closure.summary:
`WarmStandbyPolicy` refuses on `UNKNOWN_BATTERY` with a reason the owner can read, and the conversion in `VanApplication` is gone. Charging does not override it: being plugged in says nothing about whether this phone can afford the radio time, and a test asserts that too.

The sentinel is copied rather than imported, so the pure file stays pure — and a third test pins the copy against `RuntimeReading.UNKNOWN`, because a copied constant with no test is how two packages drift.
closure.counterexample: Refusing on unknown only when discharging passes the obvious test and restores the hole for a charging phone, which is the common case for a device sitting on a desk overnight. `charging does not buy a spare socket the battery could not be read for` is what separates them.
closure.residual: `VanApplication` is Android and cannot be executed here; what is checked is that the conversion is gone and that the policy refuses.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container, so CI compiles the app module.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The session outbox used an insert API where it needed an upsert, three ways
findings.description:
`EncryptedSessionOutboxStore.persist` was `queue.remove(entry.messageId)` followed by `queue.enqueue(...)`. Three separate failures came out of that one choice, and no test in the repository could see any of them because the tests exercised a nine-line fake while the adapter itself was unexecutable — it took `EncryptedCommandQueue`, which needs a Keystore and a disk.

1. Two persistent operations. A process death between them lost the owner's command outright, which is the exact failure a durable outbox exists to prevent.
2. `enqueue` mints a fresh row id, so the record was never keyed by the message id. The `remove` matched nothing and neither did `forget`: a delivered command stayed on disk and was restored and re-sent after every restart.
3. `enqueue` de-duplicates on the idempotency key and returns the existing row unchanged, so a reconfirmation — the owner's "yes", already stamped on the entry — was silently discarded, and the owner was asked the same question again after the next process death.

Raised by external review, which identified the first and asked for an atomic upsert. The second and third were found while fixing it.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§2.7, 20.14
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The adapter was written against whatever API the queue happened to expose. `enqueue` is an insert — it mints an id and de-duplicates — and the outbox needs replacement keyed on the message id. Nothing forced the difference into view because the adapter could not be executed.
findings.remediation: `OutboxRecordStore` — upsert, remove, recordsOfKind — added to the pure queue model, with `EncryptedCommandQueue` implementing it and the adapter depending on it. One `upsert` per persist, the record keyed on the message id, and the whole adapter now executed in `android/verification` against a store that can be killed between operations.

closure.summary: `persist` is one `records.upsert(...)`. `EncryptedCommandQueue.persist` and `remove` were each two SharedPreferences editors with asynchronous `apply()` — three non-atomic writes in total, not the one the review named — and are now a single editor with `commit()`, so the blob and the index move together and the caller is not told the command is queued before it is on disk.
closure.counterexample: A fault-injection sweep that finds nothing passes. `the previous two-step persist does lose the command, which is why the sweep exists` keeps the old adapter executable and asserts it still fails, and the sweep's bound is asserted to exceed the number of operations a persist actually performs — so neither the sweep nor its range can go quiet.
closure.residual: Part of the remediation is in `EncryptedCommandQueue`, which needs a Keystore and a disk and is therefore compiled by CI and executed nowhere here: the single-editor `commit()` that makes the blob and the index move together is read, not run. What is executed is the adapter — one mutating call per persist, keyed on the message id, and no kill point within a persist that loses a command.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: A resume asked by message id, was answered by command id, and dropped every unknown
findings.description:
§20.12's reconciliation was three lines: send `inFlight.keys` as `pending_command_ids`, then `states.keys().forEach { inFlight.remove(it) }`.

Two independent defects that cancelled each other out. The phone sent *message* ids and the Gateway resolved each one as a *command* id against the mission table, so every answer came back `UNKNOWN`. The phone then removed every key it had asked about, the `UNKNOWN`s included — and `UNKNOWN` is the Gateway saying it has never heard of this, which is the one answer that means resend.

The effect: every reconnect silently discarded every unacknowledged owner command. Nothing was resent because nothing was recognised, and nothing looked wrong because nothing was left behind. Restored outbox entries were not reconciled at all, so a process death between the socket write and the durable `forget` delivered the owner's command a second time.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.11, 20.12
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A command id and a message id are different identities on the same envelope, and the question and the answer were produced in different files. Neither side was checkable against the other, because the one case that distinguishes them — a partial answer — is not produced by a healthy network.
findings.remediation: `SessionReconciliation` — pure — produces the identity asked about and matches the answer by the same function, and returns a plan of resend and settle. `submit` now puts the command id on the envelope, where the Gateway records it. `_resume_snapshot` answers from §20.12's admission table when there is no mission, scoped to the asking session, and answers `UNKNOWN` explicitly rather than omitting the key. Restored outbox entries are reconciled with the in-flight ones and durably forgotten when the Gateway holds them.

closure.summary: One function produces the question and matches the answer, so asking by one identity and settling by another is no longer expressible. Absent and `UNKNOWN` both mean resend; anything else settles, which now includes a message the Gateway admitted without opening a mission for it.
closure.counterexample: A Gateway that answered something for every id would pass the "is not reported unknown" test and lose the owner's command instead — the phone would settle work that never arrived. `a message the gateway has never seen is reported unknown` and `the answer is scoped to the session that asked` are what separate the two.
closure.residual: The Gateway's half and the reconciliation decisions are executed. The wiring in `VanHermesSessionManager` — which identities are collected, what a settle does to the queue and the store — needs OkHttp, is not in the JVM harness, and is compiled by CI only. That half is a read of the source.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: Three of the four session kinds had no delegate, and the refusal burned the key
findings.description:
`SessionRouter` knows four upstream kinds. `app.py` wired one. `decision.answer`, `mission.cancel` and `mission.message` sent over the durable session were refused `session_kind_unknown`.

Worse than a missing feature, because the router admitted the envelope into §20.12's table *before* discovering it had nobody to hand it to. The idempotency key was now taken with a null result, so the phone's retry — the correct response to a refusal it cannot interpret — came back `ALREADY_KNOWN` with no result, which reads as success. The owner's "cancel it" was acknowledged, never performed, and could not be sent again for the life of the session.

Found while writing a route-level test for §20.12's resume answer: the test needed a kind the Gateway would record, and `mission.message` returned 400.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.2, 20.12
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: `SessionDelegates` made three of the four optional, so an unwired authority was a default rather than a build failure — and the admission table was written before the router knew whether it could carry the message.
findings.remediation: The delegate is resolved before admission, so nothing is written down that cannot be carried out. A delegate refusal un-records the message, releasing the key so the owner's corrected resend is admitted; an unexpected exception does the same and is re-raised. All four delegates are wired to the authorities that already exist — `DecisionService.resolve`, `MissionService.transition`, `MissionService.record_event` — and a malformed command payload is now a refusal rather than a 500, because a 500 means "try again" and this payload never will succeed.

closure.summary: §20.2 is delegation to an existing authority, and all four kinds now delegate. No envelope enters the admission table before the Gateway knows it can carry it, and no refusal leaves a row behind.
closure.counterexample: Wiring the delegates without moving the admission would pass `the owner can cancel a mission over the session` and leave the key burned for every payload a delegate refuses. `a refused message does not take its idempotency key with it` fails under exactly that fix, and `a refused message is not left in the admission table` ties it back to the resume answer: a row with no result would tell a reconnecting phone the Gateway holds a command it never performed.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: A restore read the queue through a filter that drops the commands it exists to recover
findings.description:
`EncryptedSessionOutboxStore.restore` read `queue.peekReady()`, which filters on `isReplayEligible` — and that drops a `NO_STALE_REPLAY` command once `attemptCount > 0`. That is precisely the §20.14 class a restore exists for: a command that was tried, was not acknowledged, and must be put back to the owner rather than sent on their behalf.

So a restart silently discarded the commands the owner most needed to be asked about, with every test of the mapping still green, because the mapping was never the broken half.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.14, 20.15
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: `peekReady` is the dispatcher's reader and answers "what may be sent now". A restore asks "what is still held", and the two differ in exactly the class that needs the owner. Reusing the nearest reader took the wrong question's answer.
findings.remediation: `recordsOfKind` reads the index directly and filters only on expiry, because a window that closed while the process was dead has closed. What may be sent is the outbox's decision, made after the restore, not the queue's.

closure.summary: The restore reader and the dispatch reader are different functions with different filters, and the difference is documented at the one that was wrong.
closure.counterexample: A test that persisted an un-attempted reconfirm-needed entry passes under both readers. `a command awaiting the owner is restored rather than filtered away` stamps the attempt first, which is the only state the two readers disagree about.
closure.residual: `recordsOfKind` itself lives in `EncryptedCommandQueue` and cannot be executed here. The test exercises the adapter over a store that honours the documented contract, which proves the adapter does not re-filter and does not prove the real method reads the index rather than `peekReady`. That is a source read and CI's compile.

findings.title: A session replacement cleared the outbox in memory and left it on disk
findings.description:
`ResumeOutcome.SESSION_REPLACED` calls `outbox.clear()`, with a comment stating the reason: work addressed to a session that no longer exists is not the same work, and replaying it into a new one is how a cancelled instruction gets performed.

The durable store was not cleared. So the very next `start()` restored those records and flushed them into the new session — the decision made here reversed by a restart. The commands were also dropped without the owner being told anything.

This defect arrived *with* durability: it was correct while the outbox was in memory, and C14 made the memory the wrong half to clear without revisiting this branch.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.9, 20.14
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: Adding a second place where state lives without auditing every place the first one is cleared. The recurring shape: two stores, one of them load-bearing, and the code that predates the second one still only knows about the first.
findings.remediation: The branch forgets each entry durably as well as in memory, and records it in `abandoned` so `undeliveredSinceLastRead` tells the owner it did not happen — kept separate from `expired` because "the time ran out" and "the conversation ended" are different things to say.

closure.summary: The decision is `DurableOutbox.abandonAll`, which forgets each record durably and returns what the owner must be told — so doing one without the other is not expressible at the call site. `undeliveredSinceLastRead` carries it to the owner, kept separate from `expired` because "the time ran out" and "the conversation ended" are different things to say.
closure.counterexample: Clearing the store and discarding the return value passes any test that checks the queue is empty, and loses the owner's work silently. The test asserts both the empty restore and the returned list, so neither half alone is enough.
closure.residual: The branch that calls it is in `VanHermesSessionManager`, which needs OkHttp and is compiled by CI only. What is executed is that the call clears the store and names every dropped command; that `SESSION_REPLACED` reaches it is a source read.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container and the class cannot be added to the pure harness without pulling OkHttp into it.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The §20 durable session is constructed, fed two inputs, and never started
findings.description:
`VanApplication.onCreate` builds `VanHermesSessionManager` and calls exactly two of its ten public methods: `setInteractionActive` and `setStandbyConditions`. `start()` has no caller anywhere in the app — four references to the field in the entire source tree, and none of them starts it.

Everything §20 describes on the device follows from `start()`. No socket is opened, so `resume()` never runs and the §20.12 reconciliation never executes; `restoreOutbox()` is reached only from `start()`, so nothing is ever restored; and `submit()` — the only way a command enters the durable outbox — has no caller either. The owner's commands go out through `VanCommandController` to `POST /v1/commands`, and events arrive by HTTP polling inside a `LaunchedEffect` on the Work screen, which also stops when that screen is not composed.

Two checkpoints made the session outbox durable (C14) and then atomic (C15) without either noticing that nothing puts anything in it. Every test passed because every one of them called the outbox directly.

`tools/audit/kotlin_reachability.py` did not catch it and could not: it asks whether anything *references* a file, and the constructor is a reference.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.1, 20.3, 20.14
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A subsystem was built bottom-up and its top was never attached. Each checkpoint improved a part of it against tests that called that part directly, and the reachability tool answers a weaker question than the one that mattered — whether anything references the file, rather than whether anything drives the object.
findings.remediation: Recorded before it is repaired. The seven matrix rows whose named consumer is a device-side §20 entry point are corrected to BUILT_UNWIRED, and `tests/contracts/test_session_is_driven.py` holds the matrix to whether `start()` has a caller — in both directions, so the check does not have to be deleted when the session is wired.

closure.summary:
The claim is corrected, not the code. RB-035, RB-061, RB-062, RB-064, RB-068, RB-069 and RB-071 now read BUILT_UNWIRED and name the one cause. A contract test asserts the agreement between the matrix and whether anything calls `start()`, and fails if a new public method on the session gains no caller.

**Repaired at C16b.** `VanApplication.startVanSession()` calls `start()` when the device is enrolled, so the socket opens, the outbox is restored and the resume runs. RB-035, RB-061, RB-064, RB-068, RB-069 and RB-071 return to WIRED_UNPROVEN; RB-062 does not, because the device still has no second transport.
closure.counterexample: A test asserting 'the session is unwired' passes today and has to be deleted the moment it is wired, which turns a correction into a fossil. This asserts the agreement instead: with RB-069 put back to WIRED_UNPROVEN and nothing calling `start()`, two of its four tests fail; wire the session and it stops objecting.

findings.title: §20.1 states two SHALLs for the device session and neither is implemented
findings.description:
§20.1 says `VanHermesSessionManager` SHALL feed durable downstream pages and events into the existing `EventStream.applyPage(...)`. It does not: `onMessage` handles `session.ack` and `session.epoch_changed` and drops everything else on the floor. The supervisor's failover target is therefore a path with no transport behind it.

findings.title: An owner command issued with no network is lost, not queued
findings.description:
`VanCommandController.submit` calls `gateway.dispatchCommand`, which rethrows on a transport failure; `recordFailure` then appends "Command dispatch failed" to the conversation and clears the submitting flag. Nothing retries it and nothing stores it.

Neither store-and-forward path catches it. §20.14's durable outbox is unreachable (P0-SESS-009): `VanHermesSessionManager.submit` has no caller. The pre-§20 path — `EncryptedCommandQueue` drained by `QueueReplayer` — is live and working, and is fed by exactly two callers, `VanNotificationListenerService` and `ShareIntakeActivity`. Both are context ingestion. The owner's own commands enter neither.

So the failure the whole of §20.14 exists to prevent is the one the app has: the owner speaks or types an instruction in a tunnel, sees an error, and the instruction is gone. §43 row 63 recorded STORE_AND_FORWARD as REPOSITORY_PROVEN throughout, and the evidence it cited was real — `DurableOutboxTest`, `OutboxPersistenceTest`, `RestartSeamTest` all pass, and all of them call the outbox directly.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.1, 20.14
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: Two store-and-forward mechanisms, each correct, each with callers that are not the owner's command path. The older queue was built for ingestion and kept its ingestion callers; the newer outbox was built for commands and never acquired one.
findings.remediation: Recorded at C16a ahead of the repair, because the §43 row that states the opposite is the one somebody would act on. The fix is RB C16b: start the session and give `VanCommandController` a failure branch that hands the signed command body to §20.14's outbox rather than dropping it.

closure.summary:
§43 row 63 is corrected from REPOSITORY_PROVEN to BLOCKED_EXTERNAL with the reason stated: the decisions are proven and the path that would reach them is not wired. The repair is code in `VanApplication` and `VanCommandController`, neither of which any test here can execute.

**Repaired at C16b.** `recordFailure` now asks `OfflineSubmission` what may happen to the command and hands a storable one to §20.14's outbox. Two things had to change underneath it: `submit` refused outright when there was no session id — which is exactly what offline means, so storage was available only when it was not needed — and an envelope stored before a session exists now carries a named placeholder that `flushOutbox` rebinds to the live session, keeping its message id and idempotency key.
closure.counterexample: Every test of the outbox passes and the owner still loses the command, which is why the check that matters is the one asking whether anything calls `submit` rather than whether `submit` is correct.
closure.residual: The repair itself. `VanCommandController` and `VanApplication` are Android and are compiled by CI only; whether a command survives a real tunnel is Gate 14's to observe.

findings.title: A command held for the owner's confirmation cannot be released by the owner
findings.description:
§20.14 classifies a command whose meaning depends on the moment — "read that back to me", "cancel it" — as REQUIRE_RECONFIRM_ON_RECONNECT. `DurableOutbox.flush` returns `NeedsReconfirmation` for one and `flushOutbox` correctly holds it rather than sending it on the owner's behalf. `VanHermesSessionManager.reconfirm(messageId)` is the only thing that releases it, and nothing calls it.

So after C16b such a command is stored, held, and stuck: correct in every respect except that the question §20.15 says to ask is asked by nothing. `awaitingReconfirmation()` and `queuedForOwner()` — the two readers a screen would use — also have no callers.

findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The storing half and the asking half are in different layers, and only the storing half had a caller. The same shape as P0-SESS-009 one level down, found by asking the same question of the entry points rather than of the files.

findings.title: The command stored for later was not one the Gateway could accept
findings.description:
C16b's storage path built the envelope payload by hand: `{text, action_class, idempotency_key}`, plus a project and turn id. The Gateway's `command.submit` delegate turns that payload straight into a `CommandRequest`, which also requires `command_id`, `issued_at_unix` and `signature` — so every stored command would have been refused as `command_payload_invalid` on the flush.

Worse than losing it. The owner is told their work is saved, and it is rejected on their behalf hours later on a reconnect nobody is watching; nothing looks wrong until it is too late to redo. Found by asking the question the previous checkpoint's own lesson names — not whether the code is correct, but whether the thing it produces can actually be used by the thing that receives it.

A second defect came out of the same check. `VanOwnerCommand.noStaleReplay` was passed as `requiresLiveOwnerContext`, and the two are not the same: `NO_STALE_REPLAY` is a contract with the orchestrator requiring an explicit expiry inside sixty seconds, so storing such a command in a four-hour outbox guarantees a denial.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.2, 20.14
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: The two sides of the store-and-forward seam are in different languages, so nothing could compare what one writes against what the other requires. Assembling the payload by hand looked reasonable because the fields it did carry are the ones a person thinks of as 'the command'.
findings.remediation: `buildCommandBody` is extracted from `dispatchCommand`, so the offline path stores the same signed body the Gateway would have received. Signed at submission rather than at flush, so `issued_at_unix` is the moment the owner issued it and the Gateway's own stale-intent refusal still means something. `noStaleReplay` is now its own parameter and produces a Drop with an owner-readable reason.

closure.summary: `tests/contracts/test_stored_command_is_deliverable.py` reads the Kotlin builder's own `body.put` calls and holds them against `CommandRequest`'s required fields — two languages, one question: is the thing written down a thing that can be delivered? It also pins that the offline path uses that builder rather than assembling its own, which is how this happened.
closure.counterexample: Checking only that the required fields are present would pass while the offline path went back to hand-assembly, describing a function nothing on that path calls. Both were reproduced against the fixed tree — a hand-assembled payload and a body with the signature removed each fail one test.
closure.residual: That the delegate accepts a real stored body is asserted from the field list, not from a round trip: nothing here can run the Kotlin builder and hand its output to the Python model in one process.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container and the two halves are different languages.

findings.title: Making the queue durable put a synchronous encrypted write on the main thread
findings.description:
C15 changed `EncryptedCommandQueue.persist` and `remove` from `apply()` to `commit()` so the outbox's "saved" is true when it is said. Correct for the outbox, and it made every mutating call an AES-GCM encryption plus a synchronous file write on the calling thread — including for callers that had always been fine.

Three of them were Android main-thread entry points. `ShareIntakeActivity.onCreate` writes when the owner shares something. `VanNotificationListenerService.onNotificationPosted` writes per notification, so a burst becomes a run of encrypted disk writes on the thread that draws. And `DeviceSignals`' `CLEAR_QUEUE` restore action called `clear()`, which looped `remove` — one synchronous write per queued command, from a button, so the deeper the queue the longer the owner waits.

Raised by external review, which asked where the synchronous write actually runs rather than accepting that durability had improved. The command path itself was never on the main thread: `appScope` is `Dispatchers.Default`. That is not a UI bug but it is the wrong pool for a call that waits on a disk, because `Default` is sized to the CPU count.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.14, 28
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: A shared primitive was strengthened for one caller's requirement without auditing the others. The outbox needs to block until the bytes are down; a captured notification does not, and its call site is a main-thread callback.
findings.remediation: All three dispatch to `Dispatchers.IO`, and `clear()` is one editor rather than a loop of commits — which also removes the window where a kill leaves a queue that is neither what it was nor empty. The two `appScope` launches that restore or write are moved from the default pool to IO.

closure.summary: `tests/contracts/test_encrypted_queue_writes_are_off_the_main_thread.py` holds every file that writes to the queue to dispatching it, and pins the two entry points that actually broke by shape — the write must come after the IO launch, not merely in a file that mentions one. The queue's own docstring now states the constraint at the place a caller reads.
closure.counterexample: A first version of the guard matched any `*queue.` receiver and reported `VoiceAudioArbiter`'s ring of PCM frames, which touches no disk. A check that cries wolf is one somebody switches off, so it is narrowed to the `commandQueue` handle — and it still fails if the share write goes back inline, or if the queue reverts to `apply()` and there is nothing left to protect against.
closure.residual: Whether the IO dispatch is enough on a real device under a notification burst is a measurement, not a source property. Nothing here runs an Android main looper; what is checked is that no call site writes on its caller's thread.

findings.title: The session socket's two frame shapes were both read wrongly
findings.description:
The Gateway sends exactly two shapes down `/v1/session/ws`. A downstream event is `{"direction": "DOWNSTREAM", "event": {seq, event_type, payload, created_at_unix}}`. Its answer to something the device sent is `{accepted, message_id, kind, refusal, admission, result}`, where `kind` is the *envelope's* kind.

`onMessage` matched neither. It read `seq` from the top of the frame, where there is none, and switched on `kind` looking for `"session.ack"` and `"session.epoch_changed"`, which the Gateway never sends — so the comparison was against `"command.submit"` and its siblings.

Three silent consequences. The event cursor never advanced from the socket, so a resume asked to replay from zero. Nothing was ever removed from `inFlight`, so every command stayed pending until a resume reconciled it. And §20.1's "SHALL feed durable downstream pages/events into the existing `EventStream.applyPage`" was not merely unmet: every event that arrived was parsed into nothing and dropped.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§20.1, 20.4
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: Two halves of a wire format written in different languages at different times, each internally consistent, with nothing that runs both. The third time this shape has appeared in this programme.
findings.remediation: `SessionDownstream` parses the frame, is pure, and is executed against the frames the Gateway actually constructs. `tests/contracts/test_session_socket_frames.py` pins both shapes against the Gateway's own construction sites and fails if the acknowledgement is matched on `kind` again.

closure.summary: The reading is pure and pinned from both sides; what is left in `onMessage` is what to do about each shape. A refusal now leaves `inFlight` too — it is an answer, and leaving it there would have the next resume send the Gateway something it has already declined.
closure.counterexample: A parser tested only against frames written by the same hand proves the two agree with each other rather than with the Gateway. The contract test reads `session/api.py` and `events/bus.py` for the literal field names, and fails if the Gateway changes shape while the device does not.
closure.residual: No socket is opened here. That these frames arrive in this form on a real connection is Gate 14's, and `VanHermesSessionManager` is compiled by CI only.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container.
closure.posture: fail-closed

findings.title: The owner's event history existed only while one screen was open
findings.description:
`EventStreamState` was held in the Work screen's `remember`, fed by an HTTP poll inside a `LaunchedEffect`. So the history existed only while that screen was composed: a mission finishing while the owner was anywhere else produced nothing they could see, and the poll's own `nextDelayMillis` could end the loop entirely under resource pressure.

It also made §20.1's SHALL unimplementable. An application-scoped socket cannot write into a composable's local state, so there was nowhere for a durable downstream page to go even once the frames were read correctly.
findings.requirement: docs/VAN_REMOTE_BROWSER_PRODUCTION_BLUEPRINT_REV_1_5.md §§5.6, 20.1
findings.authority: VAN Remote Browser Production Blueprint Rev 1.5
findings.root_cause: State scoped to the thing that first needed it rather than to the thing that owns it. The screen was the only reader when it was written, and it stayed the owner when a second carrier arrived.
findings.remediation: `VanEventStreamStore` is application-scoped and holds the history; the Work screen collects it and feeds its polled pages back into it. Deliberately not a second reducer — `EventStream` still decides what a page does — so a socket page and a polled page merge seq-keyed and the owner does not read one event twice.

closure.summary: One history for the app, executed in the harness because the cursor is an interface. The cursor is saved from the merged state rather than from the page, since `applyPage` refuses to rewind and saving the page's own number would ask the Gateway to resend a morning the owner has already seen.
closure.counterexample: Holding the history app-scoped and still saving the page's cursor passes any test that only checks the events merge. `the cursor is saved from the merged state rather than from the page` applies a page whose cursor is lower and asserts the saved one does not move.
closure.residual: The Compose side — that the screen collects and renders it — is compiled by CI and executed nowhere here.
closure.residual_reason: The AGP is unreachable in the audit container.
closure.posture: fail-closed
